title: Police commissioner may cancel tour after backlash
description: Colin Sutton is due to perform his true crime show on-stage 127 times between January and November.
body: Colin Sutton said he was "absolutely" reconsidering his UK-wide tour after the backlash Norfolk's police commissioner is considering scrapping his 127-date theatre show after a backlash from local people, he has told the BBC. Since announcing his UK-wide true crime tour, Colin Sutton said constituents had emailed him with concerns about his ability to perform his day job. He was elected to the £79,000-a-year post on a Reform UK ticket in July and announced the gig two months later. Steffan Aquarone, the Liberal Democrat MP for North Norfolk, accused Sutton of acting more like pop star Taylor Swift than a politician. Police and crime commissioners (PCCs) are elected officials who set the priorities of a police force, appoint a chief constable and hold them to account. Sutton, who led the investigation to catch serial killer Levi Bellfield, has priced tickets for his "Makings of a Murderer" show at about £40. Sutton was elected as Norfolk's police and crime commissioner in July Asked if he was now reconsidering the theatre run, Sutton said: "Absolutely. I'm in talks with the people who promote it to see how we can curtail it or, if necessary, just cut it completely. "I don't want anything to interfere with the job that I've got to do." One of the solutions he proposed was stripping the tour back to venues only local to Norfolk. Sutton is due to appear at a Norfolk police and crime panel on 2 February, before being on stage in Leeds that evening. "There are lots of people who do meetings like that by [Microsoft] Teams or across the internet now, which might be an option," the ex-detective said. "But it may well be that it's a moot point now, because I've listened and I think I should make sure the people of Norfolk still have the confidence that I would do the job properly." Sutton admitted the reaction from constituents on social media and via emails sent to his office had caught him off-guard. "That's made me think about it again," he conceded. However, the PCC said the theatre tour was not something he needed to mention to voters during the election campaign and he denied letting them down. Steffan Aquarone accused Sutton of taking voters for granted The role of PCCs in England and Wales is due to be scrapped by the government by the end of Parliament, with their powers to be transferred to newly directly elected mayors. Aquarone said Sutton had taken the voters of Norfolk for granted by not telling them about the tour. "Either the job is serious and requires somebody full time paying attention, or it's not and it's OK to go off and do nearly as many tour dates as Taylor Swift," he said. A spokesperson for Reform said the party was supportive of "celebrity detective" Sutton and pointed out half of his shows would take place at weekends. Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? title: Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption
description: Trains were cancelled or delayed on Tuesday after objects were found on tracks at multiple locations.
body: Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, have been hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks, the country's railway operator has said. ProRail warned that passengers in the country's centre and north should expect cancellations and delays on Tuesday, while several level crossings were also malfunctioning. Pipes were attached to the tracks in multiple locations, according to local media. In a statement, ProRail said the incident appeared to be "an intentional disruption... caused by human action". It added that no suspects or motives had been identified, but the national police unit was investigating. The BBC has contacted police for comment. The network's website showed that 15 disruptions had been recorded across the country on Tuesday, with routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, and Utrecht also affected. ProRail said in a statement: "Materials were found at multiple locations in the track that were deliberately placed there. This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved". Footage published by Dutch public broadcaster NOS on Tuesday showed police carrying what appeared to be metal pipes - about 1.5 metres (5ft) - away from railway tracks at Veenendaal in the central Netherlands. title: State pension likely to rise by £488 a year in April
description: The increase has reignited the debate about the state pension's long-term affordability and generational fairness.
body: The state pension is expected to top £13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness. The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by £488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday. The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest. Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age. The triple lock was designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people. Although the state pension age is rising to 67, the cost to the government has risen considerably too. Forecasts suggest state pension spending, already at £154bn this year, could go up by a further £600m a year by 2029-30. The policy is "crazy," Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation think tank, told the BBC. The triple lock is creating a "ratchet effect" where "pensioners' living standards grow even faster than just a typical worker," she added. "Pensioners have seen living standards grow three times more than typical workers over the last 20 years." Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) think tank, said: "Each increase in spending builds upon the last, and so the long-run cost is substantial but very uncertain." The state pension is expected to match wage growth in the next calculations. Average wage growth, including bonuses, stood at 3.9% between May and July, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), external. That is likely to be the key figure to determine April's rise in the state pension, although it could be revised, as it is likely to be higher than the rate of inflation. the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 – will likely be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year. That would be an increase of £488 the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 – will likely be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, an increase of £374.40 Pensioner groups have said older people face significant cost of living pressures, such as high energy bills, and the state pension itself remained relatively small compared with state provision across Europe. Almost 13 million people receive the state pension in the UK. If it does rise by 3.9%, it would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of £12,570 and therefore be liable for income tax. The Labour government - when Rachel Reeves was chancellor - promised that pensioners who rely solely on the state pension would not be required to complete a tax return, nor be chased to pay. However, when asked by the BBC on Tuesday, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds refused to confirm that pensioners reliant on the state pension will be exempted from paying income tax. Asked by BBC Breakfast whether he could reiterate that commitment, he said: "The vast majority of people in Britain have their own private pension provision alongside the state pension so this wouldn't be a substantial change for them, they'd already certainly be receiving an income in that case above the personal allowance. "Any changes to personal allowances, to tax rates, take place in the Budget, that's on October 28." He was repeatedly asked to confirm the previous pledge, but again pointed to the Budget. Analysis by consultants LCP suggested that only one in 16 pensioners would benefit if the government kept to its previous pledge, saving about £91 each a year. The majority of pensioners have additional pension income and so pay income tax already. "The government's plans to address this point are a mess," said Sir Steve Webb, a partner at LCP and a former Liberal Democrat pensions minister. The ONS also published figures on the UK labour force. While the unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.9%, the number of vacancies and employees on payrolls fell in recent months. Will the increase see you pay tax for the first time? title: Assembly to debate bill aimed at banning conversion practices
description: The bill contains provisions that could see a two-year jail sentence imposed on people who conduct conversion practices.
body: A bill aimed at banning sexuality and gender conversion practices will be debated by assembly members for the first time at Stormont later on Tuesday. It contains provisions, external that could see a two-year jail sentence imposed on people who conduct conversion practices. Alliance's deputy leader Eóin Tennyson proposed the private member's legislation, but it has been criticised by the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) which said the bill "presents a real threat to freedom". Unionist parties are expected to oppose the bill, but it is believed to have support from Sinn Féin and the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP). Advocates say the legislation is about protecting LGBT people from harmful attempts to change or suppress who they are. Critics contend it is a legislative overreach which limits freedom of choice for gay and trans people, and risks criminalising important conversations around sexual orientation and gender. 'They wanted me to repent': Inside the push to ban conversion practices What is conversion therapy and will it be banned? Jail time and unlimited fines planned under conversion practices ban Ahead of the debate, Tennyson said Northern Ireland had lagged behind on equality for too long. "No-one should face coercion, abuse or harm because of who they are or who they love. This is balanced legislation which protects LGBT+ people from harm whilst also upholding freedom of speech and freedom of religion," he added. But DUP leader Gavin Robinson has said the legislation is vague and that Northern Ireland already has laws to deal with abuse and coercive behaviour. "We can protect people from mistreatment without creating vague new offences that reach into homes, churches and private conversations," he added. Conversion practices - sometimes called "reparative therapy" or "gay cure therapy" - try to change someone's sexual orientation or gender identity, according to the British Psychological Society (BPS). In practice, it means trying to stop or suppress someone from being gay or from identifying as a different gender to their sex recorded at birth. It often includes talking therapies and prayer but more extreme forms can exist. The BPS and other professional bodies, including NHS England and the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said all types of conversion practices were "unethical and potentially harmful". The bill would make it a criminal offence to provide conversion therapy, or to engage in coercive conversion behaviour, with the goal of changing a person's sexual orientation or gender identity. It would also make it an offence to remove a person from Northern Ireland for the purposes of subjecting them to conversion practices. The definition for coercive behaviour is borrowed from the Domestic Abuse and Civil Proceedings Act (Northern Ireland) 2021. It includes violent or threatening behaviour, humiliating the victim, or controlling their to day activities. In a summary of legal advice, the Christian Institute - a nondenominational charity that states that it is opposed to abortion, homosexuality and "transgender ideology" - said Aidan O'Neill KC's critique of Tennyson's bill was "devastating". "O'Neill argues that the proposals are fundamentally illiberal, poorly drafted, and pose a severe threat to basic civil liberties," the charity said. "He ultimately concludes that the bill likely exceeds the legislative competence of the Northern Ireland Assembly." James Kennedy, the Christian Institute's Northern Ireland policy officer, said that "existing law offers strong safeguards against coercion in the home and verbal or physical abuse anywhere else, too". He called on assembly members (MLAs) to oppose the bill. Meanwhile, the Ban Conversion Practices Coalition has urged MLAs to take a "historic opportunity" to pass the bill and become "the first jurisdiction on these islands to pass a ban on these harmful, abusive practices". Scott Cuthbertson, CEO of The Rainbow Project, said "politicians have the opportunity to buck that unfortunate trend, and deliver real protections for LGBTQIA+ people in Northern Ireland". Patrick Corrigan, head of nations and regions at Amnesty UK, said the draft bill "sends a clear message that everyone has the right to be safe and live openly and fully". "LGBT+ people are not broken and do not need fixing - protection from harm is long overdue." The bill was brought to the assembly floor by Alliance Party MLA Eóin Tennyson, but Stormont politicians have debated the issue of gay conversion practices before. In 2021, MLAs passed an Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) motion calling for it to be banned in all forms, however it was not binding. However the UUP has now changed its position under new leader Jon Burrows and has said it would vote against the bill, saying it was "excessively broad, legally uncertain and potentially damaging". The Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) is also expected to vote against the legislation. The private member's bill has been brought forward by Alliance Party MLA Eóin Tennyson When Sinn Féin held the communities brief in the executive, several of its ministers advocated banning the practice - with Deirdre Hargey at the time saying her officials were drafting a bill, but a subsequent collapse of power-sharing meant this got no further. DUP assembly member Gordon Lyons became communities minister in 2024 when devolution was restored. He is expected to respond to Tennyson during the debate. Unionist parties cannot use a veto mechanism known as a petition of concern at this stage but they could seek to use it in future, if the bill passes its second stage on Tuesday. In England, the government has published its own plans to legislate to ban the practice there, which could carry jail time and fines for those found to have carried out "abusive acts" aiming to change someone's sexual orientation or transgender identity. title: We must heed warnings of AI tech developers, says UK minister
description: Louise Haigh is set to address growing concerns over AI safety in a speech at the TUC Congress.
body: Protesters warning about AI in London earlier this year The UK government must "heed the warnings" of "those who are at the forefront" of developing artificial intelligence (AI) technology, a senior minister will say later. First Secretary of State Louise Haigh will address the growing anxiety over AI safety when she speaks at the TUC congress on Tuesday. She is expected to say the government is "ready to work with international partners" to prioritise public safety and national security. Fears about the potential dangers of AI have ramped up in recent days after executives and current and former staff in the field warned the tech could endanger humanity. On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed the recent discussion of the risks, with his spokesperson saying: "It's a good thing that the companies developing the most advanced AI systems are now talking openly about the risks as well as the opportunities." Speaking at the TUC congress later on Tuesday, Haigh is also expected to acknowledge the benefits, saying: "AI has enormous potential to transform our public services, make our businesses stronger and deliver new scientific breakthroughs." In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said people should "never be complacent" about the impact AI might have but "we've got to be careful not to get hyperbolic about this either". "Of course there are risks but, let's be frank, there are some tremendous upsides, whether it's public services, healthcare, the contribution to the economy," he added. The UK First Secretary of State Louise Haigh is due to speak at the TUC Congress, a federation of trade unions It comes as MPs in the UK are seeking new laws on AI after a report found the technology was responsible for numerous abuses of human rights. "Nowhere in the world, including the UK, has a current legislative and regulatory approach to AI that is fit for purpose," Labour MP and committee chair Alex Sobel said. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? One Anthropic researcher, Evan Hubinger, made headlines after he said he believed there is a greater than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans" within the next decade. Hubinger's claim came after a researcher who quit Anthropic went viral for sounding the alarm on the "fate of humanity in the next two years" from AI. "If we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic employee, told the BBC. Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei has since called for the pace of development on AI models, such as Claude or ChatGPT, to slow down and be closely monitored. Amodei said risks associated with it were "serious" and that companies and governments must be given time to address them. Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk backed him. However, some in the AI industry have suggested the fears around it destroying humanity are overstated or may even be designed to generate hype. This video can not be played AI "more powerful by the day", Anthropic co-founder tells BBC An AI "kill switch" has also been floated by an Anthropic co-founder as a way to shut down AI software that becomes too dangerous. Jack Clark, one of seven founders of the AI company, told the BBC "most labs have different ways of being able to pull the plug", including Anthropic, but said MPs may need to enforce having one. Asked about the idea of a "kill switch", Reynolds told the BBC: "I don't think that's a particularly helpful way to think about how we manage the risks - I'm not really sure what that would mean in practice." He warned that overregulation could risk the UK losing access to models developed abroad, which he argued would make the country "less safe". The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency was brought to Parliament by Lords and MPs. But the Cabinet Office said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off". "Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News. Meanwhile, the US President Donald Trump has dismissed the idea of AI taking over the world, saying on social media that AI "destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX". In a more recent Truth post, Trump said the AI Hoax was "being perpetrated by the Radical Left Dumocrats" and likened it to what he describes as the "Global Warming Scam" by the left. The president, who frequently shares AI content on his platform Truth Social, has lauded the benefits of AI and has been public about his desire for the US to win "the AI race". title: What is the triple lock and how much is the state pension worth?
description: The triple lock guarantees that the state pension is not overtaken by inflation or wage increases.
body: The new state pension is expected to rise by £488 a year, as a result of the triple lock arrangement. The triple lock guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest. The age at which millions of people can claim their state pension has started to increase from 66 to 67. The state pension is a payment made every four weeks by the government, to people who have reached the qualifying age and have paid enough National Insurance (NI) contributions. the new flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 - is £241.30 a week, or £12,547.60 a year the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 - is £184.90 a week, or £9,614.80 a year Many people on the old basic state pension may also receive the additional state pension, external. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension. Some people may have gaps in their NI record if, for example, they have lived abroad or taken time off to care for children. It is possible to make voluntary payments to boost your contribution history. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years. Data suggested that the state pension will increase in April 2027, meaning: the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 – will likely be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 – will likely be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now The government will confirm the rise, possibly in October's Budget. Check your state pension age Check your state pension forecast and whether you can increase it Under the triple lock system, the state pension increases each April in line with whichever of three measures is the highest: inflation in the September of the previous year, using a measure called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) the average increase in total wages, including bonuses, across the UK for May to July of the previous year The rise in wages of 3.9% is likely to determine the April 2027 state pension increase. The triple lock was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010. It was designed to ensure the value of the state pension wasn't overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people. The Labour government has previously said it would keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament. But since that commitment, there has been intense debate over the cost of the triple lock and whether it is justified. In July 2025, the government's official forecaster said the cost of the triple lock guarantee was set to be three times higher by the end of the decade than was originally anticipated when it began. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said the annual cost is set to reach £15.5bn by 2030. It said the cost of the state pension has risen steadily over the past eight decades, and now equates to £138bn, or around half the total amount the government spent on benefits. Earlier in July, the influential Institute for Fiscal Studies think-tank suggested that the triple lock should be scrapped as part of a wider pensions overhaul. The expected increase in April 2027 would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of £12,570 and so liable to pay about £91 next year in income tax. The Labour government - when Rachel Reeves was chancellor - pledged that pensioners who rely solely on the state pension would not be required to complete a tax return, nor be chased to pay. However, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds was non-committal, saying that it was a decision for the new chancellor, John Healey, in the Budget. The majority of pensioners are already income taxpayers owing to the addition of other pension income, on top of the state pension. More than 12 million people currently receive the state pension. Men and women born between 6 October 1954 and 5 April1960 start receiving their pension at the age of 66. But for people born after this date, the state pension age is increasing in two phases: a gradual rise to 67 for those born on, or after, 5 April 1960 a gradual rise to 68 between 2044 and 2046 for those born on, or after, 5 April 1977 The rise from 66 to 67 began in April 2026. The first affected are those born between 6 April and 5 May 1960, who will have to wait an extra month. The increase is expected to save the Treasury about £10bn a year by 2030. But charities have warned that it will disproportionately affect areas of the UK where life expectancy is lower, and those on lower incomes. A government review is considering whether to delay the second phase, which would currently take the state pension age to 68 between 2044 and 2046. State pension age starts rising to 67 - here's how much you get and when Future pensioners to be worse off, government warns Depending on their overall income, those above retirement age may also be entitled to pension credit, external in addition to the basic state pension. Pension credit increased by 4.8% in April 2026. If your income is above the stated limits, you may still be eligible for pension credit if you have a disability or care for someone. Anyone who qualifies for pension credit may also be entitled to other financial support, including housing benefit, a reduction in council tax, help with heating costs and the warm home discount scheme. title: How did they get the Madring track so wrong? - F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Spanish Grand Prix.
body: Kimi Antonelli in the lead of the Spanish Grand Prix, with Red Bull's Max Verstappen and McLaren's Lando Norris behind Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli stretched his lead in the drivers' standings with victory at the first Spanish Grand Prix held at the Madring. Max Verstappen finished second in the Red Bull and McLaren's Lando Norris completed the top three. Norris, who was leading, lost out having passed the pit entry immediately before the virtual safety car was called. BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions. Antonelli wins as Norris loses out under virtual safety car The new Madring circuit looks like one of the worst on the calendar for entertaining racing. Given that half the track is custom built (ie not having to conform to street layouts), how did they get it so wrong and will substantial changes be made ahead of next year? - Matt It's a good question. Even before the race weekend began, drivers were predicting that overtaking would be next to impossible at the new Madring, and they were proved right. The track is effectively a start-from-scratch layout built partly as a new track and partly on existing roads around the Ifema exhibition centre near Madrid's Barajas international airport. It is, therefore, mystifying as to how they got it so wrong, as the problems could be foreseen by anyone with an understanding of F1. As Lando Norris put it witheringly after the race: "I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes: 'Mint.'" There are some key issues. The main one is the lack of a long straight leading into a big braking zone. Another is, as the drivers pointed out, a lot of the corners have entries where drivers have to combine braking and turning, which makes overtaking extremely difficult, as well as walls that come back towards the track on corner exit. And another is the ultra-long pit lane - the longest on the calendar. The longer a pit lane, the more the time loss for a pit stop, so the less chance of having more than a one-stop race. And if tyre degradation is high, that means more tyre management, driving further under the limit, and less chance of accidents and therefore safety cars. The good news is it is not hard to see how it could be fixed. As Norris said: "There's a lot of opportunity. They can make it into a track that's good for racing, and I'm excited to come back here next year if they can make these changes because I think it's a track that is good fun to drive and it can be a great race track. "To me, it's not a great race track. It's great in qualifying." Norris suggested removing turns 18 and 19 and "making a straight line from 17 to 20, have a much wider entry like Austin Turn One or Turn 10 in Austin... big hairpin". That, he said, would "create much better opportunities for everyone and you'll be able to enjoy the race". He also advocated what he called "some trickier changes", such as changing the unpopular, clumsy chicane at Turn Five, and the section from there to Turn Seven. While they're at it, it would also be worth looking at the location and layout of the pits and paddock. This was more fractured and over a much larger area than at any other track, which made working for F1 personnel difficult in a number of ways. The many large exhibition halls on what is, frankly, a pretty unprepossessing site - it's a bit like holding a grand prix at the NEC in Birmingham - clearly don't make this the easiest task. But finding a location for a pit lane that is not split in half by a building and making it somewhere the pits and paddock can be together and entirely outside would be another step in the right direction. Madrid F1 circuit set for changes after criticism 'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 hits football-obsessed Madrid Spanish GP Review: VSC or not to VSC The virtual safety car (VSC) definitely throws jeopardy into races, but it does not do virtually what the safety car does. Would it not be more balanced to have a minimum of at least one full lap? Yes, this would dampen the jeopardy effect but what happened to Lando Norris feels like a chance card in Monopoly. - Kyle Lando Norris' bad luck with the virtual safety car at the Spanish Grand Prix has certainly focused attention on the ways this can disrupt races. The VSC has always had issues - it freezes a race rather than resets it, which can be a bit boring compared to an actual safety car - but it has the benefit of minimising disruption when a track hazard can be cleared relatively quickly. It has long been an opportunity for someone to benefit over a rival, because making a pit stop under a VSC takes significantly less time than under racing conditions. But usually this has been in cases where one team has changed or deployed its strategy with the express intention of waiting for a safety car or VSC (such as Norris himself in his maiden victory in Miami in 2024), and benefiting over a rival who has run a more conventional strategy. That sort of thing is considered fair game. What happened to Norris - a driver lost a race win because his specific track positioning at the time of a VSC meant he alone was unable to pit under it - is, to the best anyone could remember on Sunday, unique. The media are not privy to conversations in drivers' briefings, and Norris in particular gets a bit sniffy when information from those meetings leaks out because they are meant to be a safe space where the drivers and FIA can share opinions without it becoming a controversy. But it emerged after the race that this issue, as Norris put it, "has been spoken about many, many times". Whether Norris' misfortune leads to a change, such as ensuring that a VSC is deployed for at least one whole lap, remains to be seen. title: Coutinho joins Neymar at Santos for rest of season
description: The former Liverpool and Barcelona midfielder joins Brazilian side Santos from his boyhood club Vasco da Gama.
body: Philippe Coutinho left his boyhood club Vasco da Gama in February Philippe Coutinho has joined his close friend and Brazil team-mate Neymar at Santos FC until the end of the season. The former Liverpool and Barcelona midfielder, 34, has been without a club since leaving Vasco da Gama in February. Coutinho returned to his childhood club in 2024 but left after 81 appearances, saying he was "tired mentally". Santos welcomed the player on social media by posting an old photo of Coutinho and Neymar as teenagers, alongside a new version of them re-enacting the pose in the gym. The club also posted a video of Coutinho walking into the dressing room where he receives a hug from Neymar and says "if it's a dream, I don't want to wake up". Neymar returned to Santos, his childhood team, in January last year and this will be the first time that the friends have played together at club level. Coutinho started his career at Vasco before joining Inter Milan and later moving to Liverpool in 2013, where he scored 54 goals in 201 games before joining Barcelona for £142m in 2018. He later had stints at Bayern Munich, Aston Villa and Al-Duhail before the return to Vasco. More dropped points at Anfield - is it too early for Liverpool to worry? title: At-home cervical screenings to roll out in city
description: Eligible women will be able to order a free self-testing kit online through the NHS app.
body: Women in Wolverhampton will be able to collect a sample from home and send it off to be tested for HPV Women in Wolverhampton who have not attended cervical screening appointments are to be offered home testing for human papillomavirus (HPV). The NHS is rolling out the self-testing kits to increase screening numbers, with data suggesting about a third of women are not up to date with appointments. HPV is a common virus and some high-risk types can cause changes to cells in the cervix, which can develop into cervical cancer. Eligible women will be able to order a free self-testing kit online through the NHS app. The kit contains a swab which is used to collect a sample at home before it is posted off for testing free of charge. If high-risk HPV is detected, the person will be invited to book a follow-up appointment at their GP surgery or a sexual health clinic. Cellular change linked to HPV can usually be treated before cancer develops, said Obaida Ahmed, City of Wolverhampton Council's cabinet member for health, wellbeing and community, who added: "Two women die every day from cervical cancer in England, yet it is one of the most preventable cancers." Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years or more frequently if HPV is detected. The HPV self-testing scheme is being introduced in phases across England, initially targeting women aged 30 to 65 who have not attended cervical screening after previous invitations. title: Rare marble sculpture mistaken for garden ornament
description: The 19th Century bust, which spent more than 70 years outside, could fetch up to £18,000 at auction.
body: The rare piece of art lay undetected in a family's garden (L) for more than 70 years until it was cleaned (R) A rare marble sculpture could fetch up to £18,000 at auction after it spent more than seven decades sitting outside, mistaken for a garden ornament. The lichen-covered bust from 1854 was discovered by Thomas Jenner-Fust, director of Chorley's Auctioneers, during a routine house valuation in the Cotswolds. What the family thought was a reconstituted stone bust turned out to be the work of pioneering 19th-Century artist and feminist figure, Harriet Goodhue Hosmer. Jenner-Fust said it is a reminder that some of the most valuable objects are not tucked away in stately homes but hiding in plain sight, waiting to be rediscovered. Three sisters rising through the ranks of bowls Boats stuck as silt builds up in city docks Jury discharged in Boris Johnson wedding plot trial The statue will go under the hammer at Chorley's Auctioneers in Gloucester later. Hosmer was an American neoclassical sculptor born in Massachusetts in 1830, and is widely regarded as the first professional female sculptor in the United States. She spent much of her career in Rome, where she developed an international reputation in a field that was overwhelmingly dominated by men. Hosmer was also openly gay during a time when same-sex relationships were widely condemned, and in some places, illegal. "She was somebody who was exceptional - a real trailblazer and a feminist icon," Jenner-Fust said. The bust is inscribed with the Latin phrase "me fecit Roma", translating to "Rome made me" The bust on sale depicts Daphne, Apollo's first love in Greek mythology, and is inscribed with the Latin phrase "me fecit Roma" - translating to "Rome made me". As Hosmer's debut sculpture, only a small handful were ever created. Historians from the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York recognise only three verified marble versions surviving today - all on display in museums across the US. It is unclear exactly how the sculpture came to be in the Cotswolds, but the family presume it was bought at auction by an ancestor in the mid 1900s. Black-and-white photographs from the 1950s show the sculpture proudly poised among the flowerbeds Jenner-Fust said the homeowners were "quite surprised" by the discovery, who had been "blinded by familiarity" after seven decades. "They had no idea it was marble, no idea who it was by, and no idea it was so valuable," he said. Jenner-Fust urged others to "be extra careful" when clearing out older homes, "to make sure you don't throw anything out that could be very important". "It's a bit like a treasure hunt. You never really know what you're going to find next, and that's the thrill of the chase," he added. "It also gives us a bit of comfort as auctioneers that there are still things out there, waiting to be discovered." title: Why is a village holding a referendum on leaving the UK?
description: Residents of Piddington, near Bicester, will vote in a symbolic referendum on Tuesday.
body: Shadow home secretary Chris Philp (centre) and shadow minister for women and equalities Joy Morrissey (centre left) with residents of Piddington Residents of a small village set to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers are due to vote in a symbolic referendum on whether it should remain part of the UK. Piddington, a village of about 400 people near Bicester in Oxfordshire, decided in July to hold the vote after the government announced plans to house asylum seekers at a nearby Ministry of Defence (MoD) site. Under the proposal, MoD Bicester could be converted into basic accommodation to house up to 1,256 male asylum seekers. The Home Office said it was "working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country" and that it had saved taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support costs since the election. The vote is taking place on Tuesday – but why is it being held, and will it make any difference? The Home Office announced the plans in June as part of wider proposals to move people out of hotels. Known as "Site A", MoD Bicester is located between the villages of Piddington and Upper and Lower Arncott. In 2005 it was the target of similar plans for an asylum seekers accommodation centre, external, which were abandoned by the then-Labour government. This year's announcement sparked widespread criticism, including from the district council and human rights groups, with many residents expressing shock. Chair of Piddington Parish Council Tim McNally said he was fearful over "security". Lib Dem MP for Bicester Calum Miller previously said the plans had been "veiled in secrecy" and that the process did not guarantee public participation "beyond a narrow list of statutory bodies". However, earlier this month the government published an Urgent Crown Development application. Miller called it a "clear win for local democracy and for every resident who refused to be shut out of a decision with profound consequences for our communities". A public consultation on the plans is now running until midnight on 17 September. This video can not be played The BBC's Jamie Morris explained in July what the vote is and what it could mean There is no legal mechanism allowing a village, town or city to declare independence from the UK. Therefore, a village holding a referendum can only be symbolic, which is what the one held in Piddington will be. McNally previously said the referendum would be an attempt to make voices in the village heard. Ahead of the vote, about 20 women gathered at the village green on Monday to meet shadow home secretary Chris Philp, shadow minister for women and equalities Joy Morrissey, and Reform UK MPs Sarah Pochin and Suella Braverman. Pochin and Braverman were among the MPs to respond to an open letter penned by a group of Piddington's female residents, addressed to all women MPs. In the letter, the group of 133 women said they faced a "crisis" and argued their "safety, security and freedoms will be under threat". "Life as we know it will be destroyed," they said. "We will not feel safe walking our streets. We are already living in fear." In a statement regarding the letter, the Home Office previously said the "concerns of communities" were central to its immigration reforms. "That is why we are closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites," a spokesperson said. A protest sign attached to a road sign pole in Piddington Gloria Brown, 69, who has lived in Piddington for 23 years, said she would stop litter-picking in the village if plans went ahead, something she takes "lots of pride" in doing. "All my friends in the village call me Madame Cholet," Ms Brown said. "I wouldn't be able to do that anymore. I do it on my own sometimes." She added: "How ever am I going to get my mental health back to scale? Because it's going to make me feel imprisoned in my own village. "I've felt very emotional about it just lately, and it's just not correct, and it's totally unfair." A Home Office spokesperson said: "The government is closing every asylum hotel, saving taxpayers over £1bn on asylum support since the election. "We are working to fairly house asylum seekers across the country, moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including former military sites which are designed to be self-contained to reduce impact on the local community. "As part of the process, we engage with local authorities and police forces to ensure the safety and security of those in the surrounding area." Passport to Piddington? title: Pokémon fans prepare for 'biggest day in a decade'
description: Collectors are eagerly awaiting the first release of the 30th anniversary Pokémon trading cards.
body: Pokémon collector Grace Orton hopes to secure some anniversary cards For most people, Wednesday will be just another day - the midweek hump at school or work. But not for Pokémon fans. The Japanese brand has become one of the most recognisable in the world, with its colourful creatures appearing in video games and on shop shelves across the world. But perhaps most synonymous with the Pokémon phenomenon is its trading card game, which has been played, bought and sold between collectors for the last three decades. Wednesday marks the release of Pokémon's 30th anniversary range - a day one collector described as the brand's biggest day "in the last decade, if not more". Gus Hall, owner of Evolution Games in Halifax, said he expected fans to queue before shops open to get their hands on the first release of the cards. A long-term Pokémon collector himself, Hall said he was "massively excited" about the anniversary range. "If you want my personal opinion, I would say this is the biggest release for a good while for Pokémon. Some of the products and the cards they've leaked... are crazy," he said. Gus Hall sitting in front of just some of his personal Pokémon collection Pokémon's popularity has exploded over the years, with some cards originally worth just a few pounds now selling for eye-watering amounts. Hall said a box that may have been worth £200 in the late 1990s would now sell for about £35,000. As a child, Hall would spend about £1.99 of his pocket money on a new Pokémon card. His parents would "go ballistic" at him for what they believed was a waste of money. He said: "They'd say to me: 'Why are you wasting your money on these types of things?'… Now I get the exact same from parents who come into my store and say to their children: 'Why are you wasting your money on these [cards]?'… But, you know, look who's laughing now!" But what has made these cards so popular - and so valuable? "Pokémon is different to other things in society these days - there's nothing electronic in trading cards," Hall said. "Parents quite like it because it's healthy; it creates friendships and trading and gaming, and incorporates all these wonderful things that aren't detrimental to a child or young person's mind." Hall said the satisfaction of collecting a set and "chasing certain cards" in that set was a huge part of the enjoyment, and described the moment of pulling the desired card as "euphoric". Phoebe Watson is "super excited" at the prospect of anniversary Pokémon cards Phoebe Watson, an employee at Evolution Games, has been collecting Pokémon cards for the last 20 years. She said she was "super excited" for the first release of the anniversary range and was hoping to secure some of the cards, which feature some of her favourite Pokémons. But Watson is realistic - she expects the first release to sell out quickly. "It is going to be big. We get collectors in every single day, multiple times a day, and I've had hundreds of people ask me: 'When is the set dropping? Do you know how much you're getting?'." Lee Glen, owner of trading card stores Rocket's Hideout in York and Selby, said Pokémon cards had "exploded" in the last five years, which he largely attributed to the hobby being "multi-generational". "I got back into collecting five years ago with my son. It was something nostalgic that I used to do, and then got back into it with my son… You have sons, daughters, mums, everyone - and they can do it together," Glen said. He said Pokémon was "constantly reinventing" products, and was "really good at bringing people back in". Glen's York store is usually closed on Wednesdays, but it will open specially for the first release, when Glen too expects customers to flock to York to get their hands on the stock. Lee Glenn at the Rocket's Hideout store in York Among those hoping to secure some anniversary cards is 21-year-old Grace Orton, who said she was willing to queue up to get her hands on them. "I'll definitely be trying at some point to get some. I know it'll be really difficult if I'm not [at a shop] immediately", Orton said. Despite only starting her Pokémon card collection three years ago, Orton said she was "looking to spend quite a bit of money, unfortunately" on the anniversary range. She said: "It's such a big, sought-after set. A lot of the artwork is really nice; I really want some of it for my personal collection." Another Pokémon fanatic, Ash Mehr, said he started collecting the cards between 20 and 30 years ago. After a brief hiatus, Mehr began his collection once again after his son took an interest in Pokémon. He said: "I feel like I'm sort of dragging my son to these events to try and get the cards, but really it's a little bit of a guilty pleasure of mine! But hopefully, we'll get a good haul and get some good pulls [from the anniversary range]". There is a huge sense of nostalgia surrounding the 30th anniversary of Pokémon cards, Mehr said, adding: "It takes me back to being a kid, really, something I don't get to enjoy now as much in my early 40s." But with high-value products comes risk - and Glen has warned of Pokémon fans being scammed around the release of the anniversary range. He encouraged people to buy the cards from national and independent retailers, and avoid "secondary markets", which may be used to re-sell the cards at "two or three times" the price. He said: "Just research and know what to spend. "If it looks too cheap, chances are it is… because of the desirability of a product, people will always try and copy [them]. Do your homework." title: ‘Great’ or ‘alarming’ - Should AI be reined in?

body: This video can not be played The rapid development of artificial intelligence and fears over the risks the technology poses to humanity have been thrust into the spotlight by a series of warnings from executives and staff at AI firms. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei over the weekend called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored. title: The Pitt is up for 25 Emmys - but the show's biggest fans are real-life doctors
description: Those in the medical profession say the HBO Max show about a US hospital emergency room is the most realistic medical drama yet.
body: The lead character Dr Michael Robinavitch, played by Noah Wyle, is a hardened and highly experienced emergency medicine consultant It's a familiar sight: a crowded waiting room, trolleys in corridors, stressed doctors and nurses. But this isn't a typical A&E unit in the NHS, it's a Hollywood set with actors recreating the drama of an emergency department for TV series The Pitt. And among its biggest fans are real-life doctors. "We finally feel validated for everything we go through every day," says Dr Tony Cirillo, President of the American College of Emergency Physicians. On Monday, The Pitt could become this year's most decorated series at the Emmys, America's most coveted TV honours, with 25 nominations. Doctors and others in the medical profession say, for them, it's the most realistic medical drama yet - which is why they love it. FOLLOW LIVE - TV's biggest stars to walk red carpet ahead of 78th Emmy Awards The show is a TV drama focusing on the staff of a fictional trauma centre in Pittsburgh Wyle (right) is a producer on the show as well as part of the writing team The series covers the life and work of the staff of Pittsburgh's Trauma Medical Centre, with each episode representing an hour of a day and there are 15 in each series. A constant thread through each episode is the noise, the pace of activity and the constant demands on the staff who never seem to get a break. Complex procedures and life-saving interventions are shown in graphic, and often, gory detail. The lead character Dr Michael Robinavitch, known as Dr Robby, is a hardened and highly experienced emergency medicine consultant (in US hospitals a senior emergency attending physician). Played by Noah Wyle, previously in the cast of mid-90s medical drama ER, he is an executive producer as well as part of the writing team, which includes qualified doctors. Wyle was invited to take part in a platform discussion at a prestigious conference with more than 6,000 emergency medicine experts in the audience. "People came up to him and, as opposed to actors and athletes where they say they are amazing or love their work, people just said thank you to him," Cirillo says. "The Pitt is more than just a good TV show – the term I use is validation." Social and ethical issues are often reflected. A stressed daughter who is caring for her sick mother leaves her in the emergency department and then can't be found. There are anguished conversations with parents who are desperate for their child to be kept alive, despite doctors saying there is no hope. Health inequalities are highlighted, with some patients struggling with the payments required in the US health system. Long waits and patient frustration are obvious shades of the NHS. And, based on our conversations, the series has become more popular in the UK with medics. Doctors say they like to see themselves represented on screen in shows like The Pitt Doctors seem ready to watch even in weeks when they have had punishing days or nights in A&E. One of them is Dr Fiona Hunter, vice president of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine in Scotland. "I wouldn't do it straight after a shift," she said. "We all need to decompress and debrief what we have experienced. "But in between shifts, when I have got downtime, it's watchable, relatable. It makes me feel other people might get it." North Wales consultant Dr Rob Perry is another fan. "I think it is reassuring when you see people portraying doctors and nurses in a similar job to your own and, though its not in the UK, they are doing their level best to give the best care they can," he said. Doctors we spoke to do point out that each episode of The Pitt brings together several urgent trauma cases which typically might be spread across 24 hours or more. But Prof Damian Roland, a practising emergency medicine consultant, notes that the drama does illustrate wider health challenges. He thinks it puts the problems of the NHS in perspective. "Virtually every emergency department in the world at the moment has not enough space to see patients," he says. "It's a very common theme in The Pitt about the central character arguing with hospital management saying 'I need more flow, you can't just leave these patients here' – that's a very common problem." "In my work in the NHS, its very much we all work for one another and I like that we represent that on the show," says Sarah Tosh, a senior NHS nurse who is the series medical adviser. "In The Pitt they've got a bit about the characters' day-to-day life, but it's more about their medicine, which patient they are doing and what they are going on to next." Gerran Howell (right) is a British actor nominated for an outstanding supporting actor award at the Emmys One of the stars of The Pitt, Gerran Howell, was born and brought up in South Wales. With other actors he was put through a medical boot camp for speed learning of medical techniques and jargon. This included training on dummies and CPR practice. In a BBC Wales interview he was asked if he would like to train to be a doctor. "I have such a newfound respect for the medical profession. It's maybe made me realise that I don't know how I would do this. I will stick to acting." Howell is nominated for an outstanding supporting actor award at the Emmys. The winners will be announced on 14 September at a ceremony in Los Angeles. The Pitt is available to stream on HBO Max in the UK and US. title: Police officer who put suspect in headlock and punched him 9 times faces misconduct hearing
description: PC Richard Williams faces eight allegations relating to an arrest in a police misconduct hearing.
body: This video can not be played PC Richard Williams was filmed punching a suspect with one hand as he gripped the man's neck with his other arm A police officer who punched a suspect nine times in the head used unreasonable force on multiple occasions, a police misconduct hearing has been told. PC Richard Williams faces eight allegations relating to the arrest of Steven Clark, including using a headlock or "choker", unreasonable use of incapacitant spray, and throwing or dropping Clark into the back of a police van. A misconduct hearing at North Wales Police headquarters in Colwyn Bay heard Williams denies wrongdoing. He was cleared of assault and intentional strangulation following a seven-day trial in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, in 2025. In May 2023, police were called to Porthmadog in Gwynedd, following a report of a domestic argument. A woman told officers, Clark, then 34, was "off his head on wacky backy" and possibly other drugs. The misconduct hearing was played several clips of police body-worn camera footage, as well as mobile phone video recorded by onlookers. When police tried to arrest Clark, the misconduct hearing was told things "take a turn", and the suspect ended up on the ground. It is alleged Williams used handcuffs to "cause pain to Clark's wrist", who "winced and reacted". PC Richard Williams was cleared of assault and intentional strangulation following a trial in 2025 It is also alleged he put Clark in a headlock, which it is claimed was "unreasonable". Clark claimed he "could not breathe", and later suggested during police interview he was losing consciousness. It is also claimed Clark "is punched by Williams nine times in the face or head", and that "punching Clark nine times in the face was not a reasonable use of force". The hearing was told "it is nine pretty quick punches" with no pause for reflection. Four allegations relate to the use, or apparent use, of incapacitant spray. Another is that Clark was "thrown or dropped into the van" while trying to resist. It is claimed the eight allegations "amount to an unreasonable use of force". The hearing was adjourned until Tuesday. title: Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today'
description: Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026.
body: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has said two big donations given to his party are "100% compliant with the law today", but was not able say whether they would be permissible if a rule change, currently being debated in Parliament, were passed. Ministers are seeking to put a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British expats, backdated to 25 March 2026. Farage argued the government should not retrospectively declare donations illegal and threatened to retaliate by limiting trade union donations, if elected PM. Trade union leader Paul Nowak said there was no similarity between "care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires." Over the weekend, Reform announced that it had received two donations of £36m each from wealthy businessmen Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British but have until recently lived abroad. Speaking to the BBC, Farage said there was "no question" their donations - the largest in British political history - were within the law "as it stands". Asked if the two men were resident in the UK by 25 March, Farage said: "I'm not going into their particular details." He went on to criticise the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal, saying: "This cannot be." "If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way. "We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'." Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public. Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees. Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change? Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo? On Monday the House of Lords debated the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at £100,000. The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than £100,000. The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap. It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK. Education Minister Georgia Gould told the BBC's Today programme the government was "really worried about the big money that is coming into politics... and sometimes money from overseas that is shaping politics rather than the ordinary voters". She said the new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March. The two £36m donations to Reform have reignited questions about political funding. Speaking to Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live, Sir Philip said examining domestic donations had not been within the remit of his review but that there was a case for capping all donations, whether they came from British citizens living in the UK or overseas. "I don't see any reason why we should have these mega sums of money coming into British politics," he said. He added that the government's decision to retrospectively ban certain donations was "going to be controversial" but said: "If you say, you're going to change the rules to cap donations at some point in the future, then clearly the risk is that you get a lot of those donations coming through the door before you're able to do that." Farage said the donations would allow his party to "catch up with the other big parties" and enable them to "professionalise". He argued that trade unions gave money to Labour so that it would enact their policies and that donors gave money to the Conservative Party in order to get "knighthoods and peerages". By contrast he said neither Harborne or Delo would get peerages or government contracts, if Reform won the next general election. Asked if the two men had influence over Reform's policy on cryptocurrency, Farage said he had shown them his party's paper on the subject and they both "thought it made sense". He added that the two men "will not benefit" from Reform's policies, which he said aimed to properly regulate cryptocurrency. Farage was speaking on the same day as the Trade Unions Congress, the federation of trade unions, held its annual conference. TUC general secretary Nowak said Reform were a "party for sale" and their donations were "a crisis for democracy". Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite union, said the government should go further and put a cap between £500,000 and £1m on individual donations made by UK residents Speaking on Sunday, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free". Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. Similarly, the Green Party urged the Labour Party to "find its spine and support a tight cap". title: Farm tax a mistake, Lord Blunkett says in call for Burnham 'rural reset'
description: The former mentor to Prime Minister Andy Burnham has joined ex-PM Lord Cameron in criticising rural policies.
body: Lord Blunkett spoke at a countryside campaigning event in central London An inheritance tax for farms was "a mistake" and Andy Burnham should use his premiership to listen to the countryside more, his longtime mentor Lord Blunkett has said. The former Labour minister hit out at "Treasury economic orthodoxy" over the 20% tax on inherited agricultural assets worth more than £2.5m that came into force in April, ending a waiver farms had since the 1980s. He spoke at the launch of a new campaign by the Countryside Alliance for a "rural reset" to reverse what the group says is a current set of policies "treating rural people as the enemy". The government said it was "determined to rebuild trust" with farmers and that most estates were unaffected by the tax hike. The tax, announced in last year's Budget under Sir Keir Starmer at half the 40% rate of standard inheritance tax, was initially proposed for inherited agricultural assets worth more than £1m. A backlash led to it being watered down in December - to a raised threshold of £2.5m. Some rural campaigners say this still impacts ordinary working family farms and are calling for it to be scrapped. Burnham has not hinted any change or U-turn on the issue, but Lord Blunkett said he was confident the now-prime minister, who he hired as his parliamentary private secretary back in 2004, would get the message "very clearly and act accordingly". "I think the family tax, the family farm imposition, was a mistake," the former Labour minister said, adding it "touched a nerve". "It's very strange because we've never won so many rural seats since 1945 - around 135 Labour MPs are either rural or semi-rural - and their voices need to be heard much more clearly," he told the BBC. "If you're an urban dweller all your life and you've got Treasury economic orthodoxy in your soul, you won't understand that family farms are only family because they are passed down from one generation to another." He said the countryside fits neatly into Burnham's self-professed focus on local postcodes and urban and rural areas "need each other". Lord Blunkett also branded the government's planned ban on trail hunting a mistake, saying the practice was "doing no harm". Farmers have held tractor protests in London and elsewhere over the last year Trail hunting was introduced after the Hunting Act 2004 as an alternative to hounds chasing foxes and involves using an animal-scented rag. Labour first announced a planned ban in its 2024 election manifesto. The government said there was strong support for a ban on trail hunting and that it posed risks to wildlife and pets. Former Prime Minister Lord Cameron criticised both policies at a Countryside Alliance event in Westminster on Monday, calling the inheritance tax on farm assets "stupid" and the trail hunting ban "completely wrong". Also taking aim at the government's call for evidence on game shooting in England, Lord Cameron warned further crackdowns risk eroding all facets of rural life including pubs and local services. "Some of these things we should be angry about," he added, a week after being spotted filming an episode of Prime series Clarkson's Farm which has popularised various issues facing farmers. The Countryside Alliance says its campaign is a non-political effort to encourage Burnham to work with rural people to address their concerns about policies on issues like farming, horseracing and greyhound racing. Farmers have held tractor protests in parts of the country over the last year. The government said: "This is the start of a new conversation with farmers and rural communities as we work together to build a stronger future for British farming and unlock growth in rural areas." title: No police collusion in sectarian murder but multiple RUC failings included tip-off to suspect
description: Robert Hamill died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh.
body: Robert Hamill was killed by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh An inquiry into the sectarian murder of Robert Hamill has found police officers who were in a vehicle near the attack did not condone or collude with the attackers. However, the inquiry said there were multiple police failings in the investigation, including a tip-off to a suspect to destroy the clothing he wore that night. The report, published on Monday, external, highlighted multiple wrongful omissions in the subsequent murder investigation including a failure to properly search the home of a key suspect. Robert Hamill was 25 when he died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh, in 1997. The inquiry concluded in 2009 and its report was completed in 2011 but the findings could not be published until three prosecutions in connection with the case concluded. The inquiry concluded: "We find that Robert Hamill had been assaulted before the Land Rover officers got out of their vehicle. "However, they were not aware of the assault and after they had got out of their vehicle, they attempted to restore order. "They did not in any way condone or collude with attackers." Although the inquiry found that the four officers in the police Land Rover could not have prevented the murder, the police investigation was flawed – both at the scene and in the days that followed. "The inquiry found that serving RUC [Royal Ulster Constabulary] officers were guilty of wrongful omissions and that those omissions arose both at the scene and during the initial investigation," it said. The inquiry concluded that some of the mistakes in the investigation were negligent, while others were deliberate. The 290-page report followed an inquiry which cost approximately £33m. The actions of the officers in the Land Rover have been the subject of many claims and counter-claims in the past three decades. Given how close they were to the scene, questions have been asked about why they did not intervene sooner. The inquiry found that they were "distracted talking to two members of the public". On whether they could have done more, the three-person inquiry panel did not have a unanimous view. Two members concluded that the officers in the police vehicle were not guilty "of any wrongful act or omission in relation to the death of Robert Hamill". However, on this issue the chairperson Sir Edwin Jowitt "expressed a dissenting view". The inquiry report identified a number of key mistakes in the police investigation. Failure to keep full records of the investigation Failure to properly search home of a key suspect Failure to carry out full debriefing of officers at scene of attack Nobody has been convicted of the murder. This video can not be played My brother's killers "were never fully held accountable" Speaking after the report's publication, Hamill's sister Diane said the family had "some reservations about aspects of this report". "We as a family feel totally vindicated by the clear and unequivocal findings of the panel," she said. "It documents multiple and shocking wrongdoing, some of it delivered by state agencies. "These failings have led to those who murdered our brother evading justice." She added that the family was "disappointed" that the panel could not agree "on the consequences of the police officers in the Land Rover failing to intervene while Robert was being attacked". "I just want to reiterate that the people who killed our brother were never fully held accountable due to the obstructive conduct of the state justice agencies," she said. In terms of deliberate mistakes, the actions of now-retired RUC officer Robert Atkinson were highlighted. Atkinson was jailed in 2024 for conspiring to pervert the course of justice. The inquiry found he was "guilty of a wrongful act" for making a telephone call to the home of a suspect. The report said this resulted in that individual "destroying or putting beyond the reach of police the clothes he had been wearing that night". "This obstructed the investigation and was deliberate," stated the report. It said Atkinson subsequently conspired to cover up the "tip-off telephone call". This was "an obstruction of the murder investigation and was deliberate" according to the three-person inquiry panel. This video can not be played Robert Hamill killed "because he was Catholic", says secretary of state Northern Ireland Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said it is "especially disturbing" that Atkinson "carried an RUC badge for years when he had so evidently and heinously failed in his duty and acted as an criminal". Sir Chris added that it is "difficult not to agree" that there was a "catalogue of failures". He said the report's publication is a reminder of the "long shadow of the troubles" and how other families "yearn for answers about how their loved ones were killed". "He would have been coming up to his 55th birthday in December - younger than me," Sir Chris said in the House of Commons on Monday. "He might have become a grandfather or a great uncle by now but he was murdered and murdered just for being a Catholic." The former Police Ombudsman Baroness Nuala O'Loan told BBC's Evening Extra programme there had been a "pattern of failures to investigate". Listen: Robert Hamill's family were "failed": Baroness O'Loan on sectarian murder inquiry Hamill and a friend were attacked and beaten by loyalists as they walked along Portadown's Market Street after a night out in April 1997. He suffered serious head injuries and died 11 days later. Hamill's murder was the subject of a public inquiry because it was alleged officers were parked in a police Land Rover nearby but did not intervene. That inquiry ran for 77 days between 13 January and 17 December 2009. It heard evidence in person from 174 witnesses and witness statements from a further 37 witnesses. No one was convicted of the murder and in the decades after, Hamill's family demanded answers. T

title: Tice apologises for not declaring Israel trip during debate
description: The visit, funded by Reform Friends of Israel, was declared in his register of interests but not during the debate.
body: Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice has apologised in the House of Commons for failing to declare a trip to Israel during a debate on pro-Israel influence on UK politics. The MP for Boston and Skegness said he did not mention the visit, which was funded by Reform Friends of Israel, during a speech he made in a Westminster Hall debate on 22 June. Although the trip was recorded in his register of interests, Tice acknowledged he should have declared it during his speech. The parliamentary commissioner for standards has been investigating whether Tice broke rules requiring MPs to be "open and frank in declaring any relevant interest" during debates in Parliament. The visit to Israel took place between 26 and 30 September 2025 and was declared in Tice's register of interests on 19 October 2025. According to the register, external, the trip cost an estimated £6,250, covering flights, accommodation, transport and hospitality for two people. It states that Tice met Israel's foreign minister and president during the visit. Tice told MPs: "Whilst the trip is properly recorded in my register of interests I should have declared it during the speech. That is a breach of the rules and I apologise to this good House." Rule 6 of the parliamentary code of conduct says: "Members must always be open and frank in declaring any relevant interest in any proceeding of the House or its committees, and in any communications with ministers, members, public officials or public office holders." The parliamentary commissioner for standards opened an investigation into whether Tice had failed to declare an interest on 28 July, with the inquiry extended on 20 August. The commissioner has not yet published his decision and the inquiry is ongoing. Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. title: Key convicted Palestine Action member on the run
description: Sean Middlebrough is convicted in his absence over a break-in at a British defence firm in Bristol.
body: Sean Middlebrough: Caught on a doorbell camera shortly before the break-in A key member of Palestine Action, who is currently on the run, has been convicted in his absence over a break-in that caused damage put at £1.2m to an arms firm. Sean Middlebrough, 33, originally from Liverpool, absconded in October last year after being granted bail for his brother's wedding. The self-proclaimed revolutionary communist has since sent messages to supporters describing himself as a "prisoner of war". His trial began this summer in his absence and last month the jury convicted him of criminal damage by a majority of nine-to-one. Prosecutors told the court Middlebrough had helped to plan and organise the August 2024 break-in at Elbit Systems in Bristol, a British defence firm with an Israeli parent company. The break-in happened 10 months before the government banned the group under counter-terrorism powers. Four people were convicted over the break-in that left a police officer injured During the break-in, other members of Palestine Action rammed the van into Elbit's factory and, once inside, set about destroying as much equipment as they could find, including military drones that they believed would be used in Gaza. The firm says that claim is untrue and that nothing produced at the Bristol facility goes to Israel. Prosecutors told the court that Middlebrough's role included taking part in a planning meeting in Liverpool arranged with the help of encrypted communications. He provided £890 to fund the the plot, including £600 that prosecutors said was used by another organiser to buy equipment used for the break-in. That kit included sledgehammers, one of which was used by Samuel Corner to severely injure a police officer by fracturing her spine as she crouched on the ground. The raid was live streamed and posted online Corner is now serving a seven year and eight month jail sentence for criminal damage and inflicting grievous bodily harm on Sgt Kate Evans. The jury at Middlebrough's Old Bailey trial was not told why he was not in the dock along with the seven other alleged organisers. While he was convicted in August of criminal damage, the trial of all eight defendants on other charges came to a halt when the jury failed to reach any other verdicts. A retrial has been provisionally listed for June 2028. Seven of the eight face an allegation of criminal damage. All but one of the defendants, including Middlebrough, face a further allegation of violent disorder. They deny all outstanding charges. When Middlebrough was first charged over the incident, he was remanded into custody and he then began sending a podcast to supporters from jail, describing himself as a political prisoner. The recordings were published on Spotify and later stopped by the prison authorities. Prison life: Sean Middlebrough sent pictures and messages to supporters from jail - until he was found out On 20 October last year a senior judge granted him temporary bail to go to his brother's wedding. Middlebrough was permitted to first go to Liverpool and then briefly stay in West Yorkshire and was ordered to surrender to HMP Wandsworth in south London on 24 October. He never showed up and a judge later issued a warrant for his arrest. Police believe Middlebrough, known to friends as Shibby, was helped to leave the UK by a well-organised network of supporters. Since his disappearance, he has sent messages to supporters, which have been published, saying he refuses to be "held as an Israeli prisoner of war in a British prison". Reporting of Middlebrough's conviction was delayed because of a separate prosecution in which he and another man were accused of planning to carry out a Palestine Action-themed protest at Boris Johnson's 2022 wedding party. Middlebrough's trial on that allegation has now been put back indefinitely for legal reasons. Judge Patrick Field KC, the judge in Middlebrough's trial over the Elbit break-in, lifted the reporting restriction on his conviction at a hearing on Monday morning. He is the fifth Palestine Action supporter to have been convicted over the attack. Two more trials of alleged participants are expected. BBC News has contacted the police for comment. title: Ex-Met detective to stand for Reform in by-election
description: Pete Newman will contest the Holborn and St Pancras by-election for Reform UK on 8 October.
body: Pete Newman says he is a former detective Reform UK has chosen a former Metropolitan Police detective to contest the Holborn and St Pancras by-election on 8 October. The party says Pete Newman served at the Met between 2004 and 2009, working on crime reduction and counter-terrorism across London. It says he helped lead the force's response in Westminster after the 7 July 2005 bombings. Newman has since worked as a security and investigative consultant. He joins the Conservatives' Ewan Cameron, Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali, Lib Dems' Patrick Stillman and Green Party leader Zack Polanski on the ballot. "As a former police detective, it depresses me to see the state of crime and policing in our capital," Newman said. "Residents no longer feel safe, and our police officers are struggling to cope."
