title: Chief coroner calls for inquiry into Manchester synagogue attack
description: The chief coroner says sensitive MI5 evidence means inquests may not be suitable.
body: Members of the Jewish community comforted each other after two people were killed in the attack The chief coroner overseeing inquests into the deaths of two men killed in the attack on a Manchester synagogue is to ask the government to hold a public inquiry instead. Judge Alexia Durran, chief coroner of England and Wales, said she would write to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to recommend the inquests be converted into a public inquiry after being told some MI5 material could not be heard in open court because of national security concerns. Inquests were planned into the deaths of Adrian Daulby, 53, and Melvin Cravitz, 66, following the attack by Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, on Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue in Manchester last October. Inquests have no mechanism to hold secret or private hearings, excluding press and public. Adrian Daulby and Melvin Cravitz were killed in the attack on the Heaton Park Synagogue in Manchester To carry out a full investigation, involving hearing sensitive material in private, would require a public inquiry, which can hold some of the hearings behind closed doors with press and public excluded. Judge Durran made the decision to ask for a public inquiry be established following the pre-inquest hearing on 4 September. At the hearing, lawyers for the government said if the MI5 material was released, it would harm national security. Lawyers for the families of the two victims questioned why private hearings were necessary for the disclosure of MI5 material, as the authorities had stated publicly that Al-Shamie was not known to security services. Al-Shamie launched his attack on 2 October last year by driving into the perimeter gates of the synagogue then attacking worshippers with a knife while wearing a fake suicide belt. Cravitz died from multiple knife wounds, while Daulby was killed by a bullet fired by armed officers who had been scrambled to the scene. title: Lib Dem councillor to contest Starmer's seat
description: Patrick Stillman is the Liberal Democrats' candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election.
body: Patrick Stillman says his party has "a distinct, confident liberal message" on issues like housing and safety The Liberal Democrats have selected Camden councillor Patrick Stillman as the party's candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election on 8 October. The seat became vacant when Sir Keir Starmer stood down as an MP to take a role in international affairs. Stillman became a councillor for the West Hampstead ward earlier this year and is the outgoing chairman of Camden Liberal Democrats. He said he was "proud" to have been selected to stand in next month's by-election. "Voters here deserve better than a Labour government in chaos, or a Green Party using this seat to prop up its leader's ambitions," he said. Stillman added: "We have a distinct, confident liberal message - on housing, on safety, on giving young Londoners like me a fair shot at building a life here - and I'm going to make that case on every doorstep between now and 8 October." He will face Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali for Labour, Green Party leader Zack Polanski and former Conservative councillor Ewan Cameron. Nominations close at 16:00 BST on Tuesday. title: Opera singer leads Scottish takeover of the Last Night of the Proms
description: Nicky Spence from Dumfries got the crowd laughing and cheering with a mash-up of traditional and modern music combined with dance moves and patriotic outfits.
body: Nicky Spence's two costume changes revealed a pair of red tartan trews and gold-sleeved T-shirt When opera singer Nicky Spence took to the famous stage of London's Royal Albert Hall for the Last Night Proms, just a tartan scarf hinted at his roots. But when he ripped off his "boring black trousers" to reveal a pair of tartan trews during a rendition of Donald, Where's Your Troosers? there was no doubt of his heritage. It was part of Scotch Snap - a medley of traditional and modern classics - which the Dumfries native combined with dance moves and a series of patriotic outfits. And it ensured the audience were treated to performances of The Proclaimers' I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles) and Bacara's Yes Sir, I Can Boogie alongside the more traditional Rule Britannia! and Sit Down, Your're Rocking the Boat. Last Night of the Proms: The Finale Katie Derham and Nick Mohammed host classical music's biggest party, with star soloists, all the traditions and sing-along fun Spence, who now lives in Paisley with his husband and child, told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that the show was "such a blast". "Everybody loved it, it was amazing - like a chip fire," he added. "Like Bucks Fizz when there was lots of Velcro, I came on with some very boring black trousers and then whipped them off during Donald, Where's Your Troosers? "I think that got everybody's pulses racing a la Magic Mike." It was the world premiere of the medley, which was arranged by Stuart Calvert, and also featured traditional songs like The Bonnie Banks o' Loch Lomond. Dance routines with two dancers dressed in red tartan kilts and bonnets accompanied the music. But laughter came from the audience when Spence pulled off two costume changes. He closed out his performance in a black T-shirt with gold sequined sleeves and a red pair of tartan trews, while a traditionally-dressed bagpiper accompanied the orchestra. Spence said he spent a lot of time working with the arranger to choose the music, curate and trim the showcase. "I put my finger up the zeitgeist to see what was hot at the time and I thought we have got to include Yes Sir, I Can Boogie," he said. The Spanish duo Baccara's disco hit from 1977 became Scotland's unofficial national anthem ahead of Euro 2020. The song travelled with the Tartan Army to the World Cup this summer, where it continued to be belted out by fans at home and at the tournament. For Spence, however, the song did not even touch the sides of his vocal range, who is a specialist opera singer and has toured with Katherine Jenkins and Dame Shirley Bassey. "It was really fun," he said. "Singing things like this is like sorbet compared to the rest of my life, which is like a heavy meal. "Richard Wagner, Strauss and Mozart are beautiful but quite heavy weather stuff and much harder to sing than Yes Sir, I Can Boogie." He added he was more concerned about the dancing than the singing during his performance. Spence performed Rule Britannia! in a red kilt and black Loch Ness Monster jacket Spence said it had been a long time since he had worn Scottish dress on stage but he had recently moved back to Scotland and was happy to be back. "I had a record contract when I was about 21 years old with Universal Records and I was called The Scottish Tenor so I sang a lot of Robert Burns and wore a kilt most of the day," he said. "Then I ditched it all and went into opera." He joked if anyone wants to hear Yes Sir, I Can Boogie, he will sing it again. Spence trained as an opera singer at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama The tenor also portrayed the prince from Rusalka during Vidino divná (wonderful vision) from Dvořák's Rusalka during the final evening of the BBC Proms. He followed Scotch Snap with Sit Down, You're the Rockin' the Boat - a famous show tune from the Broadway musical Guys and Dolls. Spence went on to kick off the final stretch with Rule Britannia! He received applause for his fourth costume of the evening - a jacket and kilt combo, featuring the Loch Ness Monster. Spence also recorded a version of Nessun Dorma, filmed on the steps of the Royal Albert Hall, to mark the aria's centenary. The evening concluded with a tribute to Dolly Parton, God Save the King and Auld Lang Syne. title: London musical cancelled after Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey pull out
description: Sunday in the Park With George was supposed to make its debut next year at the Barbican.
body: The upcoming London revival of Sunday In The Park With George has been cancelled after A-listers Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey dropped out. The Wicked stars had been due to reunite on stage in the Stephen Sondheim show at the Barbican next year. Last month, Grande announced she was pulling out of the musical as part of her decision to take a break from the spotlight after completing her Eternal Sunshine Tour. Earlier this month, Bailey also revealed he was withdrawing from the show. Production company Empire Street Productions initially said it would continue as planned but on Monday announced the musical would no longer be staged in 2027. A statement from the company said: "The planned 2027 production of Sunday in the Park with George at the Barbican will no longer proceed as scheduled. "Empire Street Productions will retain the rights with a view to presenting the production in 2028. Further details will be announced in due course." US composer Sondheim and playwright James Lapine created the original musical, which debuted on Broadway in 1984. Sunday in the Park with George was inspired by French painter Georges Seurat's A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, in which a fictional version of the artist is consumed by his work. Grande and Bailey played Glinda and Fiyero in the film adaptation of Wicked and its sequel, Wicked: For Good. Grande's publicist announced in August that the singer and actress would be "taking a step back from visibility" after her recent tour ended. A representative for the US star told People magazine that she "will be taking a step back from visibility" when the tour ends, after her appearances led to "endless, ongoing public scrutiny". Grande's physical appearance and health have been a topic of speculation in recent years. She later told fans at a Chicago concert: "The announcement that was made yesterday was not a reactive or impulsive thing. It is something that I had decided to plan... quietly, a long time ago." "I heard my fans were worried negativity was ruining things for me but... that could not be more than the opposite. "Boundaries need to be set, human beings do need a break sometimes." When Bailey pulled out of Sunday in the Park with George at the beginning of September, he voiced support for its director Marianne Elliott, external and said: "I so look forward to seeing what the team, and the two actors who will now take on these roles, will create with it," he continued. "I wish the very best to the entire company. I will be cheering them on as they continue with this production." Bailey previously collaborated with Elliot on the play Cock and Sondheim's musical Company in the West End. title: Speedboat killer jailed for attack on girlfriend
description: Jack Shepherd was sentenced at Isleworth Crown Court after previously admitting the violent assault.
body: Jack Shepherd was originally jailed for six years for manslaughter in 2018 Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd has been jailed for 20 months with a further four years on extended licence for violently assaulting his girlfriend, including hitting her chest with a set of hot barbecue tongs. The 38-year-old had pleaded guilty to two counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and damaging property at Isleworth Crown Court in July. The attacks happened in February and June last year and sparked Shepherd's recall to prison. He was originally jailed in 2018 for six years and six months for manslaughter over the death of 24-year-old Charlotte Brown when his speedboat crashed during a first date. Shepherd was jailed for a further four years at Exeter Crown Court in 2019 for a drink-fuelled attack on a barman in March 2018 at a Devon hotel. He was released on licence in January 2024, but faced recall to prison in September last year after he was accused of violence towards the woman. According to a prosecution summary of the case, Shepherd started dating his former partner in August 2024, but towards the end of the year she accused him of being abusive and threatening. In February 2025, he admitted pinning down the woman and "punching her several times, causing bruising to her arm and top of leg" during an argument. In the second incident, in June 2025, Shepherd got angry with her after she said that he had burned a pizza on the barbecue, and "proceeded to hit her with the barbecue tongs on her left breast which caused a permanent scar". Mitigating, George Payne said Shepherd, who attended by videolink from HMP Swaleside in Kent, was "genuinely very ashamed of his behaviour". "The behaviour is driven by his abuse of alcohol and is a feature that has existed for a long time," Payne said. Judge Martin Edmunds rejected that, and said he had "no faith" in Shepherd's remorse, adding: "Your pattern is to commit offences and afterwards apologise, and produce excuses. Your prepared statement sought to shift blame anywhere but yourself." Speedboat killer admits violent attack on woman Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd returned to jail Speedboat killer jailed after fleeing UK Judge Edmunds previously told the court the law did not allow him to add any more time to the term Shepherd was already serving, and his most recent sentence would be served concurrently to his current sentence. He is due to be released in January 2029. Charlotte Brown died in December 2015 when Shepherd took her on a date on his speedboat Following Brown's death, Shepherd went on the run in Georgia. He was convicted in his absence of manslaughter by gross negligence following an Old Bailey trial, and was eventually extradited back to the UK to serve his sentence. Brown, from Clacton, Essex, was fatally thrown from his speedboat boat on the River Thames, when it hit a submerged tree trunk, in December 2015. Shepherd was pulled out of the Thames alive, but Brown was found unconscious and unresponsive and died later in hospital. title: Driver who killed Team GB triathlete to be deported
description: Romanian van driver Visile Barbu's appeal against deportation was dismissed by a judge.
body: Rebecca Comins' family said they are "so proud of what she achieved in her life" A Romanian van driver jailed for killing a Team GB triathlete by driving into the back of her bike has lost an appeal against being deported. Visile Barbu, 50 was delivering furniture to a driver in Calais when he hit Rebecca Comins' bike in June 2022. Barbu drove straight into the back of Comins rather than move into an empty lane of the dual carriageway. He was was found guilty of causing her death by dangerous driving following a five day trial. At the hearing in Newport, immigration judge Ian Boyes said: "The nature of the offending is important. This was not an accident. It was not a slight misjudgement. It was committed using a vehicle which should not have been on the road." Vasile Barbu told police during interview that he could not explain how he hit Rebecca Comins Comins, 52, was nine minutes into a cycling time trial on the A40 near Raglan, Monmouthshire, when Barbu tried to overtake. He said he had seen her, but did not know why he hit her, claiming he would ask himself the question for his "whole life". When his van was examined following the crash it was found to be unfit for the road and its load overweight which would have increased the emergency braking distances and reduced the ability to turn the wheel, according to a vehicle examiner. Barbu moved to Britain in 2002 to become a pub chef at Old Pandy public house and eventually owned the pub. Barbu married a Romanian woman, Maria, in 2004 and had twins, who are now adults. The Crash Detectives: The Last Ride When a cyclist dies just nine minutes into a time trial on a dual carriageway, a van driver’s arrested. But a single mark on the road surface raises more questions than answers. He filed an appeal to stop him from being deported, and said it would be "unduly harsh" for both him and his family to relocate permanently to Romania, where he said he has no home or source of income. He said he identified closely with British culture and traditions and regarded the UK as his permanent home. His wife Maria said she would not relocate to Romania, and would be unable to cope without her husband. On 7 September, Boyes said as Barbu's children were adults and do not depend on him, it would not be "unduly harsh" to remove him. He said "the very significant public interest in deportation outweighs the appellant's private and family life considerations." title: What you need to know about the huge donations to Reform UK

body: This video can not be played Reform UK's Deputy Leader Richard Tice has said the government is trying to "retrospectively change the rules" on political donations, ahead of a debate on Monday in the House of Lords. The party announced £72m in donations from two billionaires days before a bill that could introduce a £100,000 cap on donations from British voters living abroad returns to Parliament. The huge donations, worth £36m each, came from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas. title: Campaigners told to respect rivals as local election abuse rises
description: A survey suggests more than half of candidates in the May 2026 polls in England faced harassment or intimidation.
body: Local elections were held in England earlier this year across 5,000 seats,136 councils and six mayoralties Political parties should require members to respect one another during elections, the Electoral Commission has said after finding rising levels of abuse. More than half of candidates in the May 2026 English local and mayoral polls experienced a problem with harassment or intimidation, the highest level over the last four years, according to its survey of 25,000 who stood. A report, external published on Monday said such issues were most likely to affect women, people from ethnic minority backgrounds and those with a disability. The watchdog is calling on political parties to make clear in their own rules that members "must respect other campaigners", with potential disciplinary action if they do not. The report also recommended requiring social media companies to improve protections for electoral candidates online, including rapidly removing abusive content and identifying perpetrators. Inappropriate contact through social media was the most frequently experienced scenario of harassment or abuse for local candidates, the survey found, with disinformation through generative AI also flagged as an issue. One candidate told the survey their daughter had "called me from school crying" because she had seen posts online branding them "racist, fascist and Nazi". Another candidate reported being screamed at with death threats while leafleting on doorsteps, but could not run away because of their disability. Reform UK and Labour candidates were more than twice as likely as Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to say they had experienced such issues in the May 2026 elections in England, with the Greens and independents between both groups. Some 79% of female respondents reported avoiding the campaign trail on their own at least once, compared to just under half of male counterparts. One female candidate said they felt the need to bring their husband with them. And a third of respondents overall considered not standing for election because of harassment, intimidation or concerns about future abuse. Only 15% of those surveyed had reported such experiences to the police. "These elections demonstrate the growing threats posed to democracy," the Electoral Commission's chief executive Vijay Rangarajan said. He added: "Without improvements to candidate safety, there is a significant risk that people will be put off standing in future elections." title: Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall
description: The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats.
body: Nigel Farage's party has accused Labour of trying to "rig the system" The House of Lords will debate changes to the laws on political donations later on Monday after Reform UK received £72m from two billionaires in 24 hours. Calls for restrictions are growing after huge donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas. The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March. The leader of one of Labour's biggest funders, Unite the Union, is among those backing limits on individual donations. In response, Reform UK's deputy leader Richard Tice said the proposed change shows Labour was "terrified" of the party. "We believe that we've done everything in complete accordance with the laws," he told BBC Breakfast. He accused Labour of trying to "retrospectively introduce legislation in order to significantly disadvantage another political party". Tice said the party's donations would enable it to "get on a level playing field" with other parties, likened it to Labour receiving donations from trade unions, and that "competition is a good thing". But Paul Nowak, the leader of Britain's trade unionists in his role as TUC general secretary, rejected comparisons between donations from wealthy individuals and unions. Speaking at the TUC's annual congress in Brighton on Monday, Nowak said: "Let no-one tell you there is any similarity between care workers chipping in a few quid a year through their union and a party bought and paid for by billionaires." He added a "proper conversation about how we clean up our politics" is required. The sheer scale of Reform's record-breaking donation windfall has prompted an urgent debate across the parties. On Monday, the bill that would introduce a £100,000 cap on donations from British voters living abroad returns to the House of Lords. The rules were proposed in a review by former civil servant Philip Rycroft aimed at countering foreign influence in UK politics. The self-described entrepreneur and philanthropist, Ben Delo, made headlines over the weekend with a record-breaking £36m donation to Reform UK. The Labour peer Lord Wills told Radio 4's Westminster Hour he intended to amend the bill so that donations from those living in the UK could also be capped. Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite, also told the BBC a limit on individual donations was necessary. Her union has donated large sums to Labour in recent years, but she argues that "billionaires splashing out millions" is different from "everyday workers giving 10p a week to a political fund". Reform have said "Labour and their union pals know they can't win an election fairly so now they want to rig the system". Questions remain over whether Reform will be able to keep all of the £72m. Robert Jenrick, the party's economic spokesman, told the BBC on Sunday the donations were "entirely in line with the law as it is, and as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future". The government has also proposed a minimum residency period in which the £100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK. This would be in place for the rest of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money". Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she did not "understand" their "circumstances". The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong. BBC News has been told both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year. The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this. Do you have any comments or questions about this story? title: Tories pick ex-councillor to contest Starmer's seat
description: Ewan Cameron, a Camden councillor from 1998 to 2002, will stand in the by-election on 8 October.
body: Ewan Cameron has been selected as the Conservative candidate The Conservatives have selected former Camden councillor Ewan Cameron as the party's candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election on 8 October. The seat became vacant when Sir Keir Starmer stood down as an MP to take a role in international affairs. Cameron was a councillor for the Belsize ward from 1998 to 2002 and sat on the council's development control committee. He stood again in May's borough elections, finishing 10th of 14 candidates in West Hampstead with 376 votes. He said he was "honoured" to have been selected to stand in next month's by-election. "This is the community where I have lived, raised my family and call home," he said. Cameron added: "Under Kemi Badenoch's leadership the Conservative Party has changed, we have clear, fully costed plans to recruit 10,000 more police officers, scrap stamp duty on family homes and cut bills with our Cheap Power Plan. "That is the message I look forward to campaigning on over the coming weeks." Cameron will face Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali for Labour and Green Party leader Zack Polanski. Nominations close at 16:00 BST on Tuesday. Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. title: Deep-fried food banned under new school dinner rules in England
description: The government describes its new school food standards as "once-in-a-generation changes".
body: There will be a boost for fresh fruit and vegetables and deep-fried food will be banned in what the government has called the biggest shake-up to school dinners in England in over a decade. Under new school food standards, fibre and wholegrains will also be increased, and breakfast clubs will have to follow nutrition rules for the first time, with schools also being monitored. The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) welcomed the changes, but said they hoped the new rules would not become "another stick with which to beat head teachers". The changes will come into effect from 2027 and be funded with existing money for schools, the government said. As part of the new framework, sweet desserts, like cake, will be reduced from a regular lunch offer to twice a week in secondary schools, and once a week in primary schools. They also must now be served with a portion of fruit. Servings of processed meats such as ham, sausages and chicken nuggets have been reduced to once a week and must come with a side of vegetables or fruit. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said they were "once-in-a-generation changes" which would "transform school food for children across the country". The Department for Education said it hoped the reforms would tackle childhood obesity, improve nutrition and support children's concentration, learning and wellbeing. Schools will be required to publish food policies and menus online with monitoring arrangements set to be developed alongside the Food Standards Agency, it said. Pepe Di'Iasio, ASCL general secretary, said parents would feel "reassured" that schools were providing children with a healthy diet. But on plans for enforcement, he added: "None of us would consider ourselves experts in health and nutrition. Don't create another stick with which to beat head teachers when they are trying to do their very best to provide a healthy, balanced meal for those in our schools." He said schools needed "more investment" in catering facilities and in the "professional development" of school chefs to develop menus that "meet the ambitions" of the government. Schools Minister Georgia Gould told BBC Breakfast she was confident schools could deliver healthy meals within existing budgets, without diverting funding from elsewhere, like teaching, and that schools would be given a year to implement the changes. She said the government was "absolutely determined to support schools" to redesign their menus affordably. As part of the changes, deep-fried chips will have to be oven-baked instead, and pasta dishes will need to be 50% wholewheat once a week. High-fibre bread will also become a requirement. Under the new rules, all dishes must come with at least one portion of fruit or vegetables Breakfast clubs will undergo one of the biggest changes. Historically, there has been no guidance on what they should provide, but from next September pastries and fried-eggs will be off the menu and there will be a sugar cap when it comes to cereals. The government said Coco Pops would no longer be an option and chocolate spread was "not permitted". Since February this year, 1,250 schools have offered free breakfast clubs to their pupils. One of those was Oasis Academy Blakenhale in Birmingham, where principal Farzana Ahmed said the school welcomed the changes. "The more children that can access a hot, nutritious meal, the better it is for us, the better it is for them, and actually it really supports families with the reduction of their financial pressures at home," she said. Ahmed said it was "important" that schools are monitored, but added that they "probably need some more guidance from the government on what that's going to look like on a day-to-day basis". Farzana Ahmed welcomed both the new school food standards and the expansion of free school meals eligibility About 60% of pupils at the inner-city school receive free school meals, and Ahmed said they were already providing a healthy, balanced diet. With free school meal eligibility expanding this year to all families who receive Universal Credit, Ahmed said there had been an "influx of parents" applying, and expects around 70% of pupils to benefit going forward. "It's a really positive move," she said. "We know how important a nutritional diet is to the wellbeing, to the behaviour, to the learning of our pupils." This video can not be played 'My favourite is pizza' - Children give their views on school dinners Working mum-of-three Kinza Butt said the free school meals her son was now getting at Blakenhale Juniors had lifted a "burden off the shoulders". "He doesn't have to eat those cold sandwiches anymore," she said. "By the end of the day he used to be starving. But now he's coming home all happy because he's having good, healthy meals with a snack as well." Newly-eligible parent Kinza is delighted her children can now have free school dinners The new food standards will apply to primary and secondary schools in England, but rules for school dinners vary across the UK. In Wales, new guidance will come into force by the end of the year with a greater focus on at least two portions of vegetables being offered every day, with only water, milk or plant-based drinks allowed for hydration. Scotland updated its legislation in 2020. It requires students to be offered at least two portions of vegetables and one portion of fruit every day and oily fish must be served at least once every three weeks. Northern Ireland last updated its regulations in 2007. They include providing bread everyday, without spread, and offering two portions of fruit and vegetables a day. It also stipulates that if beans or pulses form the protein part of a main course, another vegetable must be available. Are you a parent or a teacher? Get in touch. title: The Papers: 'Compulsory lentils' and 'Boris flees Vlad drone blitz'
description: New school food rules for England and ex-PM Boris Johnson "flees Vlad drone blitz" are the top stories in Monday's papers.
body: Comments by President Donald Trump lead the Financial Times after he rejected increasing demands for restrictions on the growth of artificial intelligence , external(AI). The paper highlights the "rare show of unity" from AI leaders in calling for a more cautious pace of development - but says Trump responded by stressing it was imperative for the US to retain its international leadership in the field. The Guardian warns that the US president "appears reluctant to confess to any AI fears" - with "losing to China" a bigger worry in his "calculus". The Daily Telegraph features the call from hospitality bosses, external for Andy Burnham to implement a cut in VAT. It says the appeal comes days after the prime minister "blindsided the industry" by handing local authorities the power to impose unlimited tourist taxes. The Daily Express , externalsays the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, has warned that the new charge on overnight stays could "crush" family-run seaside B&Bs. The government says visitor levies will be set as a percentage of the cost of accommodation, ensuring low-cost holidays will stay low. The Times says Reform UK has accused Labour of threatening the rule of law, external - after the cabinet minister, Angela Rayner, suggested that Nigel Farage's party could be forced to return £72m donated by two crypto billionaires. The paper quotes Reform spokesman Zia Yusuf who said applying new restrictions retrospectively would amount to confiscating donations that were lawful when received. The Daily Mirror says the huge windfall, external "seems like a gift from heaven but could be a poisoned chalice" for Reform - arguing that "taking millions from crypto billionaires sits awkwardly with Nigel Farage's man of the people schtick". With the headline, "Boris Flees Vlad Drone Blitz", the Sun highlights Sunday's attack by Russia on a rail station in Ukraine, external shortly after Boris Johnson had passed through. It says the former prime minister was travelling close to the Polish border when the service behind his was blown up. Writing in the Daily Mail, Johnson accuses President Valdimir Putin of getting "absolutely desperate" - and says the strike illustrates the "bared teeth of a cornered rat". title: My son was jailed indefinitely for stealing a mobile - we've waited 21 years to see him released
description: Leroy Douglas has spent almost as long in prison as one of Wales' most notorious murderers.
body: Leroy Douglas was given an indeterminate sentence in 2005 and has been in prison ever since "It's like your son being killed - he's here but he's not." Leroy Douglas was just 24 when he was jailed in 2005 for stealing a mobile phone and handed a minimum prison term of two-and-a-half years. More than 20 years later, he is still locked up. Leroy, who had a drug addiction, had a string of convictions for offences including petty crimes and shoplifting, before being sentenced for robbery and being given an indeterminate sentence of Imprisonment for Public Protection, external (IPP). His family said this came as a "huge shock" as it meant indefinite detention. Now 45, he is set to be released in October - a decision that came weeks before Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced he would end IPPs before the end of this parliament. Anthony Douglas said years of waiting had been "torture" for his son and his family as they remained in "limbo" over his future. He added: "In that time he's lost his daughter, lost his cousin, lost my parents." Leroy's sister, Natalie Douglas [left] and his father Anthony [right] have started a petition to bring Leroy closer to Cardiff when he is released Introduced in 2005, IPPs were established to keep serious offenders, who were perceived to be a risk to the public, in prison. They imposed a minimum sentence for offenders, but no maximum or end date, with criminals having to serve the minimum term before being considered for release by the parole board. But this is not automatic. They are also subject to licence conditions which they must follow or risk being recalled to prison once they are released. IPPs were scrapped in 2012 due to criticism for being handed out for less serious crimes but it was not retrospective, meaning - as of July - there were about 2,400 people still in prison on IPP sentences, according to the United Nations, external. However, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said there were 2,271 IPP prisoners in custody, as of 30 June. The organisation, which wants an end to IPPs, said the sentence "violates serious human rights". Anthony drew parallels between Leroy's sentence and offenders such as Jeffrey Gafoor, who murdered Lynette White in one of Wales' most notorious crimes. Gafoor was was released from prison in 2025 after serving 21 years for stabbing the 20-year-old to death in 1992. "Leroy stole a phone, how is it right?" Natalie says it's been incredibly sad for her family and she cannot wait for Leroy to come home Human rights lawyer Karen Todner was instrumental in securing Leroy's release as he was one of four prisoners she submitted an application for the writ of Habeas Corpus for. The writ, which requires a person detained by authorities be brought before a court so the legality of the detention may be examined, resulted in it being agreed their detention was unlawful. Despite this, Todner, said Leroy's release conditions were "so stringent, his liberty is restricted". His relatives are also unhappy as he will have to spend six months with an electronic tag, housed three hours away from them in Cardiff. Anthony believes his son is being "set up to fail" as he feels Leroy needs to be around his family for his well being. "It's like he's being taken out of the frying pan and into the fryer," he said. Leory's sister Natalie Douglas has launched a petition for to him be housed closer to home, calling on the justice system to correct "part of the years' worth of oversight". She said his family wanted to welcome him back with open arms and provide "the support system he never had while being lost in this unforgiving system". Natalie is campaigning to bring Leroy closer to home in Cardiff "I have a lump in the back of my throat just speaking about it," Anthony said. "I'm just astounded, 20 years they wouldn't let him out, but they still put conditions on it." Leroy applied for parole five times while in prison, but was rejected each time due to what his family said was incomplete courses. While going through addiction in the past, his family said he tested negative for drugs while in prison and did not have a history of violence. Anthony added: "I want to know why is he being released so far from home, and can't come home to family. "They're putting him with people from the same environment he's trying to leave behind." Natalie [left] says she and her mother visit Leroy every month and speak to him on the phone every day Anthony said he asked the prison for answers about the conditions of his release, but got no response and feels Leroy has been "tortured" for something. He added: "He went in as a kid and will come out as a man. "He's going to need counselling, he's suffering from mental pain and been sent away from family." The MoJ said: "It is right that IPP sentences were abolished and, as the prime minister and lord chancellor announced, we will set out plans to end the historic injustice of these sentences. "This will take a cross-party approach to propose a way forward with public protection and victims at the heart of these reforms. "As the IPP annual report shows, support has significantly improved for these offenders, with greater access to rehabilitation and mental health support." The MoJ said the number of people serving IPP sentences in the community had been cut from 3,018 in December 2023 to 891 in December 2025. title: Joint-worst start since 1992 and fan protests - Man Utd's day to forget
description: Manchester United fans protested inside and outside Old Trafford before Sunday's derby, then saw their team lose to 10-man Manchester City
body: Manchester United minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and co-chair Avram Glazer were at Old Trafford for the 1-0 defeat by Manchester City Sir Jim Ratcliffe cannot have imagined it would be like this. When Ratcliffe agreed on Christmas Eve 2023 to spend £1.25bn to buy a minority stake in Manchester United, his intention was to restore the ailing club to its past glories. Sitting in the directors' box at Old Trafford watching United lose 1-0 to a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men midway through the first half was definitely not part of the plan. Ratcliffe knew major decisions needed to be made in order to slash the club's losses. And he knew they were bound to be unpopular. But nearly three years on, he presumably felt the green shoots of recovery would be starting to grow by now. After all, the project chief executive Omar Berrada spoke to staff about in September 2024 was an aspiration to win the Premier League title in 2028. In other words, next season. On the evidence of this 199th Manchester derby, United are a very long shot to achieve Berrada's target. At this point, even pacifying the thousands of fans who protested against the club's ownership before the Old Trafford defeat by 10-man City looks beyond them. United now have four points from their opening four games. It equals their worst start to a Premier League season since 1992-93. Last season under Ruben Amorim, they also had four points from four matches. Manchester United fans unfurled a banner inside Old Trafford criticising the club's owners To be clear, United's fans have - to a greater or lesser degree - protested against the owners since the Glazer family landed £600m-worth of debt on to a previously debt-free club with their leveraged buy-out in 2005. In their most recent accounts to 31 March, United had an overall debt of £1.3bn, including outstanding transfer fees. Since then they have refinanced $425m (£314m) worth of bonds at a higher interest rate than they had been previously. They also took an additional $125m (£92.4m) but are yet to explain what the additional funds will be used for. The club's current financial position will be revealed on 23 September when it publishes its full year accounts to 30 June 2026. Ratcliffe's involvement promised to change the situation. Yet many fans argue that, if anything, things have got worse. Ill feeling has spilled over since United launched a ticket-touting investigation in the summer. Although they have admitted to underestimating the number of fans who shared their account details and toned down some of the threats around season ticket confiscation if supporters failed to respond as requested, United officials defended the investigation. Last week, they revealed 685 fan accounts had been banned, with a further 464 either sanctioned or warned. However, United added that "468 cases were resolved after supporters responded with the relevant information. No further action was taken, as the information provided satisfactorily explained the activity identified". Many match-going fans felt the investigation was an attack on them and decided to use the City game to protest - inside and outside Old Trafford. Huge numbers with flares gathered outside the ground, heeding a call from the 1958 Group, before making their way through the Munich tunnel under the stadium. Inside, The Red Army group of fans opted not to bring in their usual banners - instead display a single banner above the players' tunnel stating: "The way you treat us is a disgrace." It meant the only banners in the stadium were the ones the club had themselves put up. "Unless our generational match-going support is given a real voice that is actually listened to, the little that remains of our fan culture will soon be gone forever," said The Red Army group in a statement. "TRA aren't a protest group, we're an 'atmosphere' group but we've never shied away from making our position clear when we believe not doing so would be to the detriment of the interests of match-going supporters." It was noticeable many songs were sung in direct protest against Ratcliffe, as well as the Glazers. "We wanted the Glazers out and that will never change," said Steve Compton of the the 1958 Group. "Ratcliffe came in and gave us a glimmer, but his idea of putting Manchester back in Man Utd couldn't be any further from the truth. "The club have made many statements, but one thing they haven't done is actually apologise to anyone. We've had hundreds of messages directly - this has affected people's health. "These are regular Joes, working-class people who are sent an email telling them their ticket's been suspended with no actual evidence. How do you defend something you don't know what you're defending against?" The 1958 Group's allegation, which has been voiced by other fan groups, contradicts United's own comments on Friday that state they did advise fans what they were being accused of. The club declined to comment on the protests. Foden sees red as Mainoo impresses - Manchester derby ratings The 1958 Group of Manchester United fans display a banner in their protest outside Old Trafford There were boos from the home fans at the final whistle, although it was not entirely clear whether the reaction was triggered by their team's performance or the officials over the controversial offside call that confirmed Erling Haaland's second-half winner should stand. Since Berrada spoke to staff, United have delivered their worst starts in three decades. Many United supporters feel an overall transfer spend of £148m this summer was not enough after Carrick's mid-season arrival led to an improvement that secured a third-place finish. title: Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change?
description: Andy Burnham is likely to face fresh pressure to further change the rules on party donations, writes Jack Fenwick.
body: When news of Reform UK's two record-breaking £36m donations emerged this weekend, it felt as if Nigel Farage's inner circle was attempting a fightback. The last few months have proved difficult for the party, with a dip in the polls, a spike in infighting and a series of questions about money that simply won't go away. In contrast, the mood within the ranks of Labour and the Conservatives has been fairly chipper. Most Labour MPs feel Andy Burnham has got off to an impressive start as prime minister, while many Conservatives are feeling confident about Kemi Badenoch's recent reshuffle of her top team. But Reform has been quietly - and as of this weekend rather loudly - building a formidable war chest. Even before these two mega donations, Reform had raised £30.5m since the start of the year, more than double their nearest rivals. This extra £72m takes them into uncharted financial territory, which the party says will be used to hire the brightest policy minds, as well as up to 400 campaign managers in every target seat around the country. In a world of fractured politics, when seats can be won on increasingly smaller percentages of the vote, having a ground campaign that is effective at getting out the core voter base could become increasingly important. Some in Westminster have been less than convinced by Burnham's insistence that he won't call an early general election. It might be tempting for the prime minister to go to the polls before Farage has had time to splash the cash on a shiny new party machine. Some Labour MPs think that could factor into his thinking, but one Number 10 source insisted Reform's extra cash does not make an early election any more likely. Burnham is now likely to come under increasing pressure to further change the rules on party donations. Labour is already planning to introduce a cap on the amount of money a British citizen living overseas can donate. There has been much talk about whether that could impact the donations to Reform by cryptocurrency billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, but when interviewed by the BBC, Angela Rayner refused to say whether the two would be caught up in the rule changes. The Liberal Democrats and Greens have also called for a cap for people based in Britain too, to prevent future mega donations. Burnham has indicated that he's open to having that conversation, but chose not to support an effort by some Labour MPs earlier this month to tighten the rules. Rayner confirmed this morning that it was still something being considered by ministers. The Electoral Commission is looking at what more should be done in this area and the calls from within Labour for further change will now grow stronger. Government sources insist this weekend's donations are not being viewed inside Downing Street as a game-changing moment in this debate. But people across the political spectrum are now asking whether this massive injection of money will be remembered as a key moment when politics in this country changed. title: Nepo baby is a horrific term, says Zeta-Jones
description: The Chicago star's children Dylan and Carys have both gone into showbiz, following in her footsteps.
body: Hollywood star Catherine Zeta-Jones has declared the phrase "nepo baby" is "horrific". The Mumbles-born actor told The Sunday Times: "These kids didn't ask to be born into this." The term nepo baby refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs. The 56-year-old is married to Kirk Douglas' son, Michael Douglas, and they have two children - Dylan and Carys - who have both followed their parents into showbiz. Dylan, she said, was pursuing acting while Carys was interested in directing. She insisted her children were "plugging away". Catherine Zeta-Jones describes herself as "a bit of an eclectic collector" "You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said. "It's hard for them to forge a way forward on their own. "This horrific phrase 'nepo baby' is horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life. "But they love it, and they're good. "Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'." Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, becoming a household name in the UK in 1991 when she starred in ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May with Only Fools and Horses legend David Jason. She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago. "I had a sniff of the joy of being in the theatre so young," she said. "I went, 'I want to do this. I can't imagine going through school and A-Levels in Swansea.'" Zeta-Jones met Romancing The Stone star Douglas, 81, at France's Deauville Film Festival, in August 1998. With a 25-year age gap between them, they were engaged a year later, marrying at The Plaza hotel in New York in 2000. Dylan was born in 2000 and Carys in 2003. title: Reform confident it won't need to repay any of £72m under proposed new donor rules
description: Housing Secretary Angela Rayner says rule changes on donations from UK expats would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".
body: This video can not be played Watch: Donations 'entirely in line with the law', says Jenrick Reform UK believes the £72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law", the party's economic spokesman has said. Robert Jenrick told the BBC he did not expect that the party will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas. The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March. "These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said. As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed a minimum residency period in which the £100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK. This would be in place for the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money". Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she does not "understand" their "circumstances". Answering questions about the donations following Rayner's remarks, Jenrick said: "It might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me. "But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law." BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year. Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law". In a statement after the programme, a Reform UK spokesman said: "We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to be handed back." One person familiar with the government's proposed changes said the issue of whether Delo and Harborne are affected would likely come down to how ministers choose to define UK residency. They said one way would be to adopt the same definition used in tax laws, but stressed how complex the rules around residency are. Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo? Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record The government's proposed changes were added to the Representation of the People Bill after they were approved by MPs this month. The bill still needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords. Rayner said the proposals were "directly as a result" of a review by former top civil servant Philip Rycroft, external, published on 25 March. Rayner said: "We said that because of the intention of the legislation and the recommendations, which we accepted, was known in the public domain that it would be retrospective to that date. "That legislation is going through Parliament at the moment and we've also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy." There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties. The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this. It did not support calls from some MPs for a cap but Rayner left the door open to the possibility of further restrictions. "It's not as simple as we're saying we won't put a cap [on donations], it's a question of making sure that the task and finish group look at how we implement this." Since the 2024 election, the Conservative Party has raised £37m, Reform has raised £35m before Delo and Harborne's large donations, Labour had raised £21m, the Liberal Democrats £17m and the Green Party £1.9m Rayner said the aim would be to "protect our democracy in the spirit of individuals not being able to overpower and buy their way into democracy at the expense of those people that are at the ballot box". Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free". He said people should be able to support the democratic movements they wished but added that "what we've got to be careful about is where different industries, where different financial sources raise questions". Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said there should be emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. She said: "No politician should be able to buy the keys to Number 10." A Green Party spokesperson said there needed to be "more robust laws" around political donations, adding: "The Labour Party urgently needs to find its spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals." Jenrick said Delo and Harborne - who each gave £36m to the party in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party - were "not buying anything, they simply support our agenda". Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions. The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong. Harborne wrote in the Telegraph on Saturday that Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage". title: 'Slim chance' government will hit 1.5m new homes target, Rayner tells BBC
description: High construction costs and the Iran war are threatening the key manifesto pledge, the housing secretary says.
body: This video can not be played Watch: Angela Rayner says target will be difficult to meet but government "taking action" on social housing There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC. "Headwinds" including the Iran war and rising construction costs are making it harder to meet the key Labour manifesto pledge, Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. "But I'm definitely not giving it up," she said, and stressed that the government was "making a difference" through investing billions in social and affordable homes. Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic. Labour promised to hit the target through building both private and social housing by the end of the current parliament, meaning summer 2029 at the latest. This implied an average of 300,000 new properties would be needed each year - a rate of construction not seen in decades. Rayner told the BBC on Sunday: "It's a slim chance, but I'm definitely not giving it up." She said it was important to keep the goal - which she said had always been a "stretch target" - in place, but that she was "being honest with the public" that it would be difficult to achieve. "The prime minister wants us to make sure we're building council houses. He's made that absolutely, fundamentally clear," she said. "We're seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference." Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period" - although he has not provided details on exactly what this will entail. BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives. Rayner's predecessor in the role, Steve Reed, last year admitted a sharp surge in construction would be needed to reach the goal - but said he expected it would just about be met once the impact of planning reforms took hold. Analysts have said reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government should help increase construction in the long term, including changing the rules on green belt development to increase the area in which homes can be built. But some argue that construction is being held back by factors including high house prices relative to average incomes, higher costs due to global conflict and labour shortages since Brexit. BBC Verify has been tracking performance against the target using government data on Energy Performance Certificates (EPC). Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built. Data for the 12 months to June 2026 suggested about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England that year, far short of the 300,000 needed to meet the target. title: 'Forget Notting Hill - we set our new romcom in the east end of Glasgow'
description: Romantic comedy Premature is out in cinemas next Friday, despite a microscopic budget.
body: Elle Watson and James Rottger star as mismatched flatmates in Premature Film fans have had plenty of chances to spot Glasgow on the big screen in recent years, from superhero blockbusters to futuristic sci-fi thrillers. Now the city is to star in cinemas once again - but the difference is that it won't be doubling for another location. It is actually set in the city. Romantic comedy Premature is out in cinemas next Friday, despite a microscopic budget that is the fraction of Hollywood productions like Spider-Man: Brand New Day. The indie film - by writer and director Kevin Walls - was shot across the city, meaning landmarks such as Kelvingrove Art Gallery pop up - a well as the less obvious location of an east end flat. This video can not be played Rom-com stars fall in love with filming in Glasgow The film stars James Rottger and Elle Watson as Cameron and Eilidh - mismatched flatmates who face the prospect of parenthood after a one-night stand. "We shot quite a bit in a flat in the east end, maybe about nine days there," Walls said. "There is a key scene we did in a close there. It is not necessarily the most romantic location you would think of for a romcom, but in real life that's exactly where these things happen. "Why can't we set a romcom in a flat in the east end? It looks really beautiful on the big screen." The production was shot throughout Glasgow, including in an east end flat That vibe is something the film's leading lady agrees with, despite Glasgow's film appearances often being due to it looking Gothic. "We are so used to Glasgow being this dark and gritty place, but that's not reflective of the city overall", Watson said. "It's great having it on screen as a bright and funny place, with people falling in love there. Shooting in locations I've grown up around was great too, as I've been going to Kelvingrove since I was a little kid. "Part of me wanted to run around the building when it was all quiet. But when you see it on the screen it looks beautiful. Being from Glasgow you are so used to it that you almost become immune to the spectacle of the building, and how grand it is." Director Kevin Walls and stars James Rottger and Elle Watson are delighted to see Premature getting a cinema release Walls admitted to BBC Scotland News that some of the choices were made through necessity. "The locations were tricky because we didn't have any money," she said. "So we were begging – I'd usually go down and speak to people about what I was trying to do. I explained I wasn't going to tear up their space or anything like that." Premature is the first feature film Kevin has directed, having worked on short films and adverts in the past. He has also juggled other jobs, including lecturing and editing highlights of football matches for YouTube channels, with money raised going back into Premature. A Kickstarter campaign helped secure funding needed for a cinema release. "Cinema-going is really important to me, and through sheer determination I was going to get this on a cinema screen too, as it deserves to be seen there", Walls said. City centre pubs were used by the crew as locations Watson's character Eilidh harbours dreams of being an artist, but is frustrated that life is not going to plan. Her flatmate Cameron is meticulous and career driven, but everything changes for both of them when they drunkenly sleep together. "This whole film is about two people being chucked out of any sense of control they thought they had," said James Rottger, who plays the leading man. "Particularly for Cameron, that's the point of the film – I leaned into the bit of me that's a control freak and likes to do things a certain way, and then brought that out in the character." Like his co-star, he was delighted to see so much of Glasgow on screen, and being presented in a bright light. "It's brilliant big productions are coming here and using Glasgow as a double, but it's important we see Scotland on the big screen as itself," he said. "The film Kevin has written shows Glasgow in a warm light, literally and figuratively. The red sandstone flats, Kelvingrove, the pubs – it's all there." Kelvingrove Art Gallery is a location for some of the film's key scenes Premature marks Scotstoun native Watson's big screen debut, after mostly working in theatre and short films or adverts. Unlike his co-star, Rottger has a fair number of screen credits, including roles in Gary: Tank Commander and a couple of rom-coms regarded as a bit cheesy - Irish Wish with Lindsay Lohan and festive TV film A Hot Cocoa Christmas. However, for this film both stars say they could relate to their characters. "I'm probably closer to where Cameron ends up than where he starts off," said Rottger, who has two young daughters. "As a dad waiting for a baby to be born, you are out of having any control. The nerves you feel knowing you will be a parent is terrifying for the first time." More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland For Watson, the relatability came in a different way. "Any woman in her late 20s or 30s will have thought about children, it's omnipresent," she said. "You feel you need to be confident about your choice as it will soon be taken away from you as you get older. "But it was important the film is not just about Eilidh being pregnant – it's using that for her to discover who she is and what she wants from life." Elle Watson's character Eilidh is stunned to become pregnant in Premature Walls admits he had to overcome his own doubts during the creative process, having put so much effort in. "There were so many times you'd think 'what am I doing here, this is a terrible idea and won't work' – I had to push past that and be confident," he said. title: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?
description: Millions of us do it, though few of us realise we do - but getting the right treatment can be life-changing.
body: Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teeth Ella can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing. "I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it." The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life. Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear. According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing. "It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful." Ella says constant teeth grinding enlarged her masseter muscles and widened her jaw (pictured, left, before treatment and, right, afterwards) Studies, external suggest many of us Bruxers do it because of stress - but why do our jaws carry the burden of our everyday lives? What can we do about it? And can it actually be a good thing in some cases? Bruxism is an umbrella term which groups together four different jaw movements - clenching, grinding, bracing and thrusting. Some people grind at night, others through the day. Some barely notice they're doing it, while others can gnash through mouthguards and wake even the deepest sleeping bed partners. So how can you tell if you do it? Here are the signs to look out for: Worn, chipped or flattened teeth Headaches or facial pain in the morning Disrupted sleep and daytime tiredness Earache or pain near the temples without infection Teeth grinding is also mentioned more frequently in therapy according to the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, which says people nowadays are more aware of how their mental health impacts their body. Psychotherapist Rahi Popat says more of his clients - particularly younger ones - say they or someone else have noticed they've been grinding their teeth, "and they can often link that to a really stressful time in their lives and realise that's when their teeth grinding either increased or even started". Trauma and stress can put you in "fight or flight" mode, where your heart rate increases, you release adrenaline, and your muscles tense, preparing the body for an external threat, he says. And because the jaw and the nervous system are so closely linked through the major cranial nerves, our muscles are triggered and we clench and grind our teeth. "If we do it overnight, it's a way of our bodies releasing some of the stress and tension we might have felt through the day," Popat explains. For Ella, nocturnal teeth grinding in her sleep became a way to release tension that had built up while she was awake. "I know it's to do with my stress levels," Ella says. "I have high functioning anxiety - you wouldn't think it if you met me. "I'm busy, and I go out a lot to mask it." In her 20s, she says she just "put up" with the pain. But a few years later, when her dentist told her that her teeth were at risk, Ella decided to get treatment. After her dentist injected her jaw muscles with Botox, Ella says her sleep and mental health improved Even though it's not routinely offered on the NHS, Ella decided to pay her dentist to inject Botox into her masseter muscles - the ones that control her jaw. The procedure relaxed them and reduced the tension in her face, and should last 3 to 4 months. "Over the past few months I've been able to sleep properly," she says. "I've got so much more energy in the mornings, the pain has reduced and my face is not as square." Dr Simon Cove, a dentist who treats both private and NHS patients, says the physical impact of grinding on our teeth can be huge. He uses a 3D scanner to assess his patients' teeth, and can see the wear over time. "Often people are not even aware they are doing it, but then we get to see the damage," he says. "If the teeth have been worn down to such an extent, treatment can be extremely complex and can cost thousands of pounds." But he says such cases are relatively uncommon and can take years to develop. A 3D scan can reveal the damage that teeth grinders are doing to their teeth While you can treat the symptoms - by wearing a mouthguard, for example - getting to the source of what's causing your teeth grinding is just as important, says dental sleep specialist, Dr Aditi Desai. "Too often," she says, "dentists give out mouthguards without checking why it is happening." It's vital that serious, underlying conditions like obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) are considered, she says. OSA is caused by a blocked airway, so a patient may grind their teeth to move the blockage in order to be able to breathe again. "That's a very good example of why bruxism can keep you alive," says Prof Frank Lobbezoo, a leading researcher on the condition. And even though bruxism has its negatives (tooth damage, sleep disruption, jaw ache, to name but a few), it's not always the "bad guy", he explains. "Bruxism is also important for the production of saliva," Lobbezoo says. "Moving the jaw muscles activates the big salivary glands. title: Drag Race co-creator warns of TV representation 'crisis' after BBC drops show
description: The BBC is cutting the show because of financial pressures, sparking discussion about LGBTQ+ representation on TV.
body: Drag Race UK judges Michelle Visage, RuPaul Charles, Graham Norton and Alan Carr The executive producer of Drag Race has said there is a "crisis of representation" on TV, following the BBC's decision to axe the UK edition of the show. Speaking exclusively to BBC News, Fenton Bailey said he did not believe there was a "hidden agenda" behind the decision, but feared "vulnerable communities are going to be even more vulnerable". The move led viewers to raise concerns about the corporation's on-screen representation, after it also cancelled two LGBTQ+ dating shows. A spokesperson for the BBC said the decision was down to "significant financial pressures", as it attempts to make £500m of savings. Other shows being cancelled include Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank and Live at the Apollo, and more than 500 job losses have also been announced. World of Wonder (WOW) announced future series of Drag Race UK, including a new All Stars version, will be broadcast exclusively on the company's own streamer, WOW Presents Plus. BBC News spoke to Bailey, screenwriters, TV critics and former Drag Race contestants about the move and what it means for on-screen representation. When Drag Race UK launched in 2019, co-creator Fenton Bailey, who was born in Portsmouth but now lives in Los Angeles, said working with the national broadcaster felt like a "very special homecoming" for his production company, WOW. The US version of the show, created by RuPaul Charles and produced by WOW, had been on air for more than 10 years and was a runaway success, with dozens of Emmy awards and an international following. Fans were eagerly awaiting a UK series to showcase the unique British style of drag. Now, eight series and three spin-offs later, the programme will stop broadcasting on the BBC after the current series ends. "Even at the best of times, queer culture is vulnerable and you can't take anything for granted," Bailey told BBC News. "Just because a door opened yesterday doesn't mean it won't be slammed shut the next." BBC News understands discussions to renew the BBC's deal with the show lasted months, with producers hopeful an agreement could be reached, but talks ultimately failed due to the scale of the savings the corporation is trying to make. Randy Barbato (left), and Fenton Bailey (right) with Drag Race judge Ross Mathews Bailey said it was a sign of the "horrible financial situations" broadcasters are currently facing. "The team at the BBC are amazing and so passionate about the show, this is not an easy thing for any of the people I interacted with, or something they wanted to do," he added. Drag Race UK was consistently one of BBC Three's most popular offerings, but according to Barb Audiences data, while average viewing figures for the series rose between 2022 and 2024, overall they've fallen around 15% over the past four years, against a backdrop of declining TV viewing figures across the board. Bailey said the figures "haven't plummeted," but had instead fallen in line with other terrestrial TV shows, and said the number of viewers watching on social media had risen "because that's where the audience has gone." Following the announcement, some viewers speculated the show could be acquired by another UK broadcaster, but Bailey suggested the show's creators may prefer to go it alone. "We love partnerships, but in this particular moment, having the freedom to make the show the way we want may be preferable to getting into bed with another broadcaster and potentially be in the same situation a few more seasons down the road." A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly." The Vivienne rose to fame after becoming the first winner of RuPaul's Drag Race UK in 2019 Scott Bryan, TV critic and author of Out Now: A Queer Journey Through Modern Television, says the move is indicative of just how severe the financial pressures facing broadcasters have become. "I can imagine Drag Race is an expensive show to make," Bryan told the BBC, "I can see the pressures the BBC are under, but it's rather concerning in regards to queer storytelling. "You see LGBTQ+ lives reflected on soaps and primetime dramas much more casually, but there still needs to be shows specifically catering to a queer audience, and it feels like very quickly the drawbridge is pulling up." Earlier this year the BBC announced LGBTQ+ dating shows I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl were also being cancelled. The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows, but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges". Author and screenwriter Juno Dawson says viewers have begun to notice a "pattern". She said: "I think that's why perhaps eyebrows have been raised, because Drag Race hasn't been cancelled in isolation. A couple of other LGBTQ+ shows have gone as well. "It's a shame this is happening at the BBC, because commercial channels don't necessarily have an obligation to represent all the communities in the UK, but the BBC does and it's supposed to represent all of us, including LGBTQ+ people." The BBC recently announced Smoggie Queens would return for a third series The BBC recently announced Smoggie Queens, which features predominantly LGBTQ+ characters, would be renewed for a third series, and it represents the community elsewhere through storylines in shows including Mr Loverman, Amandaland, Vigil and EastEnders. A recent report from GLAAD, an American advocacy organisation, found film representation had fallen for a third consecutive year, external and more than 200 LGBTQ+ TV characters would disappear from screens in 2026 because of cancellations, endings or limited-run series.
