title: Tom Felton: I'm so excited to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again
description: The Harry Potter actor talks about taking on Broadway and his friendship with former co-stars
body: Every night on Broadway, Tom Felton walks on stage to a roar from the audience. He had expected the reaction to die down after the first week, but it never did. Almost 15 years after his final appearance as Draco Malfoy on screen, Felton has spent the past 10 months playing the character again in the Broadway production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. I meet the actor in a dressing room at NBC Studios, just off Times Square in New York. He's just finished a live television appearance and in a few hours will be back on stage for his next performance. He greets me with a hug and says he is excited to speak to BBC News because his mum and 100-year-old grandfather will see it. His family are some of his biggest supporters - his mum has seen the show five times already, while his dad is due to visit next month. That support mirrors the enthusiasm Felton has encountered from Harry Potter fans, which he says still surprises him more than two decades after he first played Draco. "I thought the applause would stop in the first week and it has not. "It's very humbling and lovely to know how much the characters still mean to people now and if it brings them to the theatre, that's the best." He is also struck by how many of the fans now approaching him were not alive when the first Harry Potter film was released. "There are fans that approach me shouting 'Draco' who weren't even born when I was in the first film," he says. Felton was the first of the original Harry Potter cast to reprise his role in the theatre show, but he will not be the only one for much longer, as Rupert Grint is set to return as Ron Weasley on Broadway in February. The 38-year-old actor says he called his former co-star as soon as he heard the news. "We are typically - and he will agree with me - pretty bad at our phone game, but when I heard the news I called him immediately and I'm so excited for him," Felton says. "Who doesn't want to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again? Come on!" I ask whether Felton offered any advice to his co-star but he laughs and says absolutely not, pointing out that Grint has already appeared on Broadway. "I don't think he needs any advice from me. If anything, I would be taking it from him." He adds that Grint has a "Ron Weasley laissez-faire approach to these things". More than two decades after they first met on the Harry Potter set, Felton says the friendships between the young cast have endured. He describes Grint, Daniel Radcliffe and Emma Watson as "best mates" and "family", even if getting them all in the same place is now difficult. "We are usually in four different corners of the Earth, so it's hard to get together," he says, adding that their support since his return to Draco has been "fantastic". Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson, Rupert Grint and Tom Felton are pictured in 2010 at the premiere of Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows - Part 1 As Felton and Grint return to familiar roles on stage, a new generation is preparing to take over the characters in HBO's television adaptation of the books set to air later this year. Felton recently met his successor, Lox Pratt, and "saw a lot of myself in him". Felton says he was struck by Pratt's confidence and describes him as a "charming young man and fabulous actor". Their families have even been in touch. "My mum is in contact with his mum and I'm encouraging him to be as cheeky as possible - but professional first." Felton says he is not worried about the level of scrutiny Pratt and the other young actors may face as they take on some of the best-known characters in popular culture. "You just enjoy it for what it is. "I'm not worried about that at all for him. He's got a very good head on his shoulders and what you don't know doesn't hurt you. I'm sure he's not one to scroll through negative comments." This video can not be played Tom Felton on Harry Potter remake Nor does Felton appear concerned that Harry Potter is being adapted again relatively soon after the films. Instead, he says the longer television format offers the chance to explore parts of the books that the films did not have time for. "We had two hours to fit in a lot of content and the wizarding world is vast, so it's exciting to know they can dive in deeper." "I hope the fans of the books and films explore more about Draco," he says. While some actors might want to distance themselves from the role that made them famous, Felton has embraced his connection to Harry Potter. He says the franchise has given him "a life I could never have imagined" and that, even today, it is "bringing people together from every corner of the earth". Asked whether this really is the last time he will play Draco, Felton is reluctant to rule anything out. "I suppose I said 15 years ago that was the end of Draco and I was leaving him forever, but here I am. "It's hard to say with any certainty what's to come." title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England
description: Changes will spell out that governments can change rules and that career choices affect repayments.
body: University applicants in England will be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out, the government has said. Ministers said they would spell out that governments can change repayment rules and that different career choices can affect how much borrowers repay. They agreed to some but not all of the recommendations made by MPs after an inquiry into student loans, and did not say whether they would reverse a freeze to the repayment threshold for some graduates. The inquiry found the way loans had been presented to teenagers amounted to mis-selling, after the BBC revealed the Department for Education (DfE) had compared repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts. The recent debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were issued in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales. The interest rate on those loans is the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus up to 3% depending on earnings, and borrowers repay at a rate of 9% of everything they earn over a repayment threshold, which is meant to rise with inflation every year. The loans are written off after 30 years. Campaigners want a lower interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse a decision last year to freeze the threshold at £29,385 for three years in England. Freezing that threshold means graduates start repaying their loans sooner and, once they do, they pay more than they would have done if it had risen with inflation. MPs on the Treasury Committee called for a U-turn on that decision as part of a series of recommendations after an inquiry this summer. The Treasury and the DfE did not say whether ministers would unfreeze the threshold in their response, but said: "We keep all aspects of the student finance system under review." The government rejected recommendations to: Split the cost of university evenly between the student and the government Stop using RPI to calculate interest rates Ensure promotional materials comply with Financial Conduct Authority's Consumer Duty, saying student loans were "very different to commercial loans" However, it agreed to "making it more prominent that... regulations may be amended by government and Parliament". It also said "more can be done to help student loan borrowers understand how their loan balance may change over the long term". The government also said giving students long-term predictions of how much they might ultimately repay risked being "misleading" because of "limited" accuracy. It proposed instead to "demonstrate how different life and career choices may affect repayment trajectories", including salary progression, retraining, part-time work, and career breaks. How student loans work for tuition fees and living costs 'Deeply misleading' school talks compared student loans to £30 phone contracts Phone contract comparisons 'amounted to mis-selling' student loans, MPs say Students starting university in England now have Plan 5 loans, which have a lower interest rate but also a lower threshold and longer repayment term. Nick Hillman, director of the Higher Education Policy Institute, who helped design the Plan 2 system, said the government had "absolutely rejected" most of what the Treasury Committee had recommended and its response would not meet the concerns of Plan 2 graduates. Oliver Gardner, founder of the Rethink Repayment campaign, said the government's response "does not go far enough" and he wanted to see "concrete action" in the autumn Budget. While Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said making information clearer was "an important step" but "doesn't help graduates who are angry that they didn't receive the same service and are now facing punitive repayment terms on a loan which keeps growing". She urged the chancellor to reverse the threshold freeze in this autumn's Budget. In March, a BBC investigation found that as well as comparing monthly student loan repayments to phone contracts, the government told presenters to "avoid words [or] phrases like debt" during presentations in schools across England a decade ago. More than 120 MPs and peers recently signed a letter coordinated by the campaign group Rethink Repayment calling for an "urgent review" of the system. One of the signatories, Liberal Democrat MP Tom Gordon, who is a Plan 2 borrower, is set to introduce a bill calling for a review in Parliament next week. Education Secretary Lucy Powell has previously said the interest rate on Plan 2 loans was "egregious" and the issue was at the top of her in-tray. The Student Loans Company said it was working with the government to "provide clear, relatable and trusted guidance". Have you been affected by the issues discussed in this story? title: Diljit Dosanjh makes history under the famous Wembley arch
description: Wembley Stadium billed Diljit Dosanjh as the first Punjabi singer to headline the iconic music venue.
body: On Saturday night, under the world-famous Wembley arch, five words rang out: "Punjabi Aa Gaye Wembley Oye!" Indian megastar Diljit Dosanjh famously starts all his concerts by announcing that "the Punjabis have arrived". But this time, it was a play on the usual catchphrase. Dosanjh is the first ever Punjabi singer to headline Wembley Stadium, the music venue has said. Addressing his fans, he reflected on the significance of the occasion. "This moment will go down in the history books," he said. And as Bhangra beats blared out, fans erupted with cheers while Dosanjh launched into his biggest hits, from Born to Shine to Lover. Over two decades, Dosanjh has built a huge global fanbase, topping charts and singing with the likes of Ed Sheeran. He has even busted Bhangra moves with Jimmy Fallon, external, with the US talk show host labelling him "the biggest Punjabi artist on the planet". His landmark concert at Wembley further cements his status as a global star. Ahead of the show, the singer spoke exclusively to the BBC backstage, describing the moment as "a dream" for him. This video can not be played The first Punjabi artist ever to headline Wembley Stadium In London, Dosanjh's crowd was largely - but not entirely - South Asian. The hype for his appearance was building all afternoon, with fans arriving early to get in place. "MJ [Michael Jackson] and Madonna, he's that level for us," said one fan. "He's so good looking, and so down to earth," said another. "Diljit. I love you more than my husband," declared a third. When he came on the stage shortly after 8pm, dressed in traditional attire, the stadium erupted and the screams barely stopped for the next two-and-a-bit hours. His soulful voice echoed around the stadium, demonstrating his range, as he blended homegrown Punjabi music with rap and hip-hop. Throughout the show, the audience waved lights, sang along and - of course - danced. At times, the standing area closest to the stage resembled an Indian wedding, with fans copying Dosanjh's energetic moves. But despite performing in such a vast venue, Dosanjh proved again his ability to connect on a personal level with fans. He brought fans on stage, giving them gifts and taking selfies, and also shouted out those in the back rows of the 90,000-seater stadium, saying they were "full of heart". There was also exciting news for fans in India, as he announced he would be performing in November at the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad. The concert was capped off with the emotion of the night - his track Main Hoon Punjab, which means "I am Punjab" - set to a spectacular firework display. "What an incredible show, the energy and vibe was unparalleled!" concert goers Amit and Rani told the BBC. They added that it was not only a privilege "but a moment to celebrate for Punjabi culture". Diljit Dosanjh performed under the famous Wembley arch From humble beginnings as a small village boy from Punjab, he made history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi-language singer to perform at the US music festival Coachella. He also famously made his Met Gala debut decked in majestic Punjabi attire. His meteoric rise has seen him perform across America and Europe, and collaborate with pop stars from Sia to Sheeran. His authenticity is a big part of his appeal. He remains true to his Punjabi roots, wears his turban as a sign of pride, and sings in his mother tongue. Away from music, Dosanjh is also a popular Bollywood actor - and a social media sensation. Even those who haven't heard his music have probably viewed his funny Instagram videos - such as him arguing with an Amazon Alexa device, external that couldn't understand his accent. From Coachella to Fallon: Decoding Diljit Dosanjh's stardom Now, he's performed on a stage that's previously been home to titans of music from Taylor Swift to Coldplay. For Dosanjh and his millions of global fans, it means Punjabi music, Punjabi culture and Punjabi vibrancy has reached an historic moment. Speaking to the BBC before his gig, he said he felt "thankful" to be here. "When we were going to book this venue, everyone said, 'Think again before you book, it's a big stadium'," he said. "I said: 'We'll see whatever comes. I want that our people are happy and can say yes, we can do this too!'" He reflected on the many artists who had performed there before him, adding that to follow their footsteps "means a lot, a lot". "It may not mean as much for someone like Harry Styles, as much as it means for us. He has performed on such stages, but for us, it's very special. Coming from a village to here - it's very special." "I feel good. I feel happy. And I feel good for my people. I feel good for the next generation," he said. And of course, there was only one way he could end. "We are here. Punjabi Aa Gaye Oye!" title: Fire at nursing home in Chile kills 16 residents
description: Ten people were evacuated from the home in Araucanía region in central Chile.
body: At least 16 elderly residents have died in a fire at a nursing home in Chile, according to authorities. Ten others were evacuated after a blaze broke out at El Edén home in Pitrufquén, around 640km (400 miles) south of the capital Santiago, on Friday evening. Jorge Granada, a prosecutor leading the case, said it was not clear at this stage what caused the incident. Chile's President José Antonio Kast said he had ordered a review into the condition of nursing homes across the country. "We will fully collaborate with the justice system to clarify what happened, determine where failures may have existed in oversight or prevention, identify what alerts were raised and what actions were taken in response to them," Kast said. "We need to know the truth and, based on that, correct whatever is necessary to do everything possible to prevent a tragedy like this from happening again," thre president added. The fire, which began at around 22:30 (01:30 GMT) was finally put out on Saturday morning. On Saturday, firefighters were still clearing debris and removing collapsed corrugated metal roofing. Police cordoned off the area for safety. "It is a situation that fills our souls with great sorrow and pain. We have been... providing support to the families," said local mayor Jacqueline Romero. title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donations
description: As Reform slip back in the polls, Labour and the Conservatives rediscover a familiar political divide, writes Laura Kuenssberg.
body: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donations Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer. Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donations putting it back in the headlines today. For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that initial £36m gift to Nigel Farage's party alone is like something from a different political universe. "It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me. That was even before another Reform donor pledged to match that astonishing sum with another £36m, saying the first donation had provoked his "competitive spirit". But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values". A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way. The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence. One senior conservative said: "It was a real line in the sand, we could never have imagined Sir Keir Starmer saying that." The party seems cock-a-hoop at a line they can use again and again, asserting the prime minister cares more about welfare than guarding against war. But there is a positive atmosphere in No 10 too, one source telling me that the face-offs between Badenoch and Burnham have "breathed new life into the Labour versus Tory dynamic". How can they both be happy, when ultimately politics is a contest and there can only be one winner in the end? Well, on the security spat, Burnham's backers are adamant he does want to cut welfare spending, and find more money for defence. How does that stack up with his words this week? I'm told No 10 will explain in more detail his belief that security also means secure communities, which aren't created by slashing benefits. Crucially, they reckon while cutting welfare might appeal to some voters, "once you dig into the 'who' and the 'how' of doing that, public support wavers, and when Kemi talks about housing benefit cuts, public opinion goes all over the shop". They even cite that moment as evidence that the prime minister is "happy to grab thorny issues and put himself at the centre of them", as he did with the early release of prisoners. He'll give a grabby-sounding view before the government has found a solution to a problem, stake part of his reputation on it, and make the case, hoping it will work out. The choices are only going to get harder and harder though. "Hope" as a slogan and a strategy could never be enough. But when politics is fundamentally a contest, how can both the traditional political tribes be buoyant? For Labour, it's not just the obvious change of leader to a more effective politician who is much more at ease talking to the public, whether that's an eight-second TikTok or his long explanations of his positions expressed in a newspaper opinion piece and posted on Facebook. It's that Burnham is making arguments that are more appealing to Labour's psychology – build council houses, take stronger action against the worst excesses of the Israeli government, stand up for those who need to rely on benefits from the state. Labour believes, for now, they have a leader who is simply a better politician, who is making arguments many of them find instinctively more appealing. The party knows what its leader believes, broadly at least. As one senior figure said: "He has a worldview which the last one didn't - he's clear what he wants and he's grabbed the reins of power." Another who has worked under Starmer and now Burnham said: "It's just chalk and cheese." And don't underestimate the importance of keeping backbenchers content, feeling understood. A government source joked the whips, the party managers, are becoming a bit "like an HR department" listening to concerns rather than driving the troops forward. But as Starmer found to his cost, backbenchers weren't prepared to be loyal to him when many felt he hadn't shown much care or loyalty to them. But Badenoch's tribe also seems more chipper because, as she has told friends, there is now a sharper ideological divide between the two parties saying, "it's much clearer to have those arguments rather than a process discussion with Starmer". Shadow ministers reckon it's easier to make classic Conservative arguments because in the words of one, "Andy Burnham is a classic old leftie and we're the obvious answer to that". Shock, horror, Labour sources I put that to dispute that is the case, one close ally calling him "a pragmatist", another denying he's further to the left than Starmer, because, "Keir was so hard to place". But one conservative source also pointedly wonders how long Labour's happiness with their new leader will last, given Burnham's rapid return to Parliament saying, "looking at the benches opposite there is a vision of somebody who has turned up to a Tinder date and doesn't quite look like his profile pic". title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
description: The proposed law sought to introduce one of the biggest societal changes in recent years.
body: This video can not be played Watch: MPs share personal stories in assisted dying debate MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end. Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270 - a majority of 16 - against the proposed legislation. The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards. A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short term. The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session. Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years had it been approved. MPs were given a free vote, meaning they were not required to vote along party lines. Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel. But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority. Please upgrade your browser to view this interactive Enter your full postcode or the name or constituency of your MP Note: a small number of postcodes do not give an accurate constituency for all properties. There were emotional scenes outside Parliament from both sides after MPs voted against giving the bill a second reading. Dame Esther Rantzen, who was unable to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC that it was "so sad that people in this country won't have the choice" that terminally ill adults in other countries have. The Childline founder said: "I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it's a tragic day." The broadcaster, 86, is terminally ill with cancer and has said she was now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic. Opponents of the assisted dying bill react after MPs voted against it Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, said: "Parliament has dropped the ball today. "It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand." Labour peer and former Home Secretary Lord Blunkett told BBC Newsnight that it was a "bad day for democracy". The issue was "clearly not going away" and would re-emerge "in a year or two's time", he added. This video can not be played Watch: A 'bad day for democracy', says Labour peer Those in favour of a change in the law have said they will try to bring forward legislation again, with Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original bill, telling the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year. Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Dame Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, who all opposed the "unsafe and unworkable" bill, welcomed the MPs' decision. They said in a joint statement: "This is not a moment for celebration, we understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law. "But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill." They said there was a need to "fix our NHS and sort out social and palliative care before we even consider introducing assisted dying". Sarah Wootton, chief executive of Dignity in Dying, said "thousands of terminally ill people will continue to suffer against their wishes in their last days and weeks". She added that she still believed law change was "inevitable". Care Not Killing chief executive Gordon Macdonald described the vote as "decisive". He said: "Our hope is that MPs now focus on repairing palliative care in the UK and securing the necessary funding to make sure that no matter what part of the country you live in, you can access the best possible care available and are treated with dignity and respect." Supporters of assisted dying react in Parliament Square following the vote in the Commons The bill in the last parliamentary session brought by Leadbeater cleared Commons with a majority of 23. But it ran out of time to progress through all the necessary stages in Parliament after some peers in the House of Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments. During the debate, Labour MP Janet Daby was among those to confirm she would vote against the bill despite previously supporting it. She told the Commons she had "nightmares about dying and death" after voting in favour of the last bill, adding: "I had to wrestle with myself, knowing that I was not entirely comfortable with the decision I had made and my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill." In another of the personal testimonies during the debate, Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove spoke about her mother's decision to bring her late-stage terminal illness to an end "on her terms". The MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke said the "harmful status quo" meant her mother had died alone in October of last year, after living with a rare blood cancer for half her life. Hazelgrove argued that "not all pain can be palliated". Conservative MP Martin Vickers said his "firm" view was that "if assisted dying is legalised we will be poorer as a society, we will have a crossed a line", adding it would also change the "relationship between doctor and patient". title: I never got to experience my baby's scan, but blind parents like me can now feel them
description: Tactile 3D models created from pregnancy scans are just one innovation to support blind parents-to-be.
body: When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the heartbeat. But now, parents like me can receive tactile 3D models created from their scans, allowing them to have a special moment with their unborn baby. Reece Finnegan-Knight, who has been blind since his teens, is one of the first people to experience a 3D-printed model of his baby's scan with his wife, Sophy, as part of a new pilot scheme. At their routine 12-week scan, Sophy had attempted to describe what she was seeing for Reece, but he struggled to feel involved in the moment. Afterwards, when the couple showed the sonogram to their loved ones, Reece said it felt like "friends and family knew more about my baby than I did". But he said the 20-week scan was more positive. "The sonographer described everything to me, and explained why what she was seeing meant that everything looked good," he says. Reece says he wants to be able to fully support his wife Sophy as her due date approaches They also now have the model of their 20-week scan picture, through the scheme by the charity Guide Dogs. "I can't stop feeling it to be honest," Reece says. "It's so nice to be able to fully access something without the need for other people's descriptions or interpretations. It has enough detail that I know what things are and it just makes everything feel more real." It's an innovation which has made me reflect on my own experiences of pregnancy and parenting. Before my partially sighted husband and I started trying for kids, I researched absolutely everything it would entail, from how to use specialist apps to read pregnancy test results, to the bells and squeaky shoes I could use to keep tabs on a fast-moving toddler. I immediately discovered a community of people in my position ready to share their wisdom, and a host of tried and tested workarounds for almost every scenario. But a decade on, there are even more advances, and I've spoken to other blind parents to find out the best ways they tackle the challenges they face. This video can not be played The 3D scans giving blind parents-to-be a new way to meet their baby For Kim and Sean Randall, who have a teenager and an 11-month-old, the progress of technology is one of the biggest changes they have noticed in the 15 years between the births of their children. For their youngest child, maternity notes came in an app which could be accessed with a screen reader on their phone, rather than being handwritten in the traditional NHS blue book. Kim says it put her on more of an equal footing with other expectant parents, and helped her feel more in control. "I could check the notes, and any test results, when I wanted rather than waiting to have them read to me," she says. For the 20-week scan, she says Sean had researched the meaning of the different numbers on an ultrasound - like the baby's thigh length or head circumference - and used a specialist AI screen-reading app to have the text read out and the images described. Some parents say they prefer this method to a 3D model, because they can get more detail from audio description of the image than from physical touch. Parents Kim and Sean Randall found that much had changed in the 15 years between the births of their two children But it's not just scans where visually impaired parents can struggle. Reece, like many blind parents, says he wants to be extra prepared for when the baby comes, "so I don't get in the way or feel like a liability". "We've been labelling clothes, putting Braille in baby books and organising the baby bag so that I know where everything is," he says. Kim, meanwhile, runs Facebook and WhatsApp groups for blind mums. Together, we have collated a host of tips and tricks from blind parents over the years for what to do when the baby arrives. Carry your own folding mat for nappy changes and always have everything you need close at hand When changing a nappy, if you think you can stop, "keep wiping" - and use barrier cream, because the start of a nappy rash can be hard to feel Score a raised mark on any syringes or scoops you might use for making up feeds so you know where to fill them to Use a baby carrier or pram which can be pulled as well as pushed, in case you walk with a guide dog or cane in front of you to get around Once they start toddling, bells clipped to clothing are a handy way of knowing where they are at home When weaning, use a wipeable high chair with a waterproof mat underneath, to keep mess contained and know what they've eaten and what's gone on the floor The Royal National Institute of Blind People , external(RNIB) has also produced guides for expectant parents and those with young children. They suggest ideas like using baby gates to block off the kitchen when you are removing something from the oven, or the hall when you are answering the door. For parents who have some but not total visual impairment, Kim says children can be dressed in brightly coloured clothing while out and about so they are easier to spot. "I put them in feelable clothes so I don't grab the wrong child," says Kim, who has no vision. "One of my favourites is a shirt with a castle on it. You open the door and there's a dragon inside." When her eldest started walking, she says "we always held hands, but had a wrist strap connecting us in case she tried to run off". For me, clothes pegs were always useful for keeping outfits together wherever possible. Also consider buying socks the same style and colour - matching those is still a nightmare for me a decade later. If two items feel the same but are different colours, cut the label on one of them. Me with my youngest several years ago - I had researched everything that being a mum could entail Parents Reece and Sophy are just at the start of their journey, but are making sure they are fully prepared for what lies ahead. title: We've followed their lives for six decades - now the stars of 7 Up are bowing out
description: 70 Up is the final instalment in a series which began in 1964 and has followed the lives of 14 people.
body: 70 Up stars from left to right: Peter Davies, Symon Basterfield, Paul Kligerman, Tony Walker, Neil Hughes, John Brisby, Andrew Brackfield, Bruce Balden, Jackie Bassett, Suzy Lusk, Sue Davis Six decades have passed since Jackie Bassett first appeared on TV aged seven, skipping down the road with her little sister. It was 1964 and she had been selected by teachers at her east London primary school to appear in a documentary called 7 Up. The show interviewed 14 seven-year-olds from vastly different socioeconomic backgrounds. Inspired by the Jesuit saying: "Give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man", it was intended as a one-off - a snapshot of Britain's class system and how it shapes us from a young age. "They only picked me because I never stopped talking," Jackie told the BBC, with an infectious giggle that hasn't changed since childhood. Little did she know then, but Jackie was being filmed for a show that would go on to be the longest-running documentary series ever made. In 2024, it was voted the most influential TV show of the past 50 years. Now the curtain is falling, with the final instalment - 70 Up - airing on ITV this Tuesday. "We didn't really know what we were doing, we had no idea what was happening," Jackie said of the day the Granada TV crew turned up at her school. In the first episode, Jackie appeared alongside her friends, Lynn and Sue, as they were asked questions about boys at school and their hopes for the future. Jackie said she would like to marry a boy "that's not got a lot of money, but has got some money". The nation was also introduced to the likes of wide-eyed Neil, who explained his plans to become either an astronaut or a coach driver; anxious Paul, who ruminated on the idea of one day marrying a woman who made him eat his greens; and pensive Bruce, who said his "heart's desire is to see my daddy who is 6,000 miles away" in Rhodesia. In 7 Up, friends Jackie Bassett, Lynn Johnson and Sue Davis were asked questions about boys and their hopes for the future 7 Up was intended to be a one-off snapshot of the class system in Britain The first episode was directed by Canadian Paul Almond, with the help of a young researcher named Michael Apted, who was involved in selecting the children. Apted then decided to follow up on the children seven years later. "The material was dreadful – as teenagers, they wouldn't say anything," he later said of the second episode, 7 Plus Seven. "Yet we started to realise the power of the idea; despite the film not being very good, everyone was interested in it." Apted went on to become a big name in Hollywood, directing blockbusters including James Bond's The World Is Not Enough, but he always returned to the show and said it was his most significant achievement. Every seven years, millions would tune in for updates on the cast's lives. Neil's dreamy outlook on the world as a child descended into battles with depression, isolation and homelessness, only to turn up as a Liberal Democrat councillor at 42 and then a lay preacher seven years later. Jackie initially said she did not want children, but by 42 Up was an adoring mother to three boys. Neil Hughes had battles with depression and homelessness but went on to be a Liberal Democrat councillor and a lay preacher As the series grew in popularity, Apted started receiving push-back from some of the participants, who felt they had been typecast based on their backgrounds. At 21, Apted asked Jackie - who had recently got married - whether she had met "enough men" before she decided to marry. For the rest of the interview, she mostly looked to the floor while Sue and Lynn answered questions. It took her 28 years to fully confront Apted over his questioning. In 49 Up, she told him: "I was really angry… you wouldn't have asked some of the other people in this programme that question. You will edit this programme as you see fit, I've got no control over that." Recalling the tense exchange, Jackie said she felt Apted could be out of touch, particularly over the changing roles of women in society. "I think he still thought we were all in the kitchen, as I mentioned to him at 21. I just thought, 'No, come on, it's about time one of us called you out on it, because he never never asked us questions about politics. It was nearly always domestic," she said. Jackie, Lynn and Sue filming 28 Up... ... and filming 35 Up with director Michael Apted on the left Jackie was not the only cast member to clash with Apted. John Brisby, who became a leading barrister, declared in 35 Up that the show felt like a "little pill of poison" injected into his veins every seven years and he wished his headmaster had never put him up for the show. He appeared in later series but refused to be interviewed by Apted. And Charles Furneaux, who later worked at the BBC before becoming commissioning editor at Channel 4, refused to appear after 21 Up following an off-camera argument in which Apted later admitted he went "berserk". Apted acknowledged flaws with the show, saying it was a "horrible error" to have only four women in a cast of 14 when making the original selection. Michael Apted became a Hollywood director, but always returned to the show Five years ago, Apted passed away, aged 79. The effect he had on the cast is clear in the final episode. Despite their differences, Jackie maintains deep affection and respect for the man she said "opened up a world to me that I would never have known". "I've always said it's a bit like having an uncle in the family. Sometimes you love him and cuddle him to death, and other times you think: I wish he'd just go away. "He would always, always help anybody and anything." Nick Hitchon died from cancer in 2023, becoming the second member of the cast to pass away after Lynn Johnson 10 years earlier. title: Running costs of vaccine damage scheme more than double amount paid to victims
description: The cost of administration and medical checks has now topped £83m, according to new figures.
body: More than 24,000 Covid vaccine-harm claims have been made - most relating to the AstraZeneca jab The government scheme to support people injured by Covid vaccines and other jabs has cost £83m to run since April 2022, new figures have revealed. The amount spent on administration costs and medical assessments is more than double the £32m paid out in financial support to victims so far. The Taxpayers' Alliance think tank said the public would be "stunned" at the cost and called for the government to urgently review the scheme. NHSBSA which runs the scheme for the government says rising numbers of claims are behind the increasing administrative and medical assessor supplier costs. Firm assessing Covid vaccine harm replaced after costs spiral to £48m Families failed by Covid jabs tell inquiry of pain The latest data, external shows there have been 24,260 claims since November 2021, although just 264 have been successful. The Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS) was set up in 1979 to provide financial support to people who, in rare cases, had been harmed by vaccines of any type. Since the pandemic the number applying for damage payments has increased sharply. The vast majority of applications are now linked to the AstraZeneca vaccine and other Covid jabs. The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But for those who were harmed, the resulting injuries are devastating. The full costs of the VDPS have now been revealed, external for the first time in the answer to a parliamentary question from the backbench Conservative MP Sir Christopher Chope. In response, health minister Dame Diana Johnson said a total of £83m had been spent on staffing costs, administration and medical reviews between April 2022 and March 2026. Under the scheme, claimants must have their application reviewed by an independent doctor, to check whether they have met the threshold of "severe disablement". If approved, they can then receive a one-off, tax-free payment of £120,000. The process can take months or even years. The costs of those medical assessments have increased from £4.3m in 2022/23 to £19.3m in 2025/26, according to new data published by the government. Based on the latest available data up to June 2026, the total amount paid out in damages to those who died or were injured after being given a Covid vaccine has risen to £31.6m. "The administrative costs and medical assessor supplier costs of the VDPS are driven by the number of claims received," said the NHSBSA, which runs the scheme on behalf of the government. "We have seen a significant increase in the number of claims received since taking over administration of the VDPS in November 2021." The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose. "It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine. Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme. Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered. The government is due to respond to her recommendations. The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments. The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed". "When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell. He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help." The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly". "In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said. NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS". title: An extraordinary result - why did MPs reject assisted dying bill this time?
description: Although supporters say they will try again, for now the momentum has fallen away from a change in the law.
body: There were gasps and – to the intense irritation of supporters – cheers from opponents of assisted dying when the vote was read out in the Commons. This was an extraordinary result. After twice voting in favour of the bill, MPs have rejected proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing to an end the latest effort to change the law. The debate itself was tetchier, more irritable than when Kim Leadbeater introduced a similar bill in 2024. Then it was the first time MPs had voted on assisted dying in nine years. Since then the Commons has voted on this issue three times and had hours of debate. The sombre, respectful tone from 2024 has become more embittered. Given the strength of feeling on both sides over such an emotive issue, perhaps that is unsurprising. But on a deeply divided issue, both sides agree on why the result was different. "We always said it would come to turnout and it did," one supporter of the bill text me. An opponent messaged to say the same. The numbers tell a story. Last time MPs voted on assisted dying in June, 315 were in favour and 291 against. Today, the numbers opposed were similar: 286. But support for this bill has ebbed away. Just 270 voted for this bill, a fall of 45. So why have fewer MPs backed it, compared to a year ago? There are a number of reasons why support for assisted dying has dropped off. Some MPs have changed their mind. Janet Daby, the Labour MP for Lewisham East, for example told the Commons that after she previously backed the bill "my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill." But in reality those switching their position are a small minority. For others, the influence of Andy Burnham may have been a factor. When MPs last gave their collective view on assisted dying, Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister and supportive of this bill. Burnham, however, is not. For Labour MPs wanting to follow Downing Street's priorities, abstaining might have seemed a more appealing option. There will be other reasons why supportive MPs did not turn up today. A wedding, I'm told, took some away from Westminster. A trip to Ukraine meant others missed the vote. Already those in favour of a change in the law promise to try again. Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original legislation last year, has told the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year. Supporters have told me they see this parliament, with such a large proportion of Labour MPs who tend to support assisted dying, as a "unique moment" to pass this change. "This result doesn't mean there isn't still a majority in parliament in favour of the principle of assisted dying," said one of those behind the bill. But for now the momentum has fallen away from a change in the law. That is a relief to those who worry such a change would risk harming vulnerable people. But it is a bitter disappointment to those who see it as a necessary and compassionate alternative to the status quo. That bitterness from supporters is aimed in part at the House of Lords. It was opponents' efforts there that ultimately led to this defeat. And it could hasten those calling for reform of Parliament's second chamber. title: Police boss criticised for 127-date theatre tour
description: Colin Sutton says it will not impinge on his police and crime commissioner work.
body: Colin Sutton was elected as Norfolk's Police and Crime Commissioner two months ago A newly elected £79,000-a-year police commissioner is facing criticism for announcing a 127-date national theatre tour. Opposition parties have questioned how Reform UK's Colin Sutton will be able to focus on his job overseeing Norfolk Police, which he was elected to in July. The former detective is due to present his true-crime show in theatres across the UK next year discussing police investigations, with tickets priced at around £40. Sutton insisted the tour "wouldn't impinge" on his day job, but Labour MP Ben Goldsborough warned "you can't police a county from the back of a tour bus". Labour MP Ben Goldsborough was surprised to learn of the commissioner's tour plan Sutton became one of the UK's most high-profile detectives in the 2000s, leading the investigation to catch serial killer Levi Bellfield, who murdered Milly Dowler, Marsha McDonnell and Amelie Delagrange. After retiring from the Metropolitan Police, Sutton wrote a book about the case, which was later turned into an ITV drama. He has also become a regular commentator in the media and last year was named as Reform's national policing and crime advisor. In July, after the former Norfolk Police and Crime Commissioner (PCC) Sarah Taylor resigned, Sutton comfortably won the election to replace her. PCCs are elected officials who set the priorities of a police force, appoint a chief constable and hold them to account. This week, promoters of Sutton's "Makings of a Murderer" show announced he was set to tour the country from January to November next year. One stretch will see him visit Consett in County Durham, Tamworth in Staffordshire, Hunstanton in Norfolk, Llandudno in north Wales and Leeds over five consecutive nights. A drive from venue to venue in that run would cover almost 700 miles (1,126km). Plan for drone-busting missile motor factory lodged New £38m jail wing adds 10 cells - not promised 170 Hosepipe ban could last until winter, firm says Promoters of Colin Sutton's show say it will offer "an unforgettable evening of real-life detective work" South Norfolk MP Goldsborough criticised Sutton's decision and said: "If Colin Sutton wants to be a celebrity that's his choice, but Norfolk deserves a police and crime commissioner whose first priority is Norfolk." Matthew Taylor, a Conservative county councillor who finished second in the PCC election, said he was "shocked" to learn of the former detective's plans for a long run in theatres. "If there is a major incident, you would expect the police and crime commissioner to be there, front and centre," he said. "Not operationally, that's down to the chief constable, but in terms of lending his support, communicating with the public, being active and visible." Defending his decision, Sutton said "I spoke to the people around me and we decided that it wouldn't impinge". He continued: "The logistics of each evening are that I turn up at about 7pm, I go on stage at 7.30pm and I'm clear by 10pm. "I don't do any rehearsal… I just literally turn up, talk and go away again. "The time I'm actually incommunicado is really reduced to the two-hour slots when I'm actually on stage talking. "I'm not a blue light service where I go round and turn up at things." Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below. title: Assisted dying: How laws differ around the world
description: About 400 million people have access to some form of assisted dying - what are the policies of other countries?
body: Around 400 million people now live in countries which have legalised assisted dying. Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Spain and Austria have all introduced assisted dying laws since 2015 – when UK MPs last voted on the issue – some allowing assisted death for those who are not terminally ill. Just last month, France adopted an 'aid in dying' law for adults with incurable conditions causing them unbearable pain. While most jurisdictions forbid medical help to die, assisted dying laws around the world vary. Across the US, assisted dying - which some critics prefer to call assisted suicide - is legal in 30 out of 50 states, as well as in Washington DC. Oregon was one of the first places in the world to offer help to die for some patients, in 1997, and so has nearly 30 years' experience. It has become the model on which other US assisted dying laws have been framed. In Oregon, assisted dying is open to terminally ill, external, mentally competent adults expected to die within six months - and must be signed off by two doctors. Since 1997, external, 5,520 people have received a prescription for a lethal dose of medication - with 3,691 deaths. In a 2025 report, external, 61% of patients who ask for help to die had cancer, 14% had a neurological condition like motor neurone disease and 11% had heart disease. Of the 400 patients who took a lethal dose of medication last year, the vast majority (89%) said loss of autonomy was a key concern, while others cited: Losing control of bodily functions (47%) Concern about being a burden on family and friends (43%) Financial implications of treatment (4%) In Oregon, as in other US states that permit assisted dying, the lethal medication must be self-administered - the same is proposed in England and Wales. Around one in three of those prescribed a lethal dose don’t go ahead with it. Oregon is important for supporters of assisted dying in England and Wales as they point out it has remained restricted to terminally ill adults since its introduction. However, opponents say some of the rules have been relaxed. A residency requirement has been lifted, which means it is open to people from outside the state. The number of assisted deaths has also risen substantially over the years. Canada is the country often cited by opponents of assisted dying as an example of the so-called "slippery slope" - a place where assisted dying has been extended and made available to more people since it was first brought in. Medical assistance in dying (Maid), external was introduced in 2016, initially just for the terminally ill. This was amended in 2021 and extended to those experiencing "unbearable suffering" from an irreversible illness or disability. It had been due to be extended to people with a mental illness but that is now on hold. Critics say the more the law is widened, the more disabled and vulnerable people will be put at risk. There has also been a dramatic growth in the number of people using Maid. Roughly one in every 20 deaths in Canada are now medically assisted, external, compared to about one in 100 in Oregon. Across Europe, six countries have some form of legalised assisted dying: Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain, Austria and - most recently - France. In all of them - unlike the proposals in England and Wales - help to die is not restricted to the terminally ill. Switzerland was the first country in the world to create a “right to die” when it made assisted suicide legal in 1942. It is one of the few countries which allows foreigners access to help to die via organisations like Dignitas, in Zurich. More than 600 Britons have died at Dignitas, external in the past two decades, including 43 last year. The lethal medication must be self-administered. The Netherlands and Belgium both legalised assisted dying more than 20 years ago for patients experiencing unbearable suffering from an incurable illness, including mental health issues. It has since been extended to children - the only European countries to allow this. Both allow euthanasia - or physician-assisted dying. Most recently, Spain and Austria have legalised assisted dying for both terminal illness and intolerable suffering. In Austria, the drugs must be self-administered, whereas in Spain a medical professional can administer them. In England, Wales and Scotland, parliament has so far rejected assisted dying proposals. But assisted dying has already been legalised in one part of the British Isles. In July, Royal Assent was given to a bill in Jersey. Unlike at Westminster and Holyrood, the legislation was introduced by the Jersey government, which says it will take about 18 months to set up the service. The first assisted death could happen late next year. There will be a residency requirement of one year, in a bid to prevent so-called 'death tourism'. The measure, which most sets apart the Jersey legislation from the rest of the British Isles, concerns the manner in which those eligible for an assisted death can end their lives. Individuals will be able to choose to have a doctor administer a lethal dose intravenously, as happens in Spain, Canada, New Zealand and most of Australia. This is, in effect, voluntary euthanasia. It has become the preferred method of assisted dying in jurisdictions which allow this choice. The laws proposed at Westminster, Holyrood and Tynwald - Isle of Man - all state that death must be by self-administration, which usually means the individual swallowing a lethal dose. The Isle of Man assisted dying bill was passed by Tynwald (the Manx parliament) in March last year. As a UK Crown Dependency - like Jersey - it could not become law until granted Royal Assent. This was declined earlier this year by the UK Ministry of Justice, but Tynwald has since passed an updated bill which has been sent back to the UK government for a second time. title: 'Game-changing' suicide prevention charity expands
description: The charity provides safe spaces for men to talk about their emotions without being judged.
body: This video can not be played A national men's mental health and suicide prevention charity marking its 10-year anniversary is expanding further in Devon. Andy's Man Club, founded in 2016 in Halifax, West Yorkshire, was named after Andy Roberts, who took his own life at the age of 23, and describes itself as a safe space where men can talk about their emotions without being judged. After opening its first Devon club in Newton Abbot in 2018, there are now 14 clubs in the county. On Monday, the charity is launching a new club in Ivybridge. Roger Bond, from Plymouth, who went to his first session when he was "in a very dark place" about three years ago, said he had "never looked back". 'Game-changing' suicide prevention charity expands. title: Polanski selected as Green Party candidate for Starmer's former seat
description: The Green Party leader said the party is the "underdog" in Holborn and St Pancras but "can win".
body: Green Party leader Zack Polanski has been selected as the party's candidate in the by-election for Sir Keir Starmer's former seat in Parliament. Polanski, who is a London Assembly member, will stand in Holborn and St Pancras on 8 October as he seeks to become an MP. He was voted to be the party's candidate by members of the Camden Green Party ahead of local councillor Hamza Chowdhury. Polanski said the Greens "might be the underdog in this election but we have the momentum and we can win". He also spoke of how he made Camden "my home" when he first moved to London 20 years ago, adding he has "lived and worked across Holborn and St Pancras for many of the years since". Polanski said: "I love this place but I also know times are tough here in Holborn and St Pancras. My story of constantly moving around flats is such a common story for Londoners and I know so many people are struggling right now." He argued that voting Green "sends a clear signal" to the council and government that "we demand better for our communities". Polanski added he is "confident but not complacent" about his chances. He also said the election is about "putting pressure" on Prime Minister Andy Burnham, noting a Green MP would "work with him constructively to challenge him on the gaps in his plans". Announcing the result, Green MP Hannah Spencer said members had "overwhelmingly" chosen Polanski. The Greens finished second to Labour at the elections for Camden Council earlier this year. The by-election is an early test of Burnham's popularity with the public and whether Labour under his leadership is able to fend off the challenge from the Greens in inner-city constituencies. For Polanski, it will be a test on whether he can provide evidence that he can deliver on his ambition for the Greens to "replace" Labour. Labour has held the inner London seat since it was created in 1983 and the party's candidate for the by-election is Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali. The seat became vacant after former Prime Minister Sir Keir announced he was standing down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs. Who are the candidates in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election? title: Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out
description: As the prime minister looks ahead to autumn, Labour figures are asking whether his government represents continuity or change.
body: At the start of summer, in the pillared room in 10 Downing Street, Andy Burnham looked out at his new special advisers, the few dozen political officials tasked with driving hundreds of thousands of civil servants to deliver his government's agenda. Some had been with him in Manchester or Makerfield. Others had spent the past few months trying everything to prevent his hostile takeover of Sir Keir Starmer's government - and the new prime minister showed he was aware of it, going out of his way to praise those who had stayed on, for their efforts in the preceding years. At that meeting, Burnham's team mapped out four key moments in the coming months. First, the return to Parliament in September, when Burnham and other leading ministers would make their first statements to MPs. Second, Labour's annual conference at the end of September - Burnham's first as leader. Third, the Budget, taking place on 28 October. And fourth, the 10-year plan for Britain which Burnham intends to unveil in November. As MPs prepare to leave Parliament on Tuesday for almost a month and party conference season gets underway, the first phase of that route map is almost complete - enough for figures at all levels of the Labour Party to begin answering some questions about the shape of this new government. Most importantly, perhaps, how new actually is it? Does Burnham represent continuity or change? That question is especially relevant because those Labour MPs who pushed for Sir Keir to be replaced always fell into two broad camps: those who wanted a change of style and emphasis but continuity in policy, and those who wanted a major shift in policy. Both groups saw what they wanted in Burnham. Andy Burnham speaks during his first Cabinet meeting since becoming prime minister Going by the words of the new prime minister himself, he represents a profound break with the past, and not only the immediate past. In his first speech as Labour leader in July, Burnham described his ascendancy as "the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years". That is the timeframe he has returned to again and again, signalling not just a desire to reverse issues he believes stem from the Thatcher era but also to break with aspects of the Labour governments since then, including his immediate predecessor's. Some in government are already quietly questioning, though, whether the ambition of that rhetoric can be squared with the early signals emerging from the Treasury under the new Chancellor John Healey. Who's in Andy Burnham's cabinet? In interviews over recent weeks, and especially in his first major speech on Monday, Healey has said he will stick to Rachel Reeves's commitments not to increase the main rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT, as well as her rules on government borrowing. In the speech, he promised to "control public spending", and hailed Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline". It led to opposition parties labelling Healey a continuity chancellor. A similar critique is being voiced among some of his government colleagues. Most are more generous for now, arguing that Healey's first imperative - especially at a time of turmoil in the global bond markets - is reassurance, and that the Budget is the moment for him to show how he plans to substantiate Burnham's rhetoric. Even one official sympathetic on that point, though, asks: "Why did he do a big speech before he has something to say?" Those close to Healey argue that his emphasis this week on securing the economic growth which has eluded successive governments by spreading wealth around the country is a clear difference from Reeves. And finding ways to boost regional growth has been one of Healey's major causes since he was a junior minister at the Treasury more than 20 years ago - long before it was at the heart of Burnham's political personality. There is no question, though, that this week the minister who most starkly signalled change from the previous government was a man who coveted Healey's job - Ed Miliband, who was instead appointed foreign secretary. In announcing new sanctions on Israel over illegal settlements in the West Bank, Miliband explicitly cast the policy as a break from Sir Keir's approach, telling MPs: "We should have acted earlier, and it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation." On the other hand, acting alongside Canada and France in announcing the sanctions represented - in form if not substance - continuity with the previous government, the three countries having moved together to recognise the state of Palestine a year ago. The sanctions announcement was received with near-universal warmth from Labour MPs, itself a marker of change from the Starmer government. It was also seen as a sign of the ability of Miliband in particular, but this government in general, to drive its agenda through the civil service machine. "There is a much clearer sense now from No 10 of what they want," one official who worked under Sir Keir as well as Burnham says. "Before there was a bit too much of 'let us know your ideas for what we should do', now it's 'this is what the PM wants, give us options to deliver it'." That is a culture shift which Burnham sought to drill into his cabinet at their weekly meeting on Tuesday, still only their third such meeting. According to one present, the prime minister said: "We need to be on the front foot. We need to be bolder. Let's get on and do things. It's about deeds not words." Burnham has called for "growth in every postcode", and the establishment of No 10 North is a key part of that agenda Perhaps the most significant way in which Burnham is trying to make boldness easier for his ministers is by encouraging them to press ahead with policies when there is a risk they will face a serious legal challenge. title: Rayner defends pause to local council overhaul
description: The cabinet minister tells the BBC she wanted to ensure the plans could survive potential legal actions.
body: Angela Rayner has defended her decision to pause plans to redraw local council boundaries, saying she wanted to ensure they would survive legal challenge. The local government secretary also told the BBC she wanted to be "clear-eyed" about what the planned shake-up in 16 areas of England was likely to achieve. It comes after earlier this week she abandoned proposals in four other areas, in the face of legal threats from Reform and Conservative-led authorities. The surprise announcement on Monday has thrown the reorganisation plans into doubt, and drawn criticism from local leaders preparing for the changes. Councils in affected areas have been drawing up proposals and consulting with residents since the reorganisation was announced in late 2024, in a process that is already thought to have cost millions of pounds. Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Rayner conceded the decision to press pause had been "difficult" and she understood local authorities had put a "lot of time and effort" into their plans. But she added she wanted to have "all the information" about the proposals before going ahead with them, after her reappointment to her cabinet role under Andy Burnham, ten months after her resignation last year. "I got the legal advice and I hadn't had the time to review and to go through all of that, and court cases were looming," she told the podcast. "If I'm making a decision that is highly likely to be in legal challenge, I want to make sure I've dotted my i's and crossed my t's," she added. Rayner also said she wanted was "really clear-eyed on where we were going" with the plans, after Burnham had asked her to look again at the blueprints, which were announced by her predecessor Steve Reed. Political Thinking with Nick Robinson Plans for major overhaul of councils halted Council to take government to court over reforms In her announcement on Monday, Rayner said she was withdrawing plans to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk. Those proposals, announced in March, were already subject to legal challenges from Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk, and the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire, which were lodged over the summer. She also said she wanted to review plans for 16 other areas, including 14 announced by Reed days before Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister and reappointed her to her old role. Some councils affected by those plans, including Kent and Leicestershire, had threatened similar bids to challenge the lawfulness of the decision-making process. The government has argued that the plans, which will abolish remaining two-tier areas in England where county and district councils share responsibility for services, would make local government more effective and cost efficient. However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities. Others have also complained that the reorganisation could stymie or delay parallel efforts to merge councils into regional authorities led by mayors, which Burnham has cited as a key part of his economic plans. Elsewhere in her interview, Rayner said Labour under Sir Keir should have been quicker to recognise a Palestinian state, having promised to do so as a "contribution to a renewed peace process" at the last election. Starmer took the move in September last year, having spent much of the prior year resisting pressure to do so from Labour MPs. "It's always been Labour policy to recognise a Palestinian state, and it felt like we got there too late. It was something that should have been really clear," she said. She also denied that UK sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, announced on Tuesday, had been made to help Labour ahead of the forthcoming by-election in Holborn and St Pancras in central London. Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months. Pointing to the fact that Western allies had also announced sanctions, she said: "The French and the Canadians are not going to be like 'oh well, we'll just signal something to help you with a local by-election in London'". Reflecting on her return to government, she said a "big difference" between Burnham and his predecessor in Downing Street was his inclination to tell "the story of why we're doing something" in government. She said both men shared "passion and the commitment" to deliver for Labour in office, but added: "Andy is probably more like me, in terms of [he] wears his heart on his sleeve". The interview with Angela Rayner will be broadcast on BBC2 at 12:30 BST on Friday 11 September, and 17:30 BST on Saturday 12 September. Do you have any comments or questions about this story? title: People long for simpler times, say Practical Magic reboot stars
description: Actresses Maisie Williams and Joey King feature in the upcoming sequel of the 1998 fantasy romcom.
body: Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast of the sequel to portray the daughters of Sandra Bullock's character Mix together a beloved film simmering for decades, a sprinkling of social media hype and a generous glug of star power and you just might conjure up the long-awaited sequel to Practical Magic. The 1998 fantasy romcom, starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as witchy sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, received mixed reviews from critics when it was first released. But it's put a spell on a new generation discovering it online, with some now regarding the film as a cult classic and autumn staple. The demand for a follow-up by this new wave of fans helped convince Bullock and Kidman to reprise their roles nearly 30 years on, they say. "You never get the opportunity to do something where people really are asking you, 'please do it'," says Bullock. "It's usually us going to them." Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast this time round to play Sally's daughters, Kylie and Antonia. Kissing Booth star King tells BBC Newsbeat she feels this desire for nostalgic content, which has become one of the defining forces within entertainment in recent years, has been influenced by "the world moving so fast". Practical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic "I think with technology moving at the speed that it is, we're really missing the times when we were less reachable," she says. "If we couldn't figure out something, we'd stare out the window until it came to us, and I think we're nostalgic for a time like that." She feels this can also be a strength of cinema as it can help "make memories" and "feelings" for people that they can revisit by rewatching. The upcoming release comes at a time when reboots, reunions and remakes are dominating film and TV lists. Game of Thrones star Williams agrees the drive for nostalgic content feels like a "symptom of people longing for simpler times", but says she is "very grateful" that they have made a sequel and not a remake. "I do believe in pushing the story forwards and I do believe in telling new stories," she says. "And I do believe stories can come back around and they can still be meaningful. "But I am not the biggest fan of the remake because I think it's a shame to withhold ourselves from telling a new story." The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the 1998 film and continues into the sequel Practical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic with the characters once again confronting a family curse which condemns anyone who loves and is loved by an Owens woman to death. There are also nods to the original throughout, with bubbling family tension, dark romantic "witchcore" fashion and the iconic midnight margaritas. US acting stalwarts Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing return to their roles for the follow-up, while Guardians of the Galaxy actor Lee Pace, Cobra Kai's Xolo Maridueña and House of the Dragon's Solly McLeod are new additions. Reviews so far have been mixed, with the Guardian describing it as a "nostalgia-bait return", external which is as "strange and messy as the first" but with "warm seasonal pleasures to be had". Meanwhile The Hollywood Reporter, external says the "slapdash" sequel "works better the less you look for any sense of logic, and the more you just lean into the transient joys of watching these actresses bounce off each other". Joey King says the idea of "being witchy" can be "empowering right now" Amid the scrutiny around the film, Williams admits joining the Practical Magic world was "a little bit overwhelming", but says the cast were "so supportive the whole time" and "welcomed us into the sisterhood". The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the first film and continues in the sequel, but Bullock has recalled this was initially one of the criticisms of the original, external, with some branding it as "too witchy" with "too many women". With women's rights under pressure in some countries, Williams says it is a "challenging time" and she feels it's "so important in a time like this for women to be supporting one another". "We are in a time when young women are staying in education longer and women, before having children, are sometimes being paid more than their male counterparts, which I do find to be really exciting," she adds. "But there's a lot of work to do. "And this feeling of witches, symbiosis and power - I feel like there's something in that which can just push us forwards."
