title: 'Like a hangover': Why your partner's snoring could be impacting your health
description: Sleeping next to a snorer could be having a negative effect on your health, experts tell the BBC.
body: Have you ever slept next to a snoring partner and woken up feeling stressed, unfocused or forgetful the next day? As snoring is relatively common, it is often left untreated and dismissed as a harmless irritation. But according to experts, sleeping next to a snorer could be impacting your health. Snoring is caused by the vibration of the soft tissues in our upper airways during sleep, explains Dr Clare Simon, a dentist with a special interest in dental sleep medicine. About 40% of the UK adult population snores, with the issue affecting more men than women, says the British Snoring and Sleep Apnoea Association (BSSAA). And 75% of people with a snoring partner say they have had their sleep impacted, according to a US survey by the Sleep Foundation. Here's what you need to know about the impact on partners - and what you can do about it. Prof Ama Johal, a consultant orthodontist and sleep expert at Aerox Health, explains that the partner of a snorer can become "so impacted upon that it's almost a last-ditch effort on their part to get up and go sleep in a separate room because they have to sleep". He adds: "As humans we physically can't function without that necessity." Prof Ama Johal says many couples put up with the negative effects snoring for too long During the night, we cycle through different stages of sleep in repeating patterns, usually every 90 minutes. The deeper stages of this cycle are important for physical restoration. If sleep is frequently disrupted, you may spend less time in the restorative stages, meaning you can wake up feeling tired, even if you've spent a lot of time in bed, the BSSAA explains. Your brain processes and stores information from the day during sleep. Fragmented sleep - which can happen if you're waking up due to a snoring partner - can interrupt this process, impacting your focus and memory. Disrupted sleep can also impact hormone regulation, which affects your energy levels and motivation. Sleep also plays a role in regulating the brain systems involved in stress and emotional response. When it is disrupted, these systems can become less balanced, which may make you feel more irritable and less able to cope with stress. This is something Meg Warren, 29, experienced when her former partner's snoring would keep her up. She says: "Without fail, after a snoring-induced wake up I would feel on incredibly high alert." Meg, a charity media officer, would prod him throughout the night and try to coax him from his back to his side. She says she would wake up "feeling groggy and dazed, sometimes so much so that it would feel like a hangover". The snoring tested the relationship, with Meg explaining: "I always said if we lived together we'd have to have a spare bedroom for the nights of truly unbearable snoring." Simon says that broken sleep, caused by a partner's snoring, can lead to irritability, arguments, and - if it is decided that sleeping in separate rooms is needed - reduced intimacy. Meg Warren felt 'groggy and dazed' after a night of little sleep due to her former partner's snoring Anna-Louise Dearden, a 52-year-old journalist, says she sometimes sleeps in a separate room from her partner due to his snoring. Having this option allows her to prioritise getting enough rest when the snoring is particularly bad. Anna-Louise Dearden says her partner's snoring has led to her sleeping in another room at times Anna-Louise said: "If you wake up and you've had a bad night's sleep, you eat more, you feel more irritable." She used to wake up often in the night due to the snoring, but has found that wearing ear plugs is a "life saver" as they allow her to sleep through most of the noise when she shares a bed with her partner. There are things that can be done, say both Simon and Johal. But first, it is important to distinguish whether your partner is simply snoring, or whether they have sleep apnoea. "What you don't want to do is simply make someone quieter at night while potentially missing an underlying sleep-related breathing disorder," Simon says. Signs of sleep apnoea, a disorder that causes a person's breathing to repeatedly stop and start during sleep, include pauses in breathing, choking at night, waking frequently, and suffering from morning headaches. If this is what you are dealing with, you could be recommended a Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machine, or even surgical treatment in some cases, Simon explains. For simple snoring, Simon said that lifestyle changes can make a difference, such as losing weight, stopping smoking, reducing alcohol intake before bed, or changing your sleeping position - such as laying on your side rather than your back. You can also suggest to your partner that they see a GP, who will be able to advise further or refer you to a specialist. An expert might suggest treating nasal obstruction or allergies, if this is what is causing snoring, or wearing a custom mouthguard to gently push the lower jaw forward and keep the airway open. Johal says too many couples put up with snoring "for too long", which impacts their relationships and wellbeing. "The key thing is that there is help out there, it's just tapping into it." title: Watch: Is the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition worth the hype?
description: Crowds have been flocking to the British Museum to see the Bayeux Tapestry as it's on public display in the UK for the first time since it was created nearly 1,000 years ago.
body: This video can not be played Visitors flocked to the British Museum in London on Thursday as the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened its doors to the general public. The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery almost 70m (230ft) in length and nearly 1,000 years old. It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066. Adult tickets to see the tapestry are priced at £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak times, with an additional £3.50 donation. The BBC's Katie Razzall asked the first visitors if it was worth the price. Read more about the Bayeux Tapestry and why it's currently in the UK. title: What in the World
description: More people are doing it to feel confident socialising - but what are the risks?
body: Use BBC.com or the new BBC App to listen to BBC podcasts, Radio 4 and the World Service outside the UK. Find out how to listen to other BBC stations World Service,·10 Sep 2026,·11 mins Available for over a year A series of recent studies suggests that drug use is increasing among Gen Z. Some young people are taking prescription anti-anxiety medications — such as propranolol and pregabalin — without a prescription. They’re buying them online or on the black market, exposing themselves to additional risks. Jacqui Wakefield, our Global Health Reporter, explains why some young people see these drugs as an alternative to alcohol. They want to reduce social anxiety on a night out and experience a feeling of euphoria, but without the calories and hangover that can come with heavy drinking. We discuss the risks associated with using these drugs without medical supervision, and the potential consequences for young people’s health. Warning: This episode includes references to suicidal thoughts. If you are affected by any of the issues discussed in this episode, or are experiencing distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. title: E-bike crime crackdown leads to 187 arrests
description: Footage released by the Met shows officers using high-powered Sur-Ron bikes to pursue suspects.
body: This video can not be played Watch: More than 185 arrested in Met crackdown on robbery and theft in central London The Metropolitan Police has arrested 187 people and seized 157 vehicles as part of a crackdown on prolific thieves using e-bikes and mopeds in Westminster. The arrests were for a variety of offences including possession of dangerous weapons, drug-related crimes, robbery and theft. The force said plain-clothed and uniformed officers carried out patrols in hotspot areas and stopped offenders known to police. The operations ran from February to July. Det Supt Gareth Gilbert, who led the operation, said officers were "staying one step ahead of the criminals who use high-powered bikes or mopeds to steal from Londoners". The Met said e-bike-related crime fell by 22% during the operation in key transport and tourist hubs in Southwark and Lambeth, including Waterloo and London Bridge. The Sur-Ron electric motorbikes are being used in several inner London boroughs Footage released by the Met shows officers using high-powered Sur-Ron electric motorbikes to pursue suspects who were trying to evade police. The force has recently expended its fleet of these bikes from five to 25. Gilbert added: "By disrupting this criminality and making hundreds of arrests, we're making London a safer place to live, work and visit. "Our approach is working, with neighbourhood crime down 14% over the past year and 13,000 fewer phone thefts." title: 'My cancer spread while I waited months for surgery': The cost of England's cancer wait times
description: Cancer care has got worse since the government announced plans to speed up waiting times and save more lives, BBC analysis shows.
body: Alan is one of thousands each month who are not being treated within the cancer target timeframe Alan was diagnosed with lung cancer after a nodule was found in June last year. The 70-year-old was meant to be operated on within weeks but ended up waiting nearly five months, by which time the cancer had spread, making his surgery more complex. "I was so frustrated and angry and couldn't understand why they would leave me like that," says Alan. On two occasions, scans were cancelled because machines had broken and for weeks he heard little or nothing from the hospital about when he would eventually have the urgent surgery. Alan is one of thousands each month in England who are not being treated within the target timeframe. Earlier this year, the government's National Cancer Plan, along with the NHS Planning Guidance, set out that 80% of patients in England would start treatment within 62 days from urgent GP referral by March 2027. This was to reach 85% by March 2029. But in the months since the government announced this ambition, performance has got worse, according to NHS England data, not better. Now, 71.2% of patients start cancer treatment within the 62 day timeframe. Previously it was 71.9%. Prof Pat Price, a leading UK clinical academic oncologist, says the government targets "are now simply impossible to hit", after what she describes as a "complete loss of momentum". Price attributes the current failures to a "complete lack of a plan or accountability". The plan stated that a new independent cancer board would be established, but it is still not known who will be leading this group. NHS data released on Thursday, for July, reveals 10 out of 120 hospital trusts in England managed to get 85% of patients to start treatment within 62 of their urgent referral by a GP. Radiotherapy UK analysis, shared exclusively with the BBC, suggests more than 2,800 extra patients would need to start treatment every month - a near 15% increase on current numbers - to achieve the March 2027 target. That is likely to grow as referrals keep rising across nearly every cancer type. Price says thousands of patients "are going to die unnecessarily, just because the government can't get their act together to treat people on time". For every month a cancer patient waits before starting treatment, their chance of survival falls by around 10%, on average. By the time Alan had his operation, the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes and the nodule "had grown at an alarming rate", according to the lung specialist. He has since been told the cancer has cleared awaiting his one-year review, but the operation has left him in debilitating pain. "I used to play golf and get out and about. Now I can't do any of the things I love," says Alan. Roughly 54,000 more patients will need to start treatment within 62 days before 2029 for the government to hit its goal. One NHS trust that is gaining traction on its waiting list numbers is Salisbury, but it is still not hitting targets. Staff say there is no single fix, just a relentless focus on getting the basics right; making sure patients know about their appointments and turn up, keeping IT systems working, recruiting the right people, making sure surgical lists are full and expanding capacity. Much of the visible progress has come through skin and prostate cancer, two of the most common cancers in the country. Diane had a cancerous lump removed from her face at Salisbury District Hospital a few weeks ago, using an innovative procedure, which checks tumour margins are clear while the patient is still in surgery. That means no follow-up operations, and it allows for complex reconstruction that leaves hardly a trace. "It's amazing, you literally can't see I had a large cancerous lesion removed from my cheek," she tells the BBC in the waiting room. Consultant plastic surgeon Neil Wickham checked her face, confirmed a biopsied lump on her arm was benign, and referred her to ENT for a separate lump in her neck. It is the kind of joined-up care the government's Cancer Plan was meant to trigger in cancer units across England. Diane benefited from an innovative procedure when she had a cancerous lump removed from her face But over in pathology at the Salisbury trust, head of department Lee Phillips is feeling the pressure. His histology lab receives cancer service biopsies from across the hospital for diagnosis. "The sheer volume of specimens we have coming in is our problem," he says. "We need more staff and more kit if we're going to keep up with demand," Phillips says. Radiotherapy is another bottleneck crying out for staff and kit. Like many trusts, Salisbury has no machine on site, so patients needing daily sessions over one to three weeks must travel up to an hour to Southampton, and sometimes Bath. But staff in Salisbury also say missed appointments, whether down to late letters, illness, transport problems or anxiety, are a constant drain on a system already stretched thin. Emilia Scutt, cancer manager in Salisbury, says that efforts to reduce missed appointments have really helped their numbers. "We know cancer can be terrifying so we are a bit like a dog with the bone, backing up patients and supporting them wherever we can." Trusts with the sharpest declines in performance - including Buckinghamshire Healthcare, Bolton NHS Foundation Trust, Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust, East Cheshire, and Torbay and South Devon - told the BBC they face pressures across the board. Rising demand, workforce shortages and diagnostic bottlenecks have all played a part. Some pointed to industrial action and staff sickness, others to reliance on outside diagnostic providers or major changes to how their systems work. All say they are investing in extra capacity, working through backlogs and redesigning pathways, and are already seeing early signs of improvement. "If government is serious about delivering on the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan

title: UK needs new laws for AI in healthcare, says watchdog
description: The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon tells the BBC.
body: The UK needs new regulations for AI products used in the NHS and other healthcare settings, says Britain's industry watchdog. The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), which regulates all medical devices and licenses treatment drugs in the UK, has published 44 recommendations to update its policies as the use of AI in the sector rises. The technology will soon be routinely used within the NHS, MHRA chief Lawrence Tallon told the BBC. "What I would expect is that patients will... increasingly see AI as part of the way that normal NHS healthcare is delivered," he said. "That should happen in a way that they can maintain their trust and their confidence in what's happening." The report was compiled by an independent commission and involved input from more than 12,000 people including patients and clinicians. Continuously monitoring AI products and removing them from regulatory approval if they malfunction or become less effective over time Giving patients the right to know whether AI is involved in their care, and easy access to information about the products involved The power to penalise the developers of an AI product if it fails to meet required standards An AI "L plate" system which would make it easier for new AI models to be trialled by healthcare professionals under close supervision "The medical devices regulatory framework predominantly dates from a period where we were thinking about things like hip replacements and knee replacements, or smaller things like stethoscopes and plasters," Tallon said. He added while current guidelines may work for simple AI products trained to spot known symptoms on scans, for example, the rules do not apply to more complex models. "Unlike most of the medical products we're used to regulating, these products continue to change after the point of authorization," he said. "As new data gets fed in, they learn, they adapt, they drift." And he acknowledged trying to regulate AI is a global challenge. "I don't think at this moment in time we can point to a single country, a single regulatory framework, and say that they have absolutely cracked it," he said. AI note-takers known as scribes, which are powered by LLMs, are reportedly used by 40% of UK-based GPs to record consultations and generate reports. But a recent study from the University of Edinburgh found patients could be less likely to share personal information such as substance abuse history if they knew the conversation was being processed by AI. Professor Henrietta Hughes, a GP who was part of the report commission, said that many of her patients were happy for AI being used during their consultations, but some chose to opt out. "Some say, 'I don't want to talk to a robot', and that is also fine," she said. Prof Hughes acknowledged that the scribes could make mistakes in their notes but said it was the responsibility of doctors to correct them. While currently AI is more likely to be used to assist with administrative tasks, or carry out symptom spotting overseen by a human expert, there is a lot of excitement about its potential in the health and medical research industries. Professor Alastair Denniston, an ophthalmologist who also worked on the report, described the technology as "an exceptional opportunity" for healthcare which was "likely to rank alongside step-changes such as antibiotics and MRI". In September Rene Haas, the boss of chip designer Arm, told the BBC he believed the tech would come up with a cure for cancer "within our lifetime". But there are also concerns about AI models making wrong decisions as a result of biases in the patient data used to train them, and incorrect medical advice being given by AI chatbots. title: Migraines and acne among five more conditions pharmacists can treat
description: Pharmacies in England will soon offer treatments for a total of 12 common conditions which save people going to their GP first.
body: People will be able to go to their local chemist in England this autumn and get on-the-spot treatment for 12 common conditions without going to their GP first. Pharmacists can already prescribe medication for seven conditions - sore throat, earache, sinusitis, shingles, impetigo, infected bites and urinary tract infections. Five more - migraines, acne, scabies, ear infections and badly blocked noses - are now also being added to that list. NHS England said the move was to ease pressure on busy GPs and A&E departments while making sure people could get treatment quickly and conveniently. After a very hot summer and three of the busiest months on record in A&Es in England, the NHS says it wants to make it as easy as possible for people to get help when they need it for everyday conditions. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said people were "fed up with the scramble for routine appointments" and wanted help close to home, with no more taking time off work or waiting to get seen. "For five more common conditions, you'll be able to walk into your local pharmacy and get treated on the spot," he said. Mr Burnham said families would feel the change, and the plan would give people back "precious time". The five conditions which can now also be treated via pharmacies are: low frequency migraines in adults hay fever or allergic rhinitis in children mild to moderate acne in young people and adults mild skin infections and scabies That's in addition to these seven: Initially, a few hundred chemists will offer treatments for the five new conditions, NHS England says. There will be a gradual rollout and the service will eventually be available at thousands of community NHS pharmacies across England. Community pharmacies also offer support with healthy eating, exercise, stopping smoking, monitoring your blood pressure, contraception, flu and Covid vaccinations. The charity the Migraine Trust said it was delighted by the news after calling for more help for migraine care in pharmacies. Chief executive Rob Music said having this support for people with migraine through their local pharmacy was "a wonderful opportunity for a faster and improved care pathway". Dr Amanda Doyle, director for primary care and community services at NHS England, said she wanted to make sure that patients can get as much support as possible in their communities, "so they do not have to be admitted to hospital unnecessarily". But bodies representing pharmacies across England have consistently said that the funding provided by the goverment does not cover the workload for the new plans. "Pharmacies are still under significant financial pressures," said Henry Gregg, chief executive of the National Pharmacy Association. "This shows why the government should go much further and invest in our pharmacy network that has the power to transform people's experience of everyday health issues." The Pharmacy First scheme started in England in 2024. NHS figures suggest it has delivered 14 million consultations since then, including two million appointments for sore throats and 1.7 million for urinary tract infections (UTIs). People can be referred to their local pharmacy via NHS111 or by their GP, or just go direct to their high street chemist. Scotland has a scheme which was seen as the model for England's Pharmacy First - Northern Ireland and Wales also have systems allowing pharmacies to treat patients with certain conditions. Patients can be treated for 27 different conditions at chemists in Scotland. Have you been treated in a pharmacy setting for one of these conditions? title: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts
description: Menstrual cycles are highly individual, making blanket advice found on social media difficult to apply, researchers say.
body: Sarah Mackay, known as @fitwsarah online, says her energy levels change through her cycle A woman points to a colour-coded grid dividing the menstrual cycle into four phases, each paired with a different list of exercises. "When you're bleeding, you want to be doing steady-pace jogging, Pilates, barre, walking, resting," she tells viewers. This is one of thousands of videos on TikTok and Instagram suggesting that people change their workouts depending on where they are in their menstrual cycles - something known as 'cycle-syncing'. So-called cycle-syncing workout plans have surged in popularity online, with Google searches for the term rising 740% since 2022 and more than 55,000 TikTok videos now using the #cyclesyncing hashtag. Most of the advice is shared by fitness and wellness creators rather than medical or research experts. They divide the menstrual cycle into phases, recommending: gradually increasing intensity in the follicular phase leading up to ovulation harder strength or high-intensity training around ovulation easing off again during the luteal phase (between ovulation and the start of your period) So what does the science say? Kelly McNulty, a researcher at Leeds Beckett University specialising in menstrual cycles and exercise, says there is evidence that some women experience changes in symptoms, energy or perceived strength across their cycle. But that is different from evidence that all women should train in a particular way at a particular point, she tells the BBC, adding that these videos are "a trend based on marketing rather than any kind of research or evidence". "There isn't any research to support that kind of phase-based prescription," she says. This video can not be played Should you sync your exercise routine with your period? A key issue is that menstrual cycles are highly individual, McNulty adds - they can differ between women, and one woman's experience can also change from one cycle to the next. That makes the blanket advice often found on social media difficult to apply, she explains. Many cycle-tracking apps and programmes are also designed around relatively regular menstrual cycles that are 21 to 35 days, which can make their recommendations less applicable to people with irregular periods, or those using hormonal contraception. "It's not so much about doing certain exercises in certain phases, it's about working with your own individual body and what your needs might be." There are now thousands of videos on Instagram and TikTok recommending women sync their workouts to their menstrual cycles Cesci Burgoyne, a nurse based in Sydney, Australia who is also a qualified personal trainer and nutritionist, adjusts her training depending on how she feels in her cycle. She doesn't follow a prescriptive plan, she says, but instead makes changes intuitively. "In my luteal phase I'll try and ease off in the training," she tells the BBC. "In my follicular phase, I'm so energised, I feel like I can lift so much heavier. I like to try and get my long runs in." Burgoyne also welcomes the growing attention on women's health, and says that exercise and nutrition research has historically focused heavily on male bodies, with findings then often applied to women. Sarah says she has sometimes hit personal records while on her period Fitness creator Sarah Mackay, known as @liftwsarah on Instagram and TikTok, has also noticed her energy, motivation, cramps and mood change through the month. But she deliberately avoids strict plans because, she says, "there are too many variables at play". Some online plans advise women to avoid intense training during their period, she says, yet she has sometimes hit personal records while menstruating. "The problem is not that the menstrual cycle is irrelevant," she says, but that "not everything is predictable". Dr Faye Bate, a trained medical doctor and women's health expert, is also wary of advice suggesting all women should train differently according to their menstrual phase. "A one-size-fits-all model of 'you should be exercising this way in this phase and a different way in a different phase' shouldn't be advice that applies to all women," she says. She is concerned that repeatedly telling women they are likely to be weaker or less capable at particular points in their cycle could create a "nocebo" effect - where negative expectations themselves influence how someone feels or performs. McNulty tells the BBC that routinely easing off resistance training could also limit progress. Strength training is particularly important for women, who face a higher risk of osteoporosis later in life. Building strength requires consistent, progressively challenging training, she says, and "we don't want to create another barrier by suggesting women train less for almost half the month." Dr Bate also warns against normalising severe symptoms: if pain, fatigue or mood changes interfere with exercise or daily life, women should seek medical advice rather than assuming it is an inevitable part of their cycle, she says. While cycle-syncing itself may not be backed by strong evidence, the experts we spoke to did suggest being "cycle-aware". McNulty says tracking your cycle can be a useful way to understand your own patterns, while Dr Bate also encourages women to become more familiar with how they feel at different points in the month. Both welcome the fact that menstrual health is being discussed more openly, but say the focus should be on individual experience, rather than rigid, phase-based rules. In practice, that might mean having painkillers ready before your period, taking a rest day when symptoms are worse, or easing off a workout if you feel unusually fatigued. For Dr Bate, "the most important part is tuning in to how you feel". In other words, use your cycle as information rather than a set of rules. title: Wellbeing walks praised for keeping people active
description: The free walks range from 10 to 90 minutes and are aimed at all abilities.
body: The free walks are held in partnership with Ramblers UK and other local partners People say taking part in free wellbeing walks has changed their lives "dramatically". Active Cornwall coordinates the walks in partnership with Ramblers UK and other local partners across the county with the aim of helping people of all ages stay healthy and connected. Led by trained volunteers and held over coast paths and garden estates to town parks, the walks range from 10 to 90 minutes and are aimed at all abilities. Kathryn, who takes part in walks at Heligan Gardens near Mevagissey, noted the walks helped lift her spirits when she felt down. Kathryn said the walks have dramatically changed her life More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall "It has changed my life dramatically, I've built up a really beautiful friendship group," she said. "We see the animals, we see the plants and every week there is something different going on. "The people I'm with, they ask how you are - it's just good to talk." Toni, who also takes part in the walks, said they provided a good opportunity to talk with others. Toni said the groups provide an opportunity to talk to others "I've also just had a knee replacement, so this is helping me along," Toni added. "I come out and walk, we have a chat and a cup of coffee, getting fresh air and being with human beings." Professor Chris Whitty, Chief Medical Officer for England, recently recommended adults aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week - and a brisk walk counts towards that amount. Active Cornwall's Rob Harrison said there were obviously physical benefits of getting out but stressed "the social element is massively important" too. "You could come to walk on your own, but you go away with friends and have that network and community," Harrison said. Follow BBC Cornwall on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. title: Alan Carr holds back tears on special night at National Television Awards
description: The comedian and Celebrity Traitors win big - see a full list of winners and nominees from the 26th edition of the awards.
body: The comedian was surprised with a top NTA honour You can see a full list of winners at the bottom of this article Alan Carr had an emotional night at the 31st National Television Awards on Tuesday as he received the Special Recognition prize following a whirlwind year for the comedian. The London audience had just been treated to a Traitors-themed musical performance in his honour, which included fellow cast member Paloma Faith emerging from a coffin, when he was given the surprise award. Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet before the ceremony, Carr had played down his chances of winning for his semi-autobiographical comedy Changing Ends. He joked: "Comedy is so subjective... Mrs Brown's Boys wins every year, why am I even here?" This video can not be played Watch: 'I still felt bad about Paloma', says Alan Carr Carr was right - Mrs Brown's Boys went on to win the Comedy prize. But the night was just beginning. The Celebrity Traitors favourite had predicted there would be "ugly crying" if he did take home a prize - and he stayed true to his word as he accepted the Special Recognition award, the only category not voted for by the public. Carr told BBC News that being part of The Celebrity Traitors had brought him a level of attention he had never experienced before. "I've never had popularity like it," he said, describing the show as a "phenomenon". The Celebrity Traitors won an award after a critically-acclaimed series Carr had more reason to celebrate when The Celebrity Traitors beat the original version of the show to win the Reality Competition prize. His co-star, singer Charlotte Church, praised the show's final, which attracted 15 million viewers within seven days, describing it as a "beautiful vignette of male tenderness and emotional expression". "Alan, Nick (Mohammed) and David (Olusoga), you were just absolutely sublime," she added. Another big win went to Sir David Attenborough, who was named Best Presenter in his 100th birthday year, beating popular duo Ant and Dec, whose 23-year winning streak was broken by Gary Lineker last year. While not in attendance, Attenborough's long-time collaborator Mark Brownlow accepted the award on his behalf and shared a message from the broadcaster urging people to help protect the planet. "Humanity has always needed the natural world for all the practicalities of life and for our mental wellbeing," Attenborough wrote. "Now the natural world needs us too: surely we must not ignore that simple fact." Clarkson's Farm won an NTA for the second year running, taking the inaugural Celebrity-Led Reality Docuseries award. The new category also featured shows from Stacey Solomon and Joe Swash, Tyson Fury, Kelvin Fletcher, and Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse. Celebrity-led programmes still featured in the Authored Documentary category, with documentaries from Olympian Sir Chris Hoy, former Little Mix singer Jesy Nelson, and Sharon Osbourne's film about her late husband Ozzy among the nominees. It was a win for a second year in a row for Jeremy Clarkson Speaking to BBC News on the red carpet, their daughter Kelly Osbourne said her family were "honoured" that the documentary about her father had been nominated, describing it as a "tragic but beautiful story". She said she had spoken to her mother Sharon just before arriving at the ceremony: "We are so close. I was on the phone with her before I got out of the car." In the end, the public chose Our Girls: The Southport Families. The BBC programme followed the families of Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, Bebe King, six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, who were murdered at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport in 2024. Accepting the award, Elsie's mother Jenni Stancombe told the audience: "We never expected to be stood up here, so I don't know what to say. "We know you didn't vote for us, you voted for our three girls." The parents of the Southport attack victims were recognised for their powerful film documenting the lives of their daughters In the drama categories, Vicky McClure won Best Drama Performance for her role in crime thriller Trigger Point, from the first all-female shortlist in the category's history. She told BBC News in the winners' room: "Over the years it has not been our space, and here we are dominating that category. "I feel honoured to be amongst those wonderful women." Vicky McClure came out on top in a list of nominees dominated by female actors Among those nominated alongside McClure was Sheridan Smith for her portrayal of campaigner Ann Ming in ITV true crime drama I Fought The Law. While Smith missed out on the individual prize, I Fought The Law went on to win New Drama. Away from the awards, nominee Graham Norton revealed his red carpet outfit had already had one high-profile outing this year. "This is what I wore to Taylor Swift's wedding," he told BBC News. Norton said guests had agreed not to reveal details of the celebrations. "I had a wonderful time and we all agreed by saying yes to going, we weren't going to blab about it." Norton, who also featured in Swift's music video for Opalite earlier this year, said working with the singer showed him "what leadership is like at that level". "It was such a happy set. Everyone was working as hard as they could for her," he said. Graham Norton revealed he wore the same suit to the NTAs as he did to Taylor Swift's wedding I'm A Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! title: Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions
description: It is hoped that coordinated action minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America, our political editor writes.
body: There is little doubt that the UK's decision to ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank is another significant shift in Britain's posture in the Middle East. The announcement from the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, with the Prime Minister Andy Burnham alongside him in the House of Commons, comes almost exactly a year after the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state. And it comes garnished with blunt language about Israel's conduct. This latest announcement is both a logical extension of that decision of 12 months ago, senior figures argue, but also, in words and actions, an expression of Burnham's desire to go further than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer was willing to. It is, Miliband believes, a re-assertion of the logic of eventually arriving at a two-state solution – a viable Palestinian state alongside Israel. The foreign secretary passionately argued that the UK did have agency and could act – and to do nothing would amount to failure. "A strategy of passivity in the face of what is happening is not a strategy," is how Miliband put it in an interview with Jewish News, external. There is a pride among his team that after a diplomatic effort over the summer, there is a breadth to the coordinated international action on this, with 11 other countries, including France and Canada, sharing the same approach. "We provided a convening and coordinating role in pulling this together," one source told me, "but we didn't have to convince others to do this. They were coming to the same view themselves, so we agreed we should all go out and say this at the same time." The hope is that coordinated action increases the likelihood that the measures will have an impact and minimises the blowback to any one country from Israel or America. UK officials had anticipated one likely reaction from Israel would be the enforced closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem, which has indeed happened. And while there is a weary acknowledgement that no one can be certain what President Donald Trump might say next about anything ever, it is noted in Whitehall that the initial reaction of the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was pretty understated. As for the domestic political context, plenty in the Labour movement and the wider British left have long clamoured for this to happen. Around 140 Labour MPs went public with this demand at the beginning of the summer, and Burnham was explicit in his criticism of his predecessor's approach to the Middle East, writing in July: "Labour's initial response to the treatment of Gaza caused huge hurt. We got it wrong and I am sorry about that." In recent years Labour has haemorrhaged support in many communities with a significant Muslim population, and so for a new Labour prime minister seeking to lure as many on the left – and beyond – under Labour's umbrella, this diplomatic intervention makes sense. But the reaction of the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, writing in the Jewish Chronicle, external, is a reminder of another challenge for Burnham, both political and societal. "Once again, British Jews find themselves warning their own government that its relentless demonisation of the world's only Jewish state risks fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home," Badenoch said. Later, the Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was "truly a dark day for Britain's Jews". Last October, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham was the local figurehead during the grim reality of an attack at the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in the city. Miliband has sought to address concerns about what Badenoch calls "demonisation" by making his view clear that "holding British Jews responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, pure and simple". But Labour figures are keenly aware that at points in the last decade, under the leadership of Jeremy Corbyn, the Labour Party's relationship with many British Jews was dire, a situation Starmer sought to rectify as a priority in the early years of his leadership. In other words, the party's recent relations with many British Jews has been fragile for some time - and many in the community already felt vulnerable after last year's attack in Manchester, and the later arson attacks on Jewish community ambulances in north-west London in the spring. Burnham has to manage that anxiety while making the case for the changing stance the government is announcing, in the weeks before he meets many of his international counterparts for the first time. title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns
description: The children's commissioner for England says many are enrolled at college but aren't showing up.
body: There could be tens of thousands more teenagers who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) than official statistics suggest, the children's commissioner for England has warned. A report by Dame Rachel de Souza said around 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England were officially classed as studying at college, but were not showing up at least half of the time. She said they had gone "under the radar" and were "not getting the support that they need". The Department for Education (DfE) said it planned to help colleges track attendance and ultimately to gather that data centrally. Unlike schools, further education and sixth form colleges in England are not required to collect or report attendance data. Dame Rachel's report is based on attendance data obtained from 262 college groups in England and says rates are "substantially lower" than in schools. It suggests that more than half (52.2%) of 16- and 17-year-olds are estimated to be persistently absent by the standards used in schools, meaning they are missing 10% or more of college sessions. And around 42,000 (5.9%) are severely absent, meaning they are missing at least half of college sessions. The DfE estimates that 57,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England are Neet, and Dame Rachel's report argues that these persistently absent teenagers should be considered as "hidden" Neets alongside them. Dame Rachel told the BBC a range of factors led to teenagers missing college, including part-time work and travel costs, and that some had been largely absent from education since the Covid pandemic. She said while those juggling part-time employment were likely to miss college every so often, it was those who are "far more vulnerable" who were likely to be severely absent. She added that it was "shocking" that the DfE did not collect the data as it meant the issue was "ignored". "It's under the radar and these kids are not getting the support that they need," she said. One in eight young people still out of work or education ahead of major review Want your job application to stand out? Employers say they look for these six skills Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise Liam Sloan, principal at Bolton College, said not many students missed more than half of classes, but those who were absent often had mental health challenges or part-time jobs. "Sometimes the student being able to be offered that £30 shift there and then means more... than the potential qualification in six or seven months' time," he said. He said there was a particular issue in English and maths GCSE classes, which students in England are required to study alongside other courses if they don't have a grade 4 or above. Attendance rates at the college had improved in recent years though, he said, and this year it has introduced full-time "positive engagement officers" to greet students each morning and contact those who do not show up. Dame Rachel said she expected the government to respond to her recommendations, including: Collecting and setting targets for attendance data for 16- and 17-year-olds "Expediting" the rollout of mental health support teams in colleges Introducing free bus travel for children Approximately one in eight people aged 16 to 24 are Neet, according to data published by the Office for National Statistics. In May, the first instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn warned that figure could be one in six within five years, and that the country was "at risk of a lost generation." The final instalment is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the problem in the coming weeks. Dame Rachel's report describes "hidden" Neets as those enrolled but persistently absent from college, while Milburn's interim report used it to describe those who are Neet and also not claiming benefits, and are therefore harder to reach. Cath Sezen, director of education policy at the Association of Colleges, said she agreed with many of the report's recommendations but said "funding pressures [were] limiting colleges' ability to provide tailored support". "We have called time and time again for increased investment, better integration of support services and a stronger national strategy for employer engagement," she said. The DfE said students in further education needed to be prioritised in future reforms to help tackle the Neets crisis. A spokesperson also said a new stepping-stone qualification would be brought in to reduce the "endless treadmill" of students failing and resitting GCSE maths and English, and that the government would track attendance in colleges and accelerate the rollout of mental health support teams. title: Very hot drinks may damage the food pipe and increase cancer risk
description: Steaming hot liquid can damage the cell lining on the way down to the stomach, experts say.
body: Regularly drinking beverages like tea and coffee at very hot temperatures increases the risk of cancer of the food pipe or gullet, known as oesophageal cancer, UK research suggests. Researchers say the findings, external, from a study of nearly a million people, make this the largest to date to establish the link. In the study, people who had their drinks "very hot" had around a three times higher risk of the cancer than "warm" tea or coffee drinkers - although experts stress the overall chances of developing this cancer are low. Steaming hot liquid can damage the cell lining of the food pipe on the way down to the stomach. The work by Oxford University, which is published in the International Journal of Cancer, defines any drink at 65 degrees Celsuis or above as "very hot" and posing a potential risk. Consuming six or more hot drinks per day also raises the risk, according to data from 977,282 middle-aged men and women. Although adding milk can cool drinks down slightly, a milky tea or coffee may still be far too hot, researchers say. Tea made immediately after a kettle is fully boiled is touching boiling point, which is 100 degrees C (212 degrees F). Once poured into a cup, that lowers to around 90 or 95 degrees C. The advice is to wait a few minutes before drinking so the beverage cools to a safer temperature. Cancer Research UK says it's difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool. "But if you're worried, we'd suggest just waiting until it's comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it's still very hot," the charity said. Lead researcher Dr Keren Papier said research in South America - where many people drink a very hot herbal beverage called mate - had already shown a similar link between hot drinks and oesophageal cancer. But she said: "More research is now needed to identify the exact drink temperatures linked to this increased risk." A separate study, external of 118 young adults who did multiple tastings of different black coffees found most only deemed the drinks to be too hot if the temperature was 70 degrees C or above. According to one takeaway coffee cup manufacturer, the ideal temperature for hot coffee on the go is between 49 and 60 degrees C. Should a barista want the coffee to stay hotter for longer - if a customer requests extra hot - it can be served at over 82 degrees C, says MTPak Coffee. The researchers suggest that around one or two in every 10 oesophageal cancers could be avoided if people stopped drinking very hot beverages. Squamous cell oesophageal cancer is rare, affecting a few thousand people a year. In the UK, around 1% of the population has a lifetime risk of being diagnosed with this type of cancer. So even if scalding hot drinks might increase someone's risk, the chances of them developing the cancer are still low. And there are other factors, such as smoking, which are a bigger risk for oesophageal cancer. Fiona Osgun from Cancer Research UK, which funded the study, stressed: "The most important ways to reduce the risk of this cancer type are not smoking and cutting down on alcohol." Symptoms of oesophageal cancer can include heartburn, indigestion or a pain in your throat or chest, especially when swallowing, along with weight loss. title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report
description: The report follows a BBC Eye investigation that found Instagram running paid ads promoting such material in India.
body: Tech Transparency Project (TTP) says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found. The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India. Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP), external says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year. When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement." The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings. About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials. After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter. The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children. When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations. The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children. But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough. Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material Bhuwan Ribhu wants India to require social media platforms to identify and report those promoting CSAM "Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu. The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC. According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act. TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad. According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year. In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website, external about how it fights child exploitation on its apps. "Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said. TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live. For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards." For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad. In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post about how it fights child exploitation on its apps When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000". TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed. This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down. Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings. TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers. title: England up in reading, maths and science rankings as Scotland and Wales fall behind
description: The latest Pisa report also warned of a global decline in teenagers' reading skills.
body: English pupils have pulled ahead of the rest of the UK in international reading, maths and science tests, new data suggests, with Scotland and Wales falling further behind. The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) saw reading and maths scores slump in each UK nation except England, while all four saw an uptick in science, with that rise again most notable in England. The latest Pisa report, which is published every three years, also warned of a worldwide decline in teenagers' reading skills. Teenagers were losing the skills that "matter most in the age of AI", such as being able to critically evaluate information from different sources, it said. The share of "hasty readers", who rush through texts to give quick, incorrect answers, has almost doubled between 2018 and 2025. The report warned the fall was greatest in those from "relatively well off" families. Run by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the Pisa tests assess teenagers on their ability to solve problems, think critically and communicate, before asking them a wider range of questions about their education in a questionnaire. Although the UK performed well overall, the rankings varied significantly again, with results showing England, where the curriculum is significantly different, pulling consistently ahead of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales. England's schools minister, Georgia Gould, said the government wanted to "build on" the positive results and "go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy". The 2025 Pisa tests were taken by a sample of 760,000 15-year-olds in 91 countries. In the UK, where education differs between the home nations, 15,566 students took the tests in 515 schools. In England, where it was recently announced that technical subjects would soon be available to students from age 14, Gould held up high-performing Estonia as an example of where "academic excellence can go hand in hand with high-quality vocational routes". "Our reforms will build on England's strong academic foundations so future generations not only perform well, but feel connected to school and excited about where their education can take them," she added. But Laura Trott, England's shadow education secretary, said the country's successes were down to previous reforms, and accused the new government of trying to "sabotage" them. Wales falls further behind rest of UK in international school tests Primary teachers hired to teach Glasgow secondary pupils to read While Wales lags behind the rest of the UK overall, on science it is ahead of other European countries such as France, Spain and the Netherlands. As the tests last year were taken by 15-year-olds, the results there largely reflect learning under an old curriculum, which has recently been changed. Anna Brychan, Wales' minister for education and Welsh language, said plans were in place to support schools, adding that the results "highlight our need to improve standards of reading and maths, as a priority". Scotland's education secretary, Mairi McAllan, said the results showed "real strengths in Scottish education, as well as areas we're already working to improve". But Scottish Labour said results had "flatlined since 2022's historically poor results", while the Scottish Liberal Democrats said the education system under the SNP had "tumbled down the rankings, lagging behind England on every measure of performance". Northern Ireland's education minister, Paul Givan, said pupils there had performed well by international standards, but that - like other countries - its education system was facing "significant challenges", adding that "there is much more work to do". Overall, the Pisa tests provide the biggest global snapshot of education systems and an independent view of how teenagers are performing compared with their peers in other countries, so it is a relative measure. Andreas Schleicher, director of education at the OECD, said reading was the "mother of all skills" and that the steep decline was a concern. He said children's ability to read complex texts had declined by the equivalent of "two school years" in the last decade. Longer-term Pisa research suggested students who read longer books performed best, he added, as it helped them to learn to hold complex information in mind. Schools like Meadow Park, in Coventry, are adopting a range of approaches to improve pupils' reading skills, including weekly book club discussions led by tutors. Year 10 pupil Ampaabeng said the sessions have had a "really positive impact" on his reading since they were brought in a year ago. The school has also invested in a wider range of books in the library, where reading for pleasure at lunchtime is encouraged. A mobile phone ban was introduced at the school two years ago to reduce distractions - an approach which is commended by the new report. "In a digital age, it's easier to pick up a phone than it is a book," head teacher Bernadette Pettman said. She said reading together had enabled the school to "break down that fear of reading" and that pupils had "absolutely embraced it". Bernadette Pettman says the school tries to make reading fun with book clubs, creative writing sessions and visits from authors One of the other big changes in education, picked up in the OECD's report, is the use of AI. It warns that excessive use can lead to pupils avoiding looking up information themselves, a process sometimes called "cognitive off-loading". In the UK, the Pisa questionnaire's results suggested a relatively high proportion of teenagers said they had never used AI for their schoolwork. But the OECD's report said countries were allowing the rapid spread of AI without evidence of its impact, likening it to rolling out an untested vaccine on children. Schleicher called on governments to provide clear guidelines, and consider whether AI could be use

title: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
description: Use our interactive tracker to explore the latest migration statistics for the UK
body: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012. How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted? Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics. Between 1 January and 7 September 2026, a total of 17,281 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 8 September 2025 to 7 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence. The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026. About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites. The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029. More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year. Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026. The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa. It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum. In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year. As of March 2026, a further 87,450 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 72% on the previous year. Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear. Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026. About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between April 2025 to March 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned. The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave. This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily. People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation. There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year. That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026: 5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026. The UK is trialing a scheme with France to return people who arrived in the country on a small boat. For every person the UK sends back to France, the UK will accept an equal number of asylum seekers. This is called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people have been returned through this arrangement. Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers. title: New mums 'left to get on with it' as C-section numbers hit record high
description: Mothers have described being left to recover from caesarean sections with "no support".
body: Carys Louise Brandon says she was completely unprepared for what came after her first C-section Mothers have described being left to recover from caesarean sections with "no support" as the number of babies being born via caesarean reaches its highest rate on record. A caesarean, or C-section, is a major operation to deliver a baby through a cut in the abdomen, usually just below the bikini line. Carys Louise Brandon, from Swansea, had an emergency C-section to deliver her first child in 2022 and said she was completely unprepared for what came afterwards. The Welsh government said every woman should receive high-quality postnatal care tailored to her needs. Carys Louise says she had many unanswered questions about her recovery Latest figures show 42% of babies in Wales were born by C-section in 2025, with just over half of those operations being emergencies. Carys' first baby was born in 2022. After needing an emergency C-section, Carys, a content creator, said she had many unanswered questions about her recovery. "I think I was thrown in at the deep end and I really didn't know how to deal with it," she said. It was almost three weeks before the 29-year-old said she felt physically able to leave the house. "And even then, I only walked up to the top of the street and back," she added. Carys has since had two more caesareans and said each experience was very different. Both times, she said the care she received in hospital and from her community midwife was good. But after getting home, she was left with questions about how her body should be recovering. "You're thrown so into the deep end and there's no sort of, 'Oh, this is how your scar should look. This is quite normal for this sort of time'." She recalled taking the dressing off her wound and fainting in the shower. "I didn't know - should my scar be recovering in a certain way, should I really be feeling like this? "There's just no support around the fact that after it, you're looking after a baby and recovering from major surgery, and everyone's recovery looks totally different." She has shared her own experiences online in the hopes of helping other women, and said expectant mums often contact her for advice. "I wish I'd had more stories that I could read to be a bit more informed before I gave birth that way." Carys has had three children, all of whom were delivered via C-section The latest figures from the Welsh government showed that 42% of births in Wales were by caesarean section in 2025 - the highest rate on record - while in England around 45% of babies are delivered in this way. According to the NHS, external, a caesarean may be recommended as a planned procedure or carried out in an emergency if a vaginal birth is considered to be too risky. Some women also choose to have a caesarean for non-medical reasons. The health service's website states that most women can go home from hospital one or two days after a C-section, but that recovery is normally slower than from a vaginal birth. A Welsh government report published in February highlighted the rapid increase in caesarean sections and inductions, saying the consequences for women, their families and the NHS had not been evaluated. The report raised concerns about staffing and support across maternity services and said postnatal care was inadequately staffed and supported. The Welsh government has committed to a three-year programme of improvements, but the Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said maternity services had not kept pace with the changing picture. New mums 'left to get on with it' after C-sections Julie Richards, director of the RCM in Wales, said postnatal care for C-sections should include support with pain relief, wound care and surgical recovery, alongside help with feeding and caring for a new baby. She said the rise in caesareans had changed the demands being placed on services. "What we may not have had is the developments in maternity care to respond to the change in landscape for maternity services." Ceri Ann says she waited seven hours to hold her newborn baby Ceri Ann Roberts, 29, from Gwynedd, said the care she received at Ysbyty Gwynedd after giving birth to her second child in 2025 had left her "traumatised". Ceri Ann had an emergency C-section and her daughter, Ania, was taken to neonatal intensive care because she was not breathing. Ceri Ann said she was then left alone on the recovery ward, unable to move. "I just wanted to see my baby but I couldn't, and the staff told me there was no-one available to take me up to see her." She said it was seven hours until she held her baby for the first time, and that was when her husband arrived back at the hospital and took her to the unit himself. "It was awful, I just cried and cried," she said. Ceri Ann Roberts says her post C-section experience was "just awful" Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board said while it could not comment on individual cases, women recovering from C-sections while their babies are in special care are supported by midwives who provide updates on their baby's wellbeing and help to facilitate visits to see their babies as soon as they are medically able to do so. It acknowledged that being separated from a baby following birth could be distressing and said its teams worked to facilitate contact "at the earliest safe opportunity". Nicola Rous-Morgan is a pregnancy and postnatal yoga teacher, and a trained midwife who works with women recovering after childbirth Nicola Rous-Morgan is a pregnancy and postnatal yoga teacher and a trained midwife, who works with women recovering after childbirth, including those who have had C-sections. She said women often tell her they feel left alone to manage their recovery by themselves. "I think one of the biggest take-homes is they felt that once they had been discharged from hospital, upon coming home, that they were just left to get on with it." She added: "The f

title: Support for disability benefits 'remarkably strong' report finds
description: About 7% of those polled wanted disability benefit cuts, according to the latest British Social Attitudes survey.
body: Protesters demonstrating against benefit cuts at a rally in Parliament Square in 2025 Support for disability benefits remains "remarkably strong" and cutting them would be "politically risky" according to a new report. The analysis, from the British Social Attitudes survey, found that fewer than one in 10 people favoured cutting welfare payments for the disabled, with almost half of people saying they would support more being spent on them, even if it led to higher taxes. The report comes amid mounting concerns among several political parties about the growing cost of disability benefits. Spending on the main disability benefit is forecast to more than double in a decade, reaching £41bn by 2030. But the report says that cutting these payments would not be easy. "Despite growing political divisions on welfare, support for disability benefits remains remarkably strong," said Dr Robert de Vries from the University of Kent, who was one of the report's co-authors. "Very few people favour cuts, disabled people are seen as among the most deserving recipients of support, and proposals to reduce disability benefits appear politically risky across the political spectrum." The analysis is based on 4,656 interviews gathered between August and October 2025. The authors noted that the timing of the interviews, just after the Sir Keir Starmer's government had failed to reform PIP, meant it was "possible that people were particularly supportive of disability benefits at the time". They cautioned that public attitudes to disability benefits "crucially depend on which disabled people are in the public's mind", referencing previous research that showed that "some types of disabled people are seen as 'deserving' by the public". The findings come despite the proportion of those who support increasing welfare spending for the poor being at a near record low. Labour, the Conservative party and Reform UK have all said there is a need to reduce the amount of money being spent on health and disability benefits, while the Liberal Democrats, Greens and SNP oppose reductions. Efforts by Sir Keir to introduce cuts last year were opposed by many in his own party, forcing a government climbdown. The proportion of GDP the UK spends on all welfare benefits for those of working age has remained broadly flat over the past 40 years, at just under 5%. It has occasionally increased to over 5%, including in the 1990s, after the financial crisis in 2008, and during the Covid pandemic. Despite that, the survey found that support for increasing welfare payments to help the poor was close to the lowest level the researchers have ever recorded. Asked if "the government should spend more money on welfare benefits for the poor, even if it leads to higher taxes," 27% replied they should while 42% were opposed. While wider welfare spending on people of working age has, proportionately, remained stable, payments for disability benefits have taken up an increasing share of the total. The latest figures show four million people in England and Wales are currently in receipt of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), the main disability benefit. Annual spending has increased sharply from £16.3bn in 2019/20 to £27.3bn in 2024/25, and is forecast to rise to more than £41bn by 2030. But around half of those polled for the survey, 49%, supported higher spending on disability benefits overall even if it led to higher taxes. Just 7% were in favour of cutting such benefits for disabled people who cannot work. A majority also strongly backed extra payments for the costs of having a disability. Around 83% of respondents supported additional payments to help with cooking, 80% for budgeting, and 78% for washing. Just 3% replied that "nobody should get any additional money" for all three tasks. Respondents were not asked if they thought it should be harder to claim those benefits. Proposals to reform PIP are due to be unveiled by the government in the autumn after an interim report published in the summer found the benefit was not fit for purpose. Around 57% of Labour voters polled for the survey favoured more spending on disability benefits. But there was broad political consensus that cuts would be wrong – just 5% of Labour voters, 7% of Conservatives and 11% of Reform UK backers said they supported cuts to those payments. The British Social Attitudes survey, carried out by the National Centre for Social Research, has been gauging public opinion since 1983.
