title: Mum 'lost trust' in surgeon review hospital
description: One parent says the number of patients involved in a review is "ridiculous".
body: Lynn said she had lost trust in Addenbrooke's Hospital, where her daughter Tammy underwent surgery A mum whose daughter was among more than 200 patients "harmed" after being operated on by a now-suspended NHS surgeon says she has lost trust in the hospital that treated her. Of the 209 patients who "experienced harm" under the care of orthopaedic surgeon Kuldeep Stohr at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge, 41 were classed as severe and one person died, as first reported by the BBC on Monday. Lynn, whose 13-year-old daughter Tammy was among the first to receive findings from an independent investigation last year, said the number of patients involved was "ridiculous". The hospital trust said it was "deeply sorry". Stohr previously said she was fully co-operating with an investigation. Kuldeep Stohr is being investigated in relation to hundreds of operations An ongoing review by the Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (CUH) has looked into the care of more than 900 patients so far. Many of the cases investigated in the review involved children operated on by Stohr. The figures were published in a report prepared for the trust's board of directors and was published on its website ahead of a meeting on Wednesday. The trust removed the report after it was contacted by the BBC for comment. It said a "confidential interim update" was "shared by mistake in our public board papers". The city grappling with unreliable phone signal 'Our son's law will save generations of children' 'I want my Bayeux Tapestry next to the original' Tammy's family was among the first to receive findings from an independent investigation last year Lynn questioned who had authored the report, "as us relatives don't trust the hospital and what they say now". "One or two can be classed as a mistake, but this amount – no. It's ridiculous, especially where parents like me have had to see their children go through additional surgery." Her family's lawyers previously said they had received a written admission of substandard surgery after screws on Tammy's hip joints, meant to improve her mobility, were inserted in the wrong place and did not properly connect to the bone. Natasha, pictured with her daughter Neave, is calling for a public inquiry Another parent, Natasha, said she was calling for a public inquiry into how children under Stohr's care – including her 19-year-old daughter Neave – came to be harmed. The trust's final findings are expected to be shared in November. Chief executive Nicola Ayton said it would be shared with patients and their families before it is published. Elizabeth Maliakal from Hudgell Solicitors, which is representing several families, said she expected the final report to be "damning". "Some of our clients, who are children, endured major surgery they didn't need, which had no positive impact on their lives, and left them in pain for years afterwards," she said. "I expect the final report from the trust, once all the findings of the independent review panel are known, to be highly critical, given we already know from those that we represent that fatal harm was caused in at least one case, and many, many more were harmed." Stohr was suspended by the hospital and has not been at work since March 2024, initially for personal reasons. Ayton said the trust was "deeply sorry to the patients and families who came to harm or experienced care below the standards they should expect". "This should never have happened and we are making changes so that something like this could not happen again," she said. Stohr's legal representatives declined to comment about the new report when approached by the BBC. Have you been affected by this story? Contact us below. title: Train station to mark World Suicide Prevention Day
description: As well as offering advice, Wellbeing Week will include poetry, gardening workshops, art and music.
body: L-R: Maria Jones and Kirsten Rose (Rethink), Jade Beddington (The Haven), Cllr Paul Singh and Mrs Ranjit Dhillon (Mayor & Mayoress of Wolverhampton), Sam Passmore and Thomas Harty (WMR) A five-day programme activities has begun at Wolverhampton's railway station to support people's mental health and wellbeing. Wellbeing Week has been timed to coincide with Thursday's World Suicide Prevention Day and is a collaboration between West Midlands Railway and Rethink Mental Illness. The event is being held at The Hub at the station, which opened in May last year to help people in crisis, and activities include poetry performances, gardening workshops, art and music. Visitors would be offered personal support and information, West Midlands Railway said while Kirsten Rose from Rethink Mental Illness said it was about raising awareness and normalising conversations about mental health. title: A&E did not get the basics right - my son's life was ruined at 32
description: Oli's experience is one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England, BBC analysis shows.
body: Oli Coppock had a career in digital marketing and was feeling positive about his future In May 2024, a few months after having treatment for a brain tumour, Oli Coppock went to Warrington Hospital's emergency department with bad headaches and dizziness. He underwent tests and assessments, but did not have a brain scan, before going home. It was a decision that ultimately ruined his life at the age of 32, his family says. A week later, with fluid building up on the brain, he suffered a cardiac arrest. He did not recover and now lives in almost complete paralysis. Oli's case is just one of a growing number of clinical negligence claims being made in England relating to A&E care. An analysis by the BBC shows there has been a 41% rise in cases over the past five years, with doctors linking it to the long delays and pressures being seen in emergency departments. Oli's father, Stephen, says he knows A&E staff are under pressure, but he cannot understand how a brain scan was not ordered, given his son's medical history. Despite the brain tumour and a recent diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Oli was otherwise fit and well and positive about his future. He had a career in digital marketing, loved going to the gym and did some DJing in his spare time. Stephen says the whole family – including Oli's six siblings - has been left "angry and broken" by what happened to him. Stephen Coppock says the whole family has been left broken by what happened to Oli "The hospital didn't get the basics right and my son has paid a terrible price – it's ruined his life. It was an awful error. He trusted the health service and believed it was there to help him, not destroy him." He says Oli's body is now twisted and paralysed and he has no ability to move around. His breathing, feeding and toileting are all done through tubes at the neurological rehabilitation centre where he is being cared for. He can only communicate through blinking, but Stephen believes he understands everything going on around him. "There is no worse space for a human to occupy – it's a permanent living nightmare." Oli, who is being cared for in a neurological rehab unit, communicates by blinking North Cheshire and Mersey NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Warrington's A&E, has now accepted a breach of duty in not ordering a CT brain scan, which on the balance of probabilities would have identified the fluid build-up in his brain and led to surgery to address it. In a statement, the trust said: "We are deeply sorry that Mr Coppock did not receive that standard of care that should be expected and we recognise the distress and lasting impact on patients and their families when harm is caused." An interim damages payment has been agreed. However, Oli's solicitor, Tanzeela Aslam, head of medical negligence at Express Solicitors, says the time taken to get to this point – more than two years – has just added to the failings, depriving him of access to funds for therapies and support that could have improved his quality of life. "Oli's case illustrates how preventable errors within the NHS can have devastating and life-changing consequences for individuals and their families." She says she is seeing more and more A&E-related cases – something she too puts down to the growing pressures. "There has been an increased reliance on corridor care for patients, and we are seeing cases across A&E departments of misdiagnoses that have led to serious injury and in some cases death." A BBC analysis of NHS Resolution figures using published data and freedom of information requests showed there were more than 1,623 A&E-related clinical negligence claims in 2025-26 in England – up from 1,151 in 2020-21. It means A&E is now the single biggest area for clinical negligence claims in terms of number. The value of those claims exceeded £550m last year. Not all claims will result in damages being paid – that happens in about half of all cases. The NHS sometimes accepts liability but it is judged compensation is not needed. And there were points during the 2010s when the number of claims were higher per A&E attendance than they were now before falling. But the sustained increase over the past five years is causing concern, say experts. The pattern is not being repeated in other areas, such as maternity or orthopaedics, and the low point in 2020-21 is thought to be unrelated to any behaviour changes by patients during the Covid pandemic as it takes three years on average for a claim to be submitted. The Royal College of Emergency Medicine told the BBC it was worried about the rise, linking it to increasing pressure and long delays being seen in A&E in recent years. Over the last two years one in 10 patients who attended A&E spent more than 12 hours waiting to be treated or discharged. RCEM's Dr Adrian Boyle said the figures were "sobering". "This is a concern. But it is not surprising when you see how busy departments are. People are staying longer and pressure on staffing is increasing." But he said clinical negligence cases were still relatively rare – happening in only around one in every 17,000 attendances. NHS Resolution, which supports NHS trusts with clinical negligence claims, said it was taking action on the "high volume" of claims and has published reports to help the NHS learn from mistakes. Such mistakes include missing the signs of acute deterioration in patients, failing to order the necessary tests and scans and making incorrect diagnoses. NHS England said claim numbers were not a good measure of current safety because of the lag between the incident happening and claims being logged, adding there were signs A&E waiting times had started improving. Matthew Hopkins, of NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, said health bosses were "making every effort is made to ensure safe, high-quality care, and that lessons are learned when that falls short". For Stephen, "every waking hour" is spent worrying

title: Oasis: Don't Look Back In Anger review - emotional documentary glosses over the hard stuff
description: The film captures the euphoria of Oasis' comeback, but fails to explore the story of their reunion.
body: Noel and Liam Gallagher premiered the documentary at the Venice Film Festival over the weekend "The little things that used to annoy us about each other have all gone away," says Noel Gallagher of reconciling with his brother, Liam. "It's not a power struggle any more." The scene comes towards the end of Don't Look Back In Anger, a sentimental and affectionate portrait of the band's comeback tour in 2025. But it's about as deep as we get into the band's 15-year hiatus. In an opening montage, we hear how Oasis conquered the world in the 1990s with hits like Wonderwall and Roll With It. As their fame grew, so did the brothers' animosity, until the party came to an abrupt halt backstage at a gig in Paris in 2009. Fan shot footage shows the promoter on stage, informing the crowd that the concert is cancelled following "a huge fight together in the dressing room". "The band doesn't exist any more," he announces, sounding more irritated than sad. According to Scottish singer Amy McDonald, who was also on the line-up, the altercation was seismic. "Liam smashed Noel's guitar, huuuge fight!" she tweeted from backstage. The film, however, never tells us what was said. Nobody explains the fall-out. We don't find out who instigated the rapprochement, nor do we hear how it affected their family. Instead, we cut to rehearsals for the comeback tour, with a caption informing us the brothers "didn't speak for 15 years", and an implication that all the wounds have been miraculously healed. Tantalisingly, the first song they practice is Columbia - a fan favourite that never made the tour's setlist - but there's a tension in the room. The band, under Noel's instruction, is piecing together the setlist. Liam won't arrive until later in the process, and no-one's sure which Liam they'll get. When he arrives, he seems fantastically grumpy, complaining about the sound-proofing panels that have been placed in front of Joey Waronker's drums. "They're already giving me the hump," he huffs. The documentary shows that the brothers' reconciliation was as genuine off-stage as it was in front of fans But when he steps up to the mic, the band relax. Guitarist Bonehead - who's strategically placed between Liam and Noel - beams from ear to ear. A couple of hours later, still in the middle of a song, Liam waves goodbye and casually strolls out of the rehearsal space. "I'm not sure whether our kid's enjoying himself," Noel says to his bandmates. In a voice-over, Liam reveals, enjoying himself wasn't the goal. "If you're not on it, chaos can ensue," he says, adding that he's given up cigarettes and alcohol (the intoxicants, not the song) for the duration of the tour. "These songs, they need to be treated with the utmost respect." The Rise and Fall of Oasis Liam's newfound professionalism is probably the biggest revelation in the documentary, scripted by Peaky Blinders' creator Steven Knight, and shot by directors Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace. To their presumable dismay, there are no scenes of the singer quitting the tour to go house-hunting, external; throwing snooker balls at Blur, external; or starting a fight on a cross-channel ferry. Instead, they complete rehearsals without incident and rock up to Cardiff's Principality Stadium for their public reunion. As the big moment looms, everyone limbers up in the corridors like middle-aged dads getting ready for a Park Run. But when they hit the stage, it's electric. The band are rumoured to be staging a second leg of their comeback tour next year Liam grabs Noel's hand and thrusts it into the air, they launch into the opening chords of Hello, and the crowd practically explodes with joy. As the gig continues, they dance and cheer and weep. During Slide Away, a man sinks to his knees and sings the lyrics, his hands clasped together as if in prayer. When the gig ends, cameras capture a young fan in an awe-struck stupor, unable to tear himself away from his spot on the stadium floor. This is where the documentary excels - capturing the sheer surge of affection that greeted Oasis's return. We visit shows in Dublin, Manchester, Sao Paolo, Tokyo and New York - and every one has a fan with a personal story to tell. One woman has named her dog Bonehead. Another is a Haenyeo - a South Korean free-diver - who says Oasis's music helped her out of depression. Noel, in particular, is blindsided by the impact. "The gravity hit me of what it meant to people and it took me by surprise," he reflects. "I have to say it actually knocked me back." During rehearsals, Bonehead jokes that he's been positioned between the Gallagher brothers as a peacemaker Structurally, though, the film has a problem. In a biopic, the triumphant night in Cardiff would have been the final scene - the moment of resolution after 15 years of pain. Here, it comes about 40 minutes into the action. Every subsequent concert just rinses and repeats the same story. The music is still thrilling. The live mix is impeccable. Liam sounds incredible. But Southern and Lovelace are left flailing around for a story. In Manchester, they focus on a priest delivering a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. In London, they follow a survivor of the Manchester Arena Bombing, who reflects on the way Don't Look Back In Anger became an anthem of resilience. But the film sidesteps the fact that Liam spent the mourning period criticising his brother for his failure to appear at charity shows supporting the survivors. It's not the only omission. There's no mention of the dynamic pricing row that overshadowed the launch of the tour (although Liam is heard apologising for the lack of "cheap seats" during one of the concerts). And while Noel praises Bonehead's contribution to the band, calling him "the sound of Oasis," we never hear from the guitarist; and the film nev

title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
description: The new leadership is trying to maintain both confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits.
body: The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning. It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minutes' drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR). In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away. Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience. The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes. So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it. In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors. The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos. "Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely. It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence? The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years. "Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th". OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock? This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable. "The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said. Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget. Chancellor refuses to rule out tax hikes in October Budget UK long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998 ahead of October Budget There was a focus on growth. As he toured the MTC, a centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing, he said the UK's "great talent and latent potential" made it the third most innovative country in the world, and he wanted to translate that into economic growth and success in more areas. Two decades ago, Healey was responsible for the Regional Development Agencies, scrapped by the Coalition Government, that helped fund this very facility. In his speech there was a big clue about how to square the circle of investing in industrial policy at a time of tricky public finances. The "Pufins" - public finance institutions - such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund can invest strategically, less constrained by the government's borrowing rules. Part of the plan is Pufins to breed more unicorns ($1bn tech startups) in the UK. This is the other part of the global backdrop. Amid the tumult of trade and military wars, there is arguably one of the biggest financial events in world history. In the coming weeks, hundreds of billions of dollars will be invested and trillions in value confirmed from flotations of big American AI firms. The UK has some standout technology in this sector. The government wants to promote it. The chancellor was also, however, cautious about the impact of AI on security and on jobs. Some degree of "public control" could be required to make these changes work for everyone. It appeared a little less cheerleading than the stance of the Starmer administration. The chancellor was perhaps mindful of the army of manufacturing robots, laser welders, 3D metal printers, whirring into action around him. Long term, it will be growth that will determine whether his borrowing rules are met, he said. Ultimately he will be judged by his actual policy choices, but where there are trade-offs between balancing the books and economic growth across the country, this sounds like a chancellor who might prioritise the latter. title: Powerlifter wins golds despite endometriosis pain
description: Lhamo Weston says it's important to be open about competing with endometriosis
body: Lhamo Weston trains for her powerlifting competitions at a gym in Redditch A teenage powerlifter managed to win double golds at a world championship despite her endometriosis flaring up to leave her in excruciating pain just before the competition. Lhamo Weston, from Redditch, also landed second on the podium with a silver and a bronze medal, across three events in the World Sub-Junior & Junior Powerlifting Championships, in South Africa last month. The 18-year-old only took up the sport three years ago, after being inspired by her brother to give it a go. Weston now uses social media to speak openly about having endometriosis and being a young woman in the sport of powerlifting, in the hope of empowering others. Lhamo Weston placed second overall at the World Sub-Junior & Junior Powerlifting Championships Lhamo told the BBC she loves competing in the sport because of its inclusivity. "I love how inclusive it is and how we're like a community," she said. "Everyone knows each other and are really supportive of each other, and I just think it's an amazing sport that really brings people together." She stood on the podium in the Under 57kg category at the championship after getting two golds in squat and deadlift, and a bronze in the bench event. "It felt incredible to be completely honest, I went into it with expectations of potentially reaching podium. I didn't initially expect to place second or even have a chance at placing first," she said. This is the first time Llamo has competed at international level But a flare up of her endometriosis, a condition which sees tissue similar to the lining of the womb grow outside of it, meant she was competing in difficult conditions: "That led to excruciating amounts of pain and a lot of issues again with making weight, which really affected me leading into comp," Lhamo continued. "It can affect my training with the pain, I get quite tired and I also get back pain which can feel the same as a back injury. It was difficult but we managed to do it." Lhamo has been celebrating back home with her medals Endometriosis affects one in 10 women in the UK, but she says many people don't know about it. "There's not enough awareness about it and how it actually impacts women and girls," she continued. "I've been dealing with endometriosis since I was 12, and I only got diagnosed last year. It was a very long journey and I just think there needs to be more awareness so we can try and find solutions to help other people. "As for powerlifting, if you want to do it, go for it. At the end of the day, there's nothing holding you back." Sam Pope from Elite Fitness in Redditch says Lhamo is an inspiration to all The teenager trains at Elite Fitness gym in Redditch and, despite recently moving to Worcester, still travels the 45 minutes to get there. Sam Pope, who works there, says Lhamo is an inspiration. "For other young people of her age, it just shows that actually if you put the effort in, the reward is there," he said. "We take pride knowing we house her here as a member because we are very much like a family. "To have her as a role model is very important because it does allow others to think 'I can do this as well' and I think that's very important not just at our gym but every gym as well." title: India's high-stakes exam system faces a crisis of trust
description: As exam scandals persist, critics ask whether fixing the centralised testing agency is enough or if the model needs to change.
body: Millions of students appear for tests conducted by India's National Testing Agency every year In 2017, India introduced the National Testing Agency (NTA) to conduct fair, transparent and standardised examinations. Set up under the federal education ministry, it was meant to make exams more efficient, consistent and trustworthy, after years of paper leaks, administrative errors and cheating allegations. Over the next few years, the agency took charge of some of India's largest and most competitive tests, including medical and engineering entrance examinations, university admissions and eligibility tests for teaching and research. But eight years later, the organisation created to restore trust in India's exams is facing a crisis of confidence of its own. In June, more than two million students had to retake a crucial medical entrance examination after the paper was leaked. The fallout triggered weeks of youth-led protests which eventually led to the resignation of the federal education minister. In response, the government appointed a high-level task force led by tech tycoon Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms and restore confidence in the examination system. For many Indians, however, the announcement prompted a sense of déjà vu. A similar panel was established in 2024 after irregularities in another medical entrance examination sparked widespread unrest. That committee proposed more than 100 reforms, a little over half of which, external have reportedly been fully implemented. The cycle has repeated: an exam goes wrong, students protest, a committee is appointed and reforms are proposed - only for another crisis to expose the same weaknesses. Experts the BBC spoke to say the problems go beyond paper leaks - from NTA's accountability and capacity to exam centralisation, design and whether India's high-stakes testing system needs a rethink. More than two million students appeared for the NEET-UG retest BJ Rao, who was part of the 2024 panel and is now head of SGT University near Delhi, says India should move more decisively towards computer-based examinations to minimise the chances of paper leaks, increase efficiency and reduce human involvement wherever possible. "Digital connectivity has vastly improved across the country, what we need to do is put in resources and focus on upgrading infrastructure and move to computer-based exams," he told the BBC. "We currently have ad hoc centres for conducting exams. We need to replace them with standardised state-controlled online centres." But technology alone will not solve the problem, he says. Rao points to the NTA's reliance on contract staff: just 24 of its 221 employees are permanent, with many from bureaucratic backgrounds, according to the government. "When you have a large portion of people who work on a temporary basis then there is no sense of belonging, and that has an impact on the functions as well. You need people who are well-versed in academia and experienced in conducting such assessments to ensure better management and oversight," he explains. Some experts argue that repeated crises have exposed flaws not only in how exams are conducted, but also in how they are designed. Keshav Aggarwal, an educationist and president of Educators Federation, says the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) or NEET-UG - whose paper leak triggered this year's protests - could be restructured along the lines of the country's engineering entrance examination, which is computer-based and conducted in two stages. Rather than relying on a single high-stakes test day, the exams could be held across multiple sessions with different sets of questions, he says. "Different stages and days with varying sets of questions" would reduce the risks associated with any one examination and make the system more resilient to disruptions, Aggarwal explains. The NEET-UG paper leak triggered massive protests in India Experts also question whether an annual exam can work when millions compete for limited university places. India needs a system where students can take important entrance exams more than once a year, as is common in some western countries, said Yamini Aiyar, senior visiting fellow at Brown University. "This would give students another chance if an exam is cancelled or they do not perform well, reducing the risk of losing an entire year," she says. For millions of Indian students, the risk is real. Many spend years preparing and tens of thousands of rupees on private tuition. A leaked, cancelled or delayed exam can suddenly upend months or years of preparation. Pari, 17, experienced that uncertainty first-hand. After taking NEET this year, she had to retake it after the original exam was cancelled following a paper leak. "It was very frustrating. All our preparation had gone to waste, and we had to start all over again," she said. The experience left her angry at repeated exam failures. "The government can form as many panels as it likes. We need a system strong enough to prevent paper leaks from happening again." Mansi Bansal, 23, has a similar story. She spent months preparing for UGC-NET, a qualification for entry-level college teaching jobs. The exam was cancelled after a 2024 paper leak and again this year after the NTA cited errors in three subjects. Bansal took the affected commerce paper and will retest on 9 September. "I put my life on hold all these months, stopping going to the gym, hanging out with friends or even attending family gatherings," she said. "I had planned my entire year but now it has all gone into uncertainty. Can the government promise a leak won't happen again?" Student activists and opposition parties have been demanding to scrap the NTA Such experiences have fuelled calls from student activists and opposition politicians to scrap the NTA altogether. title: What big issues are on the agenda as Stormont returns after summer?
description: What challenges face assembly members and ministers as Stormont returns after the summer recess?
body: Ministers and MLAs are to return to Stormont on Monday It's not even the start of a new Stormont term and already there have been leaks. Albeit it wasn't some big scoop but a rather damp surprise for the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) MLA Colin McGrath, who took to social media saying a water leak over summer had left his assembly office looking worse for wear, external. Even the most casual observers of politics here could guess, however, that Stormont's leaky roof problems are outweighed by the ever-slow drip of political activity inside the building - a place the assembly's freshest face will witness for himself from this week. On Tuesday, Paul Boggs was named Sinn Féin's new West Tyrone MLA after Maoliosa McHugh - who'd already said he wouldn't run in the next election - decided to call it quits. Boggs brings the number of MLAs who have been co-opted since the last assembly election to 14 and that figure could go up still before the upcoming election next May. Co-options aside (that's a whole other piece), the backdrop of said looming election means parties are likely to be in fighting form when Stormont sittings resume on Monday. No time for new minister to fix health service warns top doctor 'Sinn Féin will not walk away from Stormont', says Michelle O'Neill Maolíosa McHugh stepping down as West Tyrone MLA The newly-appointed Health Minister Robbie Butler will be one of those quick to feel pressure, as the 10-year anniversary of the Bengoa report - a major health reform review - approaches next month. Pay pressures in his department and the Department of Education also make for another winter of discontent, with the prospect of strike action yet to be ruled out. We know by now that Butler and other ministers argue that their hands are tied without a budget that can allow them to meet all their outstanding pressures. Executive parties have been taking part in talks with Treasury officials in a bid to break the deadlock but 36 days since the legal deadline to pass a budget expired, there has so far been little sign of light at the end of this tunnel. So much so that it prompted SDLP leader of the opposition Matthew O'Toole to issue a call to public bodies across Northern Ireland this week, asking them how the ongoing lack of financial certainty is affecting their services. Robbie Butler signing the pledge of office at Stormont after being appointed as health minister Whether point scoring or simply making a wider point about the consequences of not having a budget, others are also talking about the problems being stored up at Stormont. Think tank Pivotal published a report, external last week on the issue, noting that several departments are facing massive overspends this year, including deficits of about £800m in health and £250m in education. Money matters are a major sticking point for this executive but whether this can be resolved rests on what comes out of talks with Treasury and the secretary of state - more of those are expected to happen with the parties this week. The budget, as big as it is, is only one item on the executive's to-do list before the assembly dissolves in March ahead of the election. Already ministers have been repeatedly warned by assembly Speaker Edwin Poots that time is running out to pass remaining pieces of legislation through all their hurdles. It's not uncommon for Stormont to sit into the small hours or hold extra days of sittings as the end of a mandate approaches - this one will be no different but there are serious question marks over some key bills. Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald's so-called "Good Jobs" Bill which aims to massively reform employment laws has yet to get executive agreement, after the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said it had no support among business groups. Other flagship policies including the redevelopment of Casement Park and the A5 road project also remain mothballed due to financial and legal disputes. The reality is that as the countdown to election day gets closer the harder it will be for the executive to make decisions on major issues, for fear that any misstep could go down badly with their respective bases. The first and deputy first ministers will be feeling the heat in their own ways The largest parties - Sinn Féin and the DUP - will be feeling the heat in their own ways. Sinn Féin, which became the largest party for the first time in the last election, needs to consolidate its support and show that it can deliver - without a legislative win or two in the next few months this may be hard to demonstrate on the doorsteps. The DUP faces its own challenges of going into its first election since the conviction of former party leader Jeffrey Donaldson in June for child sex abuse offences, which he is appealing. In July, the party moved to commission an independent review over Donaldson's actions while he was a member of the DUP, but it is not yet clear when the report will be completed or published. Throw in fresh tensions over Drumcree, continuing rows over Irish language signage and pressure on Alliance's agriculture minister over a controversial cattle cull last month and it all makes for a battle a day. If this current executive has anything going for it, it's that leaks of information and counter briefings against each other are much more rare than in the last executive. Often the mood around the table is described as collegiate, even if ministers disagree on an issue. But as one Stormont source put it recently: "You can't leak anything if there's nothing to leak. This is an executive in a holding pattern." Sooner rather than later this executive will have to circle back to big issues that can't be ducked forever. title: Why Reform UK undercover donations claims are legally complicated
description: A look at the key allegations concerning foreign donations and where they sit with the law.
body: Reform UK has been hit by a row over foreign donations as the party's leaders and supporters gather for their annual conference. The row centres on allegations which surfaced during undercover filming by Verbatim Investigations - founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting - and broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday. The party denies any wrongdoing and says it is investigating. Robert Jenrick, Reform's economy spokesperson, said the two senior aides in the film had been suspended, telling the BBC's Today programme: "Nigel [Farage] got rid of the two people who did this…he acted swiftly, they've gone." Both Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported Reform to the Metropolitan Police, which says it is assessing the claims but has not launched an investigation. The Electoral Commission says it is "in touch" with the police. We have looked at each of the three main allegations and where they sit with the law. In the film, Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr suggest a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations for the party, one of which would have totaled £500,000. Jukes meets an undercover reporter posing as a UK-based son of a wealthy American financier, who voices concern that his father could not directly donate to Reform within the law. Jukes tells him: "You do realise that you can do it?" According to Channel 4, Jukes was suggesting that the donation could be in the son's name, even though the money would have come from his American father. A similar arrangement is also mooted in a meeting with Orr. Farage is shown saying "it's all above board" and expressing thanks. On Friday, Farage said he was in fact asking whether it was above board. Channel 4 says the proposed £500,000 donation was never made. Under electoral law, you must be a UK registered voter or a company registered in the UK to be a "permissable" donor to a UK political party. In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, but his father would not be. Any donation of more than £500 from an impermissible source must be declared to the Electoral Commission and returned within 30 days. If the party keeps it beyond that, it is deemed to have accepted the donation - and that could lead to a fine and potential criminal investigation. Two Reform officials step down after undercover donations report Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk' Channel 4 says Reform commissioned three opinion polls between January and July 2026, costing £32,500 in total. One was on the front page of the Telegraph newspaper under the headline "Labour would face wipeout if elections went ahead"; another on the front page of the Times with the headline "Reform vote in unions at same level as Labour". In the film, Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps the American financier could pay for opinion polling to help with Reform's campaigns. He is shown saying this would "technically be a donation in kind" but "the reality is we could easily get away with it". The public was not told who had commissioned and paid for the three polls. Polling firm JL Partners, the Telegraph and the Times have all said this was not known to them either. Farage said on Friday the polls in question had been commissioned by an independent third party and that Reform had "not done anything wrong". Any legitimate donations from permissible donors worth more than £11,180 in a calendar year must, by law, be declared to the Electoral Commission. The £32,500 polling payment does not appear to have been declared. The legal definition for a political party donation includes payments for studies and research. This video can not be played Watch: Undercover reporters posing as party donors meet with Nigel Farage The Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000 specifically outlaws knowingly taking steps to disguise or conceal that a donation has come from an impermissible source. As part of this, it can be a crime for someone to conceal money spent on expenses incurred directly or indirectly by the party - and to mislead a party on the source of a donation. The maximum sentence is 12 months in prison. It is in this context that Labour is demanding the police investigate the polling and whether there is evidence of concealing who actually paid for it. But investigating this and the other claims in the film would be hugely complex - and a 30-minute TV report could not be the sole basis for a prosecution. The police would almost certainly ask Channel 4 for all the unused filmed material, research notes and plans for the documentary. Detectives would want to interview everyone involved and understand their intentions. In a statement on Friday, JL Partners said that "sometimes people with a party alignment make suggestions about potential clients who may be interested in commissioning and paying for polling" in the UK and abroad, and that it would not expect to be told the precise relationship between Reform and the US-based company. Nick Vamos, former head of specialist crime at the Crown Prosecution Service, explained: "It is very common for allegations of electoral offences to be reported to the police, especially by political rivals looking to score points," adding the police would assess the evidence neutrally to decide whether a full investigation is required. Such offences very rarely lead to prosecution. Between 2011 and 2021, the Electoral Commission referred eight cases to the Met, none of which resulted in charges. Even if there were an investigation, it would take months to get near specialist detectives or prosecutors. Elsewhere in the film, Jukes appears to list other supporters of Reform UK who have potentially donated to the party through UK residents. The names, made in the context of discussing the proposed £500,000 arrangement, are bleeped out. He is shown telling the undercover reporter: "But,

title: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
description: Nigel Farage's admirers in the party are calling for a stronger operation as the party aims for power.
body: "It makes us look a bit like a pirate ship," a senior Reform figure acknowledges privately, deeply frustrated that after a year in which they say the party has "radically professionalised" the events of the last few days could still happen. It was the recurring conversation throughout Reform UK's conference in Birmingham: the consequences of the undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 News which has cost two senior party figures their jobs, at least for now. How much damage does it cause to Reform? And what does it tell us about them? "A key part of the appeal of us is the sense of us being cavaliers. Doing things differently. Standing out. And that's great. We have roundheads too. Those who ask the boring questions. Do the checks. We need more of them," this same senior figure adds. The story of Reform over the last 12 months can be summarised in three words: defections, elections and money. Farage says his aides' donor comments were 'loose pub talk' Reform donations row overshadows party's moment to lay out big ideas Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman. Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland. But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours. In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable. Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours. Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham. Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave. Reform wants to project itself as ready to run the country. Some saw James Orr's work as head of policy as key to that professionalisation. Orr as well as Dan Jukes, a close aide to Nigel Farage, have been suspended and both deny wrongdoing. "We need people to see the reality that Reform is getting ready for government," I am told. And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law. Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern. But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture." There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought. Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match. Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly. Both Orr and Jukes will be missed profoundly by those inside the party. Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return. Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic. Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see. Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed. The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months. title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
description: With Argentina's President Milei promising "winds of change" over the Falklands, will Donald Trump shift his stance on British rule?
body: Argentine President Javier Milei enjoys a warm relationship with President Trump The tone over the Falkland Islands dispute has been sharpening in Argentina from well before President Javier Milei's late-night national address on sanctions earlier this week. It's tempting to see a visual representation of the tension in the jubilant Argentine players celebrating their hard-fought win over England at the Fifa World Cup this summer holding a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentine - in front of their deliriously happy fans. However, the ill-feeling has been fomenting for much longer. President Milei began his Thursday address with a brief history of the Falklands, very much from the Argentine perspective. He repeated the refrain at the heart of their position: the islands "rightfully belong" to Argentina. The British had invaded and colonially occupied the islands in 1833, he said, violently wrestling the territory from Argentina's hands. UK support for Falkland Islands 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims, No 10 says The UK Government would say he conveniently overlooked a few details. The European powers interchanged control over the islands throughout the 17th and 18th centuries. In December 1831, an Argentine settlement was largely dismantled not by the British but by an American warship, the USS Lexington, amid a dispute over local fishing and sealing rights, after which many inhabitants left. An Argentine garrison which arrived in 1832 was expelled by the British when they reoccupied the land in 1833. Still, if the Americans had a hand in forcing the Argentines out two centuries ago, they may now play a central role in strengthening the Argentine claim. President Milei certainly thinks so. "Winds of change" were blowing, he assured the Argentine people, after President Trump said he was "re-evaluating" the US position on the Falklands. The US recognises Britain's rule over the Falklands - but Trump has suggested he is "re-evaluating" the US position That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982 – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict. For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran. "You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific. Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his estranged vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing. Fifa fined the Argentine Football Association after players held up a banner claiming the Falklands, breaching rules against political messaging Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it. With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added. On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have. In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally. The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas. Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics. Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship". Correction 11 September: An earlier version of this report said that a US warship had forced out an Argentine settlement from the Falklands in 1831, leaving the islands uninhabited. In fact, while many inhabitants left, some remained. An Argentine garrison was also expelled when the British reoccupied the land in 1833. The article was amended to reflect this. title: Why do ex-MPs join the 'Chiltern Hundreds' list?
description: Sir Keir Starmer is the latest person to take the office as a means of resigning as an MP.
body: Sir Keir Starmer and Boris Johnson are two of hundreds of MPs who resigned by taking the Chiltern Hundreds position Sir Keir Starmer and Boris Johnson have this in common: They both stepped down as Prime Minister before their term was up, and within three years of winning an election. Their subsequent resignation as a sitting MP means they have also shared the unusual office of "Steward and Bailiff of the Three Hundreds of Chiltern". Sir Keir is the latest person to pick up the title after resigning as an MP this week. What is it, and what does it have to do with the Chilterns? MPs across the generations have used the mechanism to resign from their role Thanks to a law dating back to 1624, Members of Parliament (MPs) in the UK are not technically permitted to resign. "Unless they die or are expelled, they must become disqualified if they wish to retire before the end of a Parliament," according to the UK Parliament website. This is because back in the 17th Century, MPs often accepted the role reluctantly, so leaving the job was not to be encouraged. A "parliamentary loophole" was created to get around this, according to the History of Parliament blog, external. "An MP can do this by requesting, and accepting, office as either the Steward and Bailiff of the Chiltern Hundreds, or Steward and Bailiff of the Manor of Northstead," wrote Dr Martin Spychal. "Both offices (or jobs) are nominal. They exist in name only, have no responsibilities and are unpaid." Anyone with these titles is disqualified from being an MP – originally in order to prevent royal influence on politics – but later used by parliamentarians who were unhappy with their lot. High Wycombe is one of the towns in the Chiltern Hundreds region The "hundreds" were areas that belonged to the Crown as far back as the 13th Century. The three Chiltern Hundreds mentioned today refer to Stoke, Desborough and Burnham in Buckinghamshire. The regions include the towns of Amersham, Beaconsfield, High Wycombe, Marlow, Eton and Chesham. Coincidentally, these are near to the prime minister's countryside residence in Buckinghamshire – Chequers. Because a steward of the hundreds might be able to benefit financially from the role, or promote the interests of the crown, it was seen as a conflict of interest. "Resourceful MPs discovered that they could request appointment to these offices, which then disqualified them from sitting in the Commons," wrote Spychal. Nigel Farage and Nadine Dorries are among those to be appointed to the Manor of Northstead or the Chiltern Hundreds The House of Commons Information Office said: "The Stewardship of the Chiltern Hundreds is thought to have been used for the first time as a means of resignation from the House of Commons on 17 January 1751 by John Pitt, who wanted to vacate his seat for Wareham and stand for Dorchester." The Manor of Northstead, in North Yorkshire, is the other remaining office given to resigning MPs. Its most recent recipient was Reform UK's Nigel Farage who resigned in order to stand for re-election in his own constituency. The titles are given out alternately, in case two MPs wish to step down at the same time, and each new appointment replaces the previous one. Spychal said there have been calls to reform the system since 1775 - but in 2026, the peculiar British formality lives on. Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. title: Michael Owen doesn't tell his children he loves them - how big a deal is that?
description: His comments sparked discussions around parenting, gender and culture, and just how important those three simple words are.
body: England football legend Michael Owen sparked debate this week after saying he "never ever" tells his children he loves them - despite them being "the most dearest things in the world" to him. "I don't say anything like that," the father-of-four told Jamie Laing in a podcast interview., external "I just assume my actions would show them that I love them. I think most of us are like that." While some were surprised at Owen's comments, saying they always make sure to tell their children how they feel, other parents say they share the ex-striker's outlook. The exchange has highlighted different attitudes around parenting, gender and culture, and raises the question - just how important are those three simple words? Experts tell us making your child feel loved comes from more than just a simple turn of phrase. Educational psychologist Dr Patricia Britto says while words can often be crucial, the most important thing is that a child feels "safe, valued and emotionally secure". "We shouldn't conclude that children have been psychologically damaged and harmed simply because they don't hear those words," she tells the BBC. "They may experience love very clearly through actions." Dr Britto says the bigger issue for many children is whether they feel affection is "consistently communicated" which can come through both words and actions, or better yet a combination of the two. "If you said to a child 'I love you, I love you' but you never turn up to any of their football games or shows, they might not actually feel loved. They might just feel they are empty words." Michael Owen with eldest daughter and Love Island star Gemma - and the pair together in 2005, when he played for Newcastle Dad Aaron Dale, host of the Raisingboys2men podcast and author of a book on parenting, agrees. "It's not words or actions - they shouldn't compete against each other, they should complement each other. "Words are to speak the message and actions are the evidence." Dale pointed to how his own father would often tell him "I love you" after letting him down, diminishing the meaning of the words. However, some parents believe it is absolutely crucial their child hears that they are loved. One father of a seven-year-old daughter, told us he was surprised by Owen's comments, describing them as "awful". "You should always tell your children you love them no matter what, when they're bad, when they're good," he said. And reacting online to the clip of Owen, another parent wrote: "Parents and potential parents do not listen to this man. Tell your kids you love them everyday, even when it annoys them." To the outside observer, Owen's love for his children is not in doubt. The trailer for his new show, Meet the Owens, shows glimpses of what appears to be a happy home life with his wife and children. And in 2024, the former England striker spoke movingly about his son James's sight loss, saying: "If I could give him my eyes... I would." Pushed by podcast host Laing to explain why he doesn't let the 'I love yous' flow freely, Owen told Laing that "I would love to be a little bit soft". "I'm definitely getting softer," he said, "but still not soft enough to say anything like that." Using the word "soft" to describe telling your children you love them reflects long-standing attitudes many fathers have towards parenting, both Dale and Dr Britto suggest. They say it's a result of different contexts, such as culture, class, gender and a generational divide "I think that's the dangerous part there," Dale says, "the belief of what men should and what men shouldn't do." Many fathers believe their role is simply to "provide", but they can do so much more, he says. "Men are much more than just providers... what about our emotional capacity and willingness to have conversations and be there as fathers? And maybe we can't provide, but you know what? Our presence is at full capacity." He adds that he thinks people's style of parenting "always stems from somewhere", including whether they were often told they were loved as a child. Aaron Dale writes and posts about parenting on TikTok, and says he believes our parenting style comes from how our own parents behaved Gender expectations and masculinity are not the only element at play, Dr Britto says. "In some cultures they don't even use those words [I love you] at all," she says. "They may ask things like 'Have you eaten?' as a sign of love rather than actually saying 'I love you'." She adds: "As an African myself, in Nigerian culture parents don't always say 'I love you'... but I still felt loved." Parents also suggest that different generations may approach showing love for their children in different ways. Reacting on social media, one says Owen is right to suggest actions speak louder than words: "My dad never said the words, but it was also never in doubt." Another writes: "What's the big deal? My dad - and I'm sure most dads of our generation - didn't. He did something far, far better than emotional words he 'showed us' by his actions." While Owen's comments may have triggered strong feelings, it is clear there are countless ways parents communicate love to their children. Above all, says Dr Britto, it's about making sure children feel a sense of belonging. "Do they feel loved?" she says. "Do they feel wanted? "Do they feel that they matter, rather than simply hearing the words?" Our family fell out. title: New GP and wellbeing hub 'a major milestone'
description: The £21m hub brings together primary care, community wellbeing and leisure services in one location.
body: Dr Paul Moore says the new hub will reinforce the message that "your GP is there for you" A cluster of empty and under‑used buildings in East Sussex has been transformed into a £21m modern health hub. Wellbeing Square in Newhaven, which brings together primary care, community wellbeing and leisure services in one location, officially opened on Thursday. The project was led by Lewes District Council, which said it would "deliver a high‑quality, modern healthcare environment that residents so richly deserve". Council leader Zoe Nicholson called the venue a "major milestone in the history of the town". "Not only is it transformational for people living in Newhaven but is also central to our wider regeneration plans," she said. The completed scheme includes two state‑of‑the‑art GP practices, a new pharmacy, an extension to Seahaven Swim & Fitness Centre operated by Wave Active, and a creative/co‑working space. Lewes councillor Zoe Nicholson says the hub is "transformational" The council says the plan is to create an environment which can offer healthcare, wellbeing and community services delivered side‑by‑side. The two GP surgeries combined will serve more than 15,000 local residents, with more than 5.500 appointments offered on the site each month. Dr Paul Moore, a GP at Quayside Medical Practice, said: "We are encouraging people to be as healthy as they can." He says the new hub will reinforce the message that "your GP is there for you". Allison Cannon, chief nursing officer for NHS Sussex and Surrey, says the new hub will make it easier for people to access support closer to home and at a convenient time. "This is exactly the kind of neighbourhood approach we want to see more of across Surrey and Sussex," she said. "It's where health services, local partners and communities come together to help people stay well, tackle health inequalities and support healthier lives." title: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
description: The party's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny, says BBC political editor Chris Mason.
body: Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in the Senedd and in local authorities. But they also gather amid significant political headwinds, much of which revolve around money. There was that whopping £5m gift to Nigel Farage from Christopher Harborne, the Thailand based British billionaire, and the long running row about whether the money should have been declared by Farage once he became an MP. Then there is, among other things, the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to the party during the last general election campaign. Reform insists that it "takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations." When the party got together in the same West Midlands venue a year ago, they were an insurgency provoking intrigue and attention and demonstrating plenty of momentum. Indeed that momentum was so significant that it was a major factor, perhaps the major factor, in accelerating the demise of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, because the potential prospect of a Reform government frightened the Labour Party to its core. Would Starmer, its then desperately unpopular leader, help or hinder their attempts to take on Farage? Hinder was the eventually overwhelming view within Labour, and so Starmer was a goner. But politics can change, and change quickly. With Starmer out and Burnham in, there is early evidence of some support for Labour picking up. No longer are Reform comfortably leading in all the opinion polls - in some they're not leading at all. Add to this a more confident and prominent Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives and the recent rise too of Restore Britain, the outfit set up by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. And the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru won and so beat them in the devolved elections in Scotland and Wales respectively. In other words, collectively Reform's opponents appear more energised and popular. Make no mistake, no party at a UK wide level is popular at the moment, but the scrap appears more evenly matched than it did. This video can not be played Watch: 'I firmly believe I have broken no rules,' Farage tells BBC Into that mix, Reform's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny. Nigel Farage is a candidate for prime minister; his senior team candidates for the great offices of state. When I interviewed Farage at Reform HQ yesterday, on the specifics of the £5m gift and the police investigation he maintained they've acted appropriately. But he offered an insight into how he perceives the hurricane of questions he faces. "I think what you're seeing is the establishment - in a very coordinated way - fighting back," he claimed. I suggested he sounded like a conspiracy theorist, implying the whole world was out to get him. His answer was instructive: "When you read in the newspaper you're under investigation, and you don't even know a complaint's been made, you can see the degree of collusion that has gone on between interested parties. This will not stop. They will continually try and do this to us." Who's they? I pressed. He mentioned the House of Commons and House of Lords – full of his political opponents – but didn't name anyone or anything else. "I'm talking about normal human behaviour. People who, people who hold positions of power, influence, and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding." Let's be clear – it is a big claim to allege collusion between institutions or organisations collectively seeking to undermine him and his party, and there is no evidence for it. But, crucially, you hear in his answer a sense of why he perceives that - that is what it feels like. The question, as Reform's conference gets under way, is how the party approaches the coming days and the coming months. Will Nigel Farage ditch the "aggrieved" tone he has been accused of adopting recently? Reform up against 'complainants' society', Farage tells BBC Yes, his clear hint to me. "I've generally, you know, gone through politics with a smile…I'll go back to doing what I've been doing for the last 34 years," he said. And as for their pitch to you at conference? A Reform government would achieve, and achieve quickly, they claim. The party is promising a list of promises it would deliver in the first 100 days of a majority government, with every senior minister in a Farage government making and delivering one clear pledge. But would they be able to if there is validity in their current claim that plenty of institutions are trying to stymie them? Do you have any views, comments or questions about this story? title: Why 'sleepmaxxing' could be making your sleep worse
description: The things you're doing to make your sleep better could actually be making your sleep worse.
body: Sleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of sleeping has become a minefield. Trying to optimise sleep in this way is called "sleepmaxxing". Take it too far, and you could end up with "orthosomnia" - the clinical term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep. While it's not formally recognised as a condition in the UK, doctors tell the BBC they've noticed signs of orthosomnia in their patients, with some bringing their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced, wrongly, that they have a sleep disorder. That fixation is actually making people's sleep worse, they warn. So how and why did sleep become so complicated? And if sleepmaxxing isn't the answer, what is the elusive secret to a good night's sleep? The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009. Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn. These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement). Many also give users a "sleep score". But the concept of a sleep score is "completely made up", according to Dr Alanna Hare, consultant of sleep medicine at the Royal Brompton Hospital in London. "There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC. "That's just been created by manufacturers." This video can not be played How sleep-tracking can make your sleep worse Hare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients. "I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says. Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds. "It's great that there's more focus on sleep as part of wellness," she adds. "But sleep just does not respond well to attempts to perfect it." One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct". In response, Oura told the BBC that it "stand[s] behind our science, research and accuracy claims". "We're committed to clearly communicating what Oura measures, what it estimates, and how members should use that information," the company added. Studies also show sleep trackers can affect how you function during the day, even if they're not accurate. In one study, external from the University of Oxford, participants were given sleep trackers which assigned them a sleep score. The scores were randomised, however, and had no relation to how the participants had actually slept. The next day participants rated their mood, fatigue levels and alertness, before tests checking their focus and reaction times. Researchers found that the people told they'd slept badly reported feeling more fatigued, and were less mentally alert - even though the sleep scores were all fake. This is something Jess Hill says she noticed in herself after getting a Garmin watch several years ago. "I started to rely on the watch as my Bible for whether I slept well or not," the 32-year-old HR professional from London tells the BBC. "I would think, 'I've had awful sleep so I'm going to really struggle today', even if I actually probably had okay sleep. If I'd slept really well, I'd be convinced I'd have to be on top - even though I was tired, I was pushing through things." Jess Hill was "obsessed" with her Garmin's sleep scores for about three years Her "obsession", as she describes it, with getting a high sleep score lasted three years, until earlier this year, when she started to notice the watch wasn't reflecting how she'd actually slept. "I was awake the other week for four hours in the night, and my watch was like 'wow, great sleep!' - I literally was awake from 01:00 until 05:00," she says. The BBC has approached Garmin for comment. Jess's sleep scores weren't matching how she actually felt Dr Neil Stanley, sleep expert and author of the book How to Sleep Well, argues that gamifying sleep is creating more disordered sleeping. "The thing with tracking your sleep is that it gives you a number, and this means you have a target," he tells the BBC. "So you get into this cycle of worrying about your quality of sleep or the quantity of sleep based on figures." He says he carried out research into actigraphy - wrist-worn sleep trackers - around 40 years ago. Though commercial trackers now are a bit more sophisticated, they work in much the same way - by measuring your movement - and have the same limitations, he says. "If you want to measure sleep, you have to measure the brain," Stanley adds. "Unless you're measuring the brain's activities, you're not measuring sleep." Keeping your bedroom cool, dark and quiet - within reason. "That doesn't mean it needs to be pitch black, exactly 16C or totally silent," she says. "It should be coolish, darkish and quietish." Seeing bright light in the morning, which is good for regulating your circadian rhythm - that is, your body's natural clock. Doing light exercise, and eating a "healthy, Mediterranean-style diet with plenty of plant variability". Above all, keeping it simple - "anything else, you don't need it".
