title: Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics
description: Burnham's exchanges with Kemi Badenoch slipped into familiar territory of trading barbs, writes Alex Forsyth.
body: Throughout the summer Andy Burnham's been attempting to cultivate a new style of communicating with a steady stream of social media videos designed to speak directly to the public. But alongside his digital push, the prime minister still has to master one of Westminster's weekly traditions; the political back and forth that is Prime Minister's Questions. To some it might seem outdated in a modern media world, but the exchange across the despatch box is still deemed vital by many in Westminster as a moment of scrutiny; a chance for the public to peer into Parliament's workings and a crucial factor in setting the mood among backbench MPs as they watch – and judge – the performance of party leaders. So the debut of a new prime minister matters. Badenoch presses Burnham on borrowing costs at his first Prime Minister's Questions Burnham took his place in the House of Commons chamber to raucous cheers from the packed Labour benches and struck a confident tone from the start, clearly keen to maintain the sense of optimism he's promised the country. His initial exchanges with Kemi Badenoch were vaguely jocular. The Conservative leader started with a joke about the prime minister's stamina after a marathon Commons' session on Tuesday when he took questions for more than three hours; there was laughter from MPs and a cautious smile from Burnham. But if there was an early twinkle in the eye of either party leader their exchanges soon slipped into more familiar territory, trading barbs over tax and borrowing with Badenoch making claims of profligate government spending. Burnham, despite his promises to end what he's called political "point scoring" was soon pointing the finger at the Tories for their economic record, referencing the budget of former Prime Minister Liz Truss while promising he'd deliver fiscal discipline. He's not the first prime minister to pledge a new style of politics only to find it hard to dodge the adversarial nature of PMQs. David Cameron said he'd end "Punch and Judy politics" when he became Tory leader only to find himself in regular political knockabouts across the despatch box. But while the political barbs continued it's clear that Burnham is a more comfortable communicator than his predecessor. His real challenge will be delivering more than a change in tone. Andy Burnham speaking during his first Prime Minister's Questions in the House of Commons, London, with Conservative MPs including party leader Kemi Badenoch watching on The backdrop to his first few days as prime minister with Westminster in full swing has been the increased cost of borrowing – a global trend but one to which the UK is exposed and which looks likely to limit the chancellor's room for manoeuvre at the budget come the end of October. Burnham has promised a transformational government but he's facing many of the same challenges as Sir Keir Starmer, with difficult decisions on defence spending, welfare and social care - to name just a few - hurtling towards him. These are the pressure points his political opponents will seek to exploit, as evidenced by Badenoch's approach at Prime Minister's Questions when she quizzed him over plans for taxes, spending and borrowing. Burnham pointed to his early actions in office, cutting VAT on domestic electricity bills and business rates for pubs and music venues as a sign of his priorities, but he gave little more away – leaning back on another familiar refrain that prime ministers don't write budgets from the despatch box. In reality, it would be unfair to expect much more in the way of detail about Burnham's plans for the economy during his very first session of PMQs, but these are questions his government will eventually have to answer. And what is clear is that despite the promise of a more consensual style of politics, when it comes to the substance there are sharp ideological differences across the Commons. Burnham's diagnosis for the country's problems centres on privatisation and deindustrialisation over recent decades, as well as Brexit. Badenoch disagrees, pointing instead to high taxes and spending as constraints on economic growth. While Burnham's early weeks in office have seen a shift in style with a summer tour around the country and heavy social media presence, the economic arguments between him and his political opponents remain, and now Westminster is back in session there will likely be a clamour for more detail about his planned direction. Today's Prime Minister's Questions is a taste of what's to come. As well as smart communications, the choices the prime minister makes against a tricky economic background will take careful navigation if he's to deliver the optimistic future he's promised. title: Five takeaways from Burnham's Commons debut as PM
description: The prime minister's first appearance in Parliament comes more than six weeks after he entered No 10.
body: Andy Burnham has taken questions from MPs in the House of Commons for the first time since taking over as prime minister. The statement on his future plans for power comes six weeks after he took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July, just before Parliament's summer recess. Here are the main points from what he said. Burnham told MPs his time as mayor of Greater Manchester had given him a "clear theory of growth" that further devolution of power away from Westminster would help boost the UK's economic prospects. But he said he wanted to avoid a "two-tier England" - where areas that have already been given greater powers pull away from those that have not. He announced that work was under way with Cornwall council and its six MPs on a devolution deal, "with or without" an elected mayor, to help the rural economy. Burnham's move to grant the county greater powers, without requiring it to team up with councils in neighbouring areas, could open the door to more devolution for other single counties. Burnham also said he would meet leaders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to explore more local powers there. The statement was the first chance for Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to grill Burnham on defence spending following headlines on the issue over the summer. Chancellor John Healey was appointed by Burnham after quitting as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer, calling for the UK to spend 3% of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence by 2030. However, since entering the Treasury, Healey is yet to attach a date to this spending target, and has faced pressure to do so in recent days. Healey has said a target date for increasing spending to 3% of GDP will be set out at the next government spending review, expected in spring next year. But in a potential signal of his intentions in this area, Burham said the arguments Healey had made about defence spending in his former role were a key reason why he had put him in charge of the Treasury. Andy Burnham chaired his first Number 10 North meeting in July Burnham confirmed he would attend the COP31 climate summit in November, as he vowed to "meet the climate challenge". The annual UN climate change conference will take place in Antalya, Turkey, allowing Burnham to come face to face with many world leaders and senior officials. While Sir Keir attended COP summits when he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak was criticised in 2022 for not going because he had "other pressing domestic commitments". Burnham's pledge to attend the summit comes as he faces a looming decision about whether to allow drilling to start in the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield, in the North Sea, which have been in legal limbo for a year. Labour's 2024 election manifesto promised to "finally bring the feudal leasehold system to an end", after campaigners said it was unfair that flat owners had little control over spiralling property costs. A draft Leasehold and Commonhold Reform Bill published by Starmer's government earlier this year included plans to cap ground rent at £250, ban the sale of new leasehold flats and give homeowners greater control over how their buildings are managed. Under the bill, leasehold would be banned "except in limited cases", and developers would no longer be allowed to sell new flats as leasehold. That bill is yet to be introduced to Parliament, but Burnham confirmed he intended to "bring forward" a Commonhold and Leasehold Bill during the current session of Parliament, which began in May and would normally last around a year. Burnham kicked off his Commons statement by paying tribute to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, who had announced he was resigning as MP for Holborn and St Pancras just hours earlier. Sir Keir had given the UK "a lifetime of service", Burnham said, including delivering the Hillsborough Law which demands more accountability from public officials during official inquiries, as well as work to achieve peace in Ukraine. He also praised Sir Keir for leading Labour to one of its "best victories" in the 2024 election. He said Sir Keir had "created a platform to change this country for the better" which the new government would "use well". Burnham to tell MPs optimism at heart of his vision for UK Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost? title: Emergency measures needed to stop teachers quitting, say Lib Dems
description: A survey by the party suggested almost half of teachers reported considering quitting the classroom in the next five years.
body: The Lib Dems say schools are approaching an "existential crisis" in teacher retention Burnt out teachers urgently need better working hours and more support to stop them leaving the profession, the Liberal Democrats say, as the new term approaches. Nearly half of the teachers surveyed by the party in England said they were planning to quit the classroom in the next five years, with many saying they felt overworked and stressed. The Lib Dems are urging new Education Secretary Lucy Powell to fully fund teachers' pay, rather than raiding school budgets to cover increases, and to bring in limits on overtime. The Department for Education said last year saw the lowest rate of teachers leaving the profession since 2010 but acknowledged there was "more to do". The survey asked more than 900 teachers, headteachers and Special Educational Needs Coordinators (SENCOs) across England how long they planned to stay in teaching. Almost half of those in post said they were considering leaving teaching in the next five years, while one in ten were planning to spend less than a year in the job. More than three quarters of those surveyed, which included former teachers, said they had felt "frequently or constantly burnt out" while at work. Respondents cited high workloads on marking, lesson preparation and other tasks, which they said gave them less time in the classroom. The Liberal Democrats' schools spokesperson Caroline Voaden said this pointed to a government that is "not listening" to the profession. "We rely on teachers to educate our children, the least we can do is make sure they want to come back after the summer," she said. Teacher retention is a challenge successive governments have had to grapple with. The National Education Union (NEU) reported that 4 in 10 teachers were planning to quit over "huge workloads and excessive accountability" in 2019. This latest survey was also conducted with the help of the NEU, as well as the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL). "After over a decade of austerity and chronic underfunding in our schools the system is on its knees" said the NEU's general secretary Daniel Kebede. "The new academic year is the perfect time for Andy Burnham to signal a fresh start for our schools" he added. "That means fully funding the pay award and properly funding all our schools and colleges to stem the recruitment and retention crisis and give children the education they deserve." "As Lucy Powell enters her first term as education secretary the Liberal Democrats are calling for her first act to be to introduce an emergency package of 'back to school' measures to face this crisis head on," Voaden said. The Lib Dem proposals include the government fully funding teacher's pay, which will increase in England by 3.5% from September, with an additional 3% the year after. Currently, half of the pay increase will come from existing school budgets. The party is also calling for proper enforcement of teacher's legally mandated working hours, the introduction of reasonable limits on overtime, and for all schools to be required to introduce flexible working policies. The party did not identify where funding might come from to pay for the policies. An education department spokesperson said: "We know teachers do an incredible job and we're determined to make sure that dedication is matched with the right support. "Last year saw one of the lowest rates of teachers leaving the profession since 2010, and a record number of teachers returning to the classroom, but we know there's more to do. "We're taking action by announcing pay awards of almost 17% over two years, funding schools to improve maternity pay and offering targeted support to normalise flexible working and manageable workloads so that more teachers stay in our classrooms and thrive." title: Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?
description: The prime minister says he will keep hundreds more criminals behind bars but doing so requires complex changes.
body: This video can not be played Watch: PM confirms PC Harper's killers will remain in prison The prime minister's announcement that he will keep hundreds of criminals behind bars who would otherwise have been released early is one he has wanted to make for weeks. Andy Burnham had already expanded the list of people ineligible for early release and had consistently said he wanted to go further. What is not clear is exactly what has changed to allow him to do so. Earlier this month, the Ministry of Justice warned that exempting any more prisoners risked "prisons reaching capacity and collapsing". The prime minister himself previously said he had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do". In his exclusive interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham picked out the release of people on controversial indefinite sentences and the deportation of foreign criminals as measures that had made his latest intervention possible. It is understood extra capacity will also be created by immediately beginning work to create new cells in existing prisons. But none of these are short-term solutions. Ending indefinite sentences will require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up. Previous governments have struggled to quickly deport foreign offenders and there are not thought to be any new returns agreements with other countries. The case of grooming gang ringleader Shabir Ahmed, who Pakistan has resisted attempts to deport, is one example. Retrofitting prisons to create more cells is also expected to take months. People in government concede that in the short-term, Burnham will only be able to follow through on today's announcement by making prisons even more full. With the adult male prison estate already running at 98% capacity, it is a move that could worry some in the sector. But in the end, the prime minister believed he simply had to act. The extra exemptions Burnham has announced are being described within government as a "political decision". That is not surprising given the intense pressure that had built up, especially around the potential for PC Andrew Harper's killers to be released early. Burnham's inner circle are mindful that political misjudgements at the start of Sir Keir Starmer's premiership caused long-lasting damage. They believe Sir Keir never recovered from early rows over freebies and winter fuel payments, and point to a lack of major mishaps in Burnham's first six weeks in office as evidence of a more slick political operation. There was some surprise in Downing Street about how much media attention the issue of early release received over the summer. That is one reason why the prime minister's aides are relishing the new parliamentary term, when news stories come along at a faster rate and so are less likely to linger in the headlines. After the initial flip-flopping on whether the government would be able to exempt more prisoners, the mother of PC Harper told BBC Breakfast that the handling of the situation had been a "hash". Government officials working on the plans have spoken to the families of victims, who made it clear they did not want the new measures to be dripped out in leaks to the media. Instead it was decided one big announcement would be the neatest option. It had seemed likely that would come in the form of a parliamentary statement on Tuesday from the justice secretary. Instead, the prime minister decided to make the announcement himself in an interview with BBC Breakfast. It is understood Burnham was mindful of mounting speculation and wanted to give victims and the public as much certainty at the earliest possible opportunity. In doing so, he may have risked the ire of the Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle, who is generally disdainful of governments that make major announcements outside of Parliament. He may also have offered up ammunition to the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who has already accused Burnham of being a "people pleaser" who finds it difficult to say no to people. That characterisation is likely to be tested again when more stories inevitably appear about the victims of prisoners who will still be released early. It already started on Sunday morning, when the domestic abuse commissioner said she remained "deeply concerned about the number of abusers" still set to be freed. While this is not the first time Burnham has said he has pushed the system to the limit, Whitehall sources are now adamant there will be no more additional exemptions. title: Six ways parents could make the return to school a little easier
description: Parenting experts give their top tips on how to make sure back-to-school runs as smoothly as possible.
body: The BBC spoke to parents and experts to find out their back-to-school tips It's back-to-school time again - and families brace for the challenge of swapping summer lie-ins for school routines, easing first-day nerves and getting ready for the year ahead. While children in Scotland returned to school in mid-August, children in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will be returning in the coming week as September begins. We spoke to experts to find out their six key tips to make going back to school as stress-free as possible. Cerys Parker, a teacher and blogger, says one of the best ways to keep organised during school time is to keep a consistent morning routine. Her morning starts 30 minutes before her children wake up, for some alone time and a hot coffee. She then makes them the same breakfast every morning, which they eat together with no screens, then it's upstairs for showers and getting ready for school. Parker also keeps copies of her children's timetables so she knows what to prepare on specific days, such as when they have PE She grabs their lunch boxes and they leave the house at 07:30 for the bus, or 07:50 if Parker is dropping them at school on the way to her own job. The night before, she makes sure school bags are packed, shoes are ready, uniform is laid out and lunch is packed for the morning. "We have things in the same place, so the bags are always in the same location, the keys, and that makes the morning smoother. There's no panic about where everything's going to be." It is easy to forget non-uniform days, sports days or study sessions. Parker recommends having a family calendar pinned to your wall or your fridge - somewhere you can easily see it every day. "It's an academic year calendar with a space for each of us, and then an events section, so as soon as a notice comes in, I write it down." This could include things like meal plans, after-school activities or - depending on your child's age - exams. Parker's calendar from June, detailing exams, activities and meal plans for herself and her children It's worth reminding yourself of the school holiday dates, while Parker also notes down key days for her children's school year, such as: Children in Need, on Friday, 13 November World Book Day, on Thursday, 4 March 2027 Red Nose Day, on Friday, 19 March 2027 Earth Day, on Thursday, 22 April 2027 She also keeps a small purse of coins throughout the year in case her children need some change for non-uniform days or bake sales. After school, many children are tired and are not up for discussion about their day, so Will Shield, professor of child and educational psychology at the University of Exeter, suggests changing your approach to the conversation. "Ask some open questions, instead of interrogating them," he says. "Ask what made you smile today? Or who did you play with at lunchtime?" These sorts of questions are a lot easier to answer for a child, he says, instead of asking what they did. Martha Deiros Collado says children getting emotional at the school gates is perfectly normal Parker suggests similar questions, like: "What was the silliest thing that happened, or what made you laugh today?" For younger children, clinical psychologist Dr Martha Deiros Collado told CBeebies Parenting Download that pick-up time should not be a "sign of alarm". "See it as part of the process of separating and loving you, missing you, which is really important." Many families will have children attending school for the first time, which can be just as big a moment for parents as it is for new pupils. Shield says parents should "reassure themselves" about the routine they will need to follow on school mornings. "Visit the school, walk or drive past it, bring bedtimes back a bit earlier so it's not just a big start in the first week," he says. He also encourages parents to introduce their child into the concept of school, through things like: Going through the school website Trying on the new school uniform or PE kit Shield adds that you don't want to overwhelm your child with information about school, but get them to a point where it feels "familiar" Deiros Collado says school readiness is not about "numbers and letters". "It's about much more basic things, like feeling comfortable and safe to be in a classroom with other children," she says. Building independence can also help bridge the gap between home and school life, she says, by encouraging your child to do some things by themselves, such as zipping up their own coat. "It's just building that sense of, I'm ready to do this without you," she says. But Deiros Collado also stresses that your child should be able to ask for help when they need it. "One of the best skills you can give your little ones is being able to say to an adult, 'Help me,' because you want your kid to be able to say that to a teacher." She also suggests a "goodbye ritual" with your child to practise separation, such as blowing a kiss. Katharine Radice says that focusing too much on the homework outcome you want for your child can be "demotivating" for them Katharine Radice, teacher and author, recommends putting together a homework timetable. "Doing this puts boundaries around homework and makes it easier to ring-fence distraction-free time," she says. This could be different every week depending on different activities, but Radice stresses there should be a plan in advance so it's not left to the last minute. For supporting children with homework, Radice suggests approaching the task in a "positive and open way" and listening to what they might be finding difficult. She also recommends looking for opportunities to praise your child's effort in doing work to help them "stay motivated." title: We helped create UK emergency alert system - but question how government is using it
description: Millions across England and Wales received a wildfire alert on their phones earlier this month, but it partly backfired.
body: There are calls for ministers to launch a review of how emergency alerts are used As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming from his phone earlier this month. What took him by a surprise was the message on the screen. Like millions of people across England and Wales, the "severe alert" on 14 August warned him of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" and against doing anything that could start a fire, including lighting disposable barbecues. It was the biggest use of the system to date - but Dowden has now weighed in to question whether it was strictly necessary. Dowden and two officials who helped create the government's emergency alert system are calling for Labour ministers to be up front with the public on what it could be used for in future. "I was surprised at the decision to issue this nationwide alert and it raises some serious questions," Dowden, who served as deputy prime minister under Rishi Sunak, tells BBC News. "The government needs to clarify the criteria for its use and why this alert met those criteria." When he fronted the launch of the alert system in April 2023, he says it was intended for as narrow a geographic area as possible where the threat to life is imminent. The government's own webpage, external for emergency alerts says they are only sent for "life-threatening emergencies", listing wildfires, severe flooding and extreme storms. Two national tests of the system took place in 2023 and 2025, while 10 local alerts have been sent since its launch, all related to weather or flooding bar one in Plymouth for a World War Two bomb removal. The day before the alert was sent earlier this month, 19 homes burned down in the west Midlands town of Stourbridge after a wildfire. The day of the alert, ministers say they were asked directly by fire chiefs to send one as crews dealt with 43 wildfires and 11 major incidents across the country. Oliver Dowden oversaw the public campaign when the alert was launched in 2023 The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August. It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk, and confusion about alerts sent multiple times. Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales. "People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it." A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts. "Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds. The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries. "By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said. But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring. He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around. "Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'." His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?" Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life. "It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out. Frazer Rhodes was closely involved in building the emergency alert system He thinks ministers should accept there has been a divided response and launch a review to ask themselves: "How do we do this differently?" Rhodes, a service delivery specialist, adds: "The national protocol should be a public document… I think that document is almost like a contract with us to say 'this is when we're going to use it, these are the parameters, this is who can use it'." Back in 2021 when designing the alerts, he says these were the scenarios considered valid for future alerts: Severe weather and environmental alerts such as flood risk Major hazards such as the Buncefield oil depot fire in 2005 When building the UK alert system, which cost up to £25.3m in its first three years, officials looked to Australia, external and New Zealand, external where emergency alerts have no "opt out" option for the public, unlike in the UK. They also considered minor types of public safety alerts which are sent in the US for issues such as missing children. The alert targets individual cell towers with a radiowave-like signal, allowing all mobile phones in the area to pick it up without needing to know people's mobile numbers. This cell broadcast technology is used instead of SMS texts or an app. It comes as the Cabinet Office plans to launch a separate campaign in the autumn about how people can make themselves and their homes more prepared for extreme weather and cyber-attacks. title: One in eight young people still out of work or education ahead of major review
description: Just under one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training (Neet).
body: Just under one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - according to data published ahead of a major report about a "lost generation". The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 were Neet between April and June. That is about one in eight people in that age group. The final instalment of a major report by former minister Alan Milburn is expected to set out recommendations for tackling the problem in the coming weeks. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden told the BBC ministers would "take those [recommendations] forward". Want your job application to stand out? Employers say they look for these six skills Competition for degree apprenticeships quadruples as university costs rise The new data suggests the number of young people who are Neet has fallen compared to the first three months of the year, when it was over one million, or 13.5% of the total population of people aged 16 to 24. But it has risen by 3% compared to the same period last year, when it was 951,000 young people. The estimates are based on information from a sample of households. The ONS says looking at a smaller subset, like Neets, leads to more "variability" - which can explain small changes from quarter to quarter and means it is best to look at long-term, rather than short-term, changes. Asia Mason, 22, from London, says she spent more than two years applying for jobs before she finally secured her first role in the NHS. After leaving college with a health and social care qualification, Mason hoped to work in maternity. She applied for more than 30 jobs but was repeatedly told she lacked experience. "I remember thinking, 'How am I supposed to get experience if nobody is willing to give me the opportunity to gain it?'" she says. She ended up securing her first NHS role after completing a social care programme run by The King's Trust charity, which helped her gain experience and confidence. Asia eventually wants to be a midwife Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the UK labour market was "in a robust position" but there had been "a long-term challenge for young people". He said he was "looking forward" to recommendations on how to tackle the issue from Milburn. "We'll have proposals, legislation, if necessary, to take those forward," he said. McFadden spoke to the BBC during a visit to Boots in Nottingham, where young people had started jobs in a pilot of the government's Jobs Guarantee scheme. Over the next three years, it aims to support 90,000 young people who have been claiming Universal Credit and looking for work for 18 months. It funds 25 hours of paid work every week for half a year. What Skills Do You Need For The Jobs Market? According to ONS data, the latest figures suggest 981,000 people aged 16-24 were Neet between April and June McFadden said there were also plans for 300,000 more work experience placements and 50,000 more youth apprenticeship starts, adding that the government had already rolled out £3,000 hiring incentives for employers who take on young people who have been out of work for six months. But shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately criticised the government's policies, claiming Labour had "destroyed job opportunities for young people" through increased taxes, such as employer National Insurance contributions. For the Liberal Democrats, Munira Wilson said the sheer number of Neets represented a "generational betrayal", and said the government needed to make it "more attractive for businesses to take on apprentices, boosting the number of degree apprenticeships, and crucially, reversing Labour's damaging job tax". The rise in the number of Neets between April and June compared to the same time last year was largely an increase among men. An extra 25,000 men were estimated to be Neet, compared to another 4,000 young women. In May, the first part of Milburn's report, which was commissioned by the government, said the reasons for the rise in rates among men were "complex", but could be down to more health issues, the "erosion of traditional employment routes" and "a growing gap in educational outcomes". He also said the "Neet problem is grounded in social disadvantage" and highlighted higher rates among certain groups, including young people who: have grown up in poverty have special educational needs or disabilities (SEND) don't have a GCSE-level qualification are Black, African and Caribbean The report warned that one in six young people would be out of work in five years without action, adding: "We are at risk of a lost generation." It said young jobseekers were submitting dozens, sometimes hundreds of applications, but rejections had become the norm. Last week, analysis by the BBC found that competition for degree apprenticeships in England through the government's "find an apprenticeship" service, for example, had quadrupled over the past three years. The second, and final, instalment of Milburn's report - including recommendations for how to tackle the problems - is expected in the coming weeks. title: What does Neet stand for and why does the UK have so many?
description: Ministers want to tackle the high number of young people not in education, employment or training.
body: There were 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 not in employment, education or training between April and June, according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Figures published earlier in the year showed the number had previously topped one million, as an independent review warned of "a lost generation" of young people, unless urgent action is taken to support them. A young person is considered Neet if they are not in education, employment or training. To be considered Neet, a person must be aged 16 to 24 and: unemployed - looking for work economically inactive - not actively looking for work and not waiting to start a job, or caring for family not in formal education, such as school or university, or on a vocational course not participating in any training schemes, such as apprenticeships or internships Want your job application to stand out? Employers say they look for these six skills Opportunities shrinking for too many young people, says major report on 'lost generation' There were 981,000 Neets between April and June, the ONS says, an increase of about 3% on the same period in 2025. The numbers are published every three months and vary throughout the year, but have been steadily increasing over time. The latest figures account for 13% - over one in eight - of all young people in the UK. There were more Neets classed as not looking or available for work than there were hunting for jobs. The number of economically inactive young people was 588,000. This group includes 310,000 women and 278,000 men. The ONS estimates that 393,000 16- to 24-year-olds were unemployed and looking for work. There were more unemployed young men than young women - 252,000 men compared with 141,000 women. An estimated one in 10 young people who are Neet are graduates. However, those who have not achieved GCSE-level qualification are more likely to remain Neet for longer periods, according to the Youth Futures Foundation, an organisation which aims to ensure young people can find work. It said those living in poverty, or with special educational needs, are also more likely to be Neet. The ONS releases figures on the number of Neets in the UK every three months. It produces its estimates from its Labour Force Survey. Fewer people have responded to the survey in recent years, which makes the results more volatile than in the past. The number of Neets tends to fluctuate throughout the year. What needs to change to get more people working? Five tips to help you get your first job Tens of thousands of jobs have been lost from the hospitality sector, which tends to employ a significant proportion of young people A major independent review of the reasons so many young people are not in education, work or training was released by former Health Secretary Alan Milburn in May. He was asked to look into the issue by the government. Milburn challenged the idea that young people were not trying, or were "work-shy, snowflakes, soft". A survey carried out for his interim report suggested that 84% of Neet young people do want a job or training. He said rejections for young jobseekers, after submitting dozens, sometimes hundreds of applications, had become the norm. The report said there is not one factor causing the crisis, with a "perfect storm" of the jobs market, spending on education and the Covid pandemic being some of the reasons highlighted. It said the number of entry-level jobs has fallen by about 1.6 million over the past 20 years. Vacancies in hospitality, for example, have halved in the last four years alone. Apprenticeships and graduate jobs have also been affected. Health issues are also a factor. The proportion of people who say they are Neet because of a work-limiting health condition has increased by 70% over the past decade, according to the Health Foundation charity. The number of those citing a mental health condition has almost doubled to more than four in 10, according to the Youth Futures Foundation. Milburn described the situation for young people with disabilities as "devastating". In 2024-2025, 29.6% of disabled young people were Neet, compared with 8.7% of their non-disabled peers, his report said. The second part of Milburn's report, containing recommendations, will be unveiled later in 2026. What is an apprenticeship and how much is the pay? Is university right for me? 'I applied for 647 jobs after uni until I got one' Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited a train maunfacturing site in Derby as he set out his plans for technical education Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden welcomed Milburn's report and said the government was already taking action. He said the government's job guarantee was supporting those "most in need", with the first young people who were supported by the scheme now in work. "Our wider £2.5bn investment will help create almost a million opportunities to earn or learn," he said, adding that further reforms would follow the full Milburn review. The government also announced a bursary of up to £4,500 for some families who would lose out on money if their children wanted to do an apprenticeship, because the child benefit they would lose out on would be worth more than the apprenticeship starter salary. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also promoted a new work experience scheme by Sainsbury's, with 10,000 places being rolled out from October 2026. However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately criticised the government's policies, claiming Labour had "destroyed job opportunities for young people" through increased taxes, such as employer National Insurance contributions. Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said her party "repeatedly warned that Labour's jobs tax would hammer job opportunities for young people and that their business rates hikes would kill off high street job opportunities". title: Off to Reading or Leeds? Here's your guide to festival make-up (without the toxins)
description: Neon is on trend, but some make-up products pose a serious risk to your health. Here's what to check for, and how to dazzle.
body: Off to Reading or Leeds? Here's your guide to festival make-up (without the toxins) Festival season is here - with Reading and Leeds taking place this weekend. So now's the time to perfect neon make-up. Bright graphic eyeliner, vampy lips and holographic highlighter are some of this year's biggest beauty trends for the main stage. But some of these make-up products, which are being sold by third-party sellers on online marketplaces such as TikTok Shop, can contain a host of toxic chemicals, warns the Chartered Trading Standards Institute, external. So here's what to look out for – and how to stay safe while serving festival glam. Use a white eye pencil on the skin first How to get the look: Dominic Skinner, make-up artist and judge on the hit BBC show Glow Up, came into the BBC's London offices to show us how to achieve the perfect festival look and make it dance and party-proof. If you want colours to "pop", he says use a white eye pencil on the skin first and then press bright eyeshadows on top. "It will make bold colours more intense, and last all night." This video can not be played How to get a festival look that isn't toxic What to be aware of: Banned ingredients can cause bad rashes and allergic reactions, so check the label and avoid products that say they're "not for cosmetic use" - even if they say they're for the skin. Also look out for banned colourants, like Solvent Yellow 172, CI 45161 (Basic Red 1:1) and CI 45174 (Basic Violet 11:1). Embrace the fun of festival make-up - the stuff you might not get away with wearing at your 9-to-5, says Skinner Be cautious of cheap products or sellers you've never heard of, says Skinner. "There are some items that are UV reflective, glow-in-the-dark or neon that are made by cosmetics brands but are quietly labelled as a 'non-cosmetic paint'," he adds. Skinner suggests using gems as they're bigger and more impactful How to get the look: Fairycore-inspired make-up is in, which means sparkles, face gems and glitter. Don't go for subtle, says Skinner. "The 'no make-up look' is gone. Clean girl is out!" There's a child-like quality to festival make-up, he says, so embrace it - think playful colour and crystals. To stand out, he suggests using glitter in hair partings or your shoulders. "Personally, I say use gems as they're bigger and more impactful, plus you can peel them off at the end of night and reuse them in the morning." What to be aware of: Skip near the eyes to avoid nasty scratches on your cornea, says the British Skin Foundation's Dr Emma Wedgeworth, and never use craft glitter. Use biodegradable, eco-friendly products that are better for the environment and softer on the skin. Safe adhesives, like lash glue, will keep it in place. Break away from summer-friendly pinks and peaches How to get the look: Vogue says 2026 is all about juicy and blurred lips, external that play with texture more than colour. Think "your-lips-but-better", using stains and glosses. InStyle magazine recommends dramatic, dark red vampy lips, external as a breakaway from summer-friendly pinks and peaches. Use a liquid lip product, Skinner says, because it won't budge. "You can do some drinking, you can do some snogging." And he says leave that lip liner until last - it'll just "highlight how wonky your drawing skills are". Colour first, liner later. What to be aware of: Whatever your look, don't share your balm or lipstick. That can spread nasty infections like cold sores. Cross-contamination is real, and why make-up artists sanitise everything in between clients. Before and after application is crucial - sunburn is not on trend Use high-protection sunscreen - at least SPF 30 - as a base before the make-up and let it soak in like any primer, says Wedgeworth. Skinner recommends matte or sweat-proof SPF to help your make-up last longer. Reapply throughout the day, at least every two hours. Don't forget your hairline and any partings to protect your scalp. Sprays let you layer over make-up, but can be difficult to apply thickly enough, so take shade breaks and bring a big hat for extra protection, says Wedgeworth. Dance and sweat-proof hair styles - sorted How to get the look: Who, What, Wear, external says think about accessories - scarfs, crochet beanie caps or eye-catching hair clips, charms or cuffs. InStyle, external suggests Mermaid waves or thin Baby Braids if your hair is long enough. What to be aware of: If you want a colour change with a spray or dye, do a patch test first to check you are not allergic. Put a small amount behind your ear or on your arm and wait 24 to 48 hours to check for a reaction, says Wedgeworth. Skinner says you probably already own products that can give you a festival look. "You just have to think creatively about how to play with it." Copyright © 2026 BBC. The BBC is not responsible for the content of external sites. Read about our approach to external linking.

title: More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs
description: Students like Jessica say they worry about missing out on student life, but feel they have no choice but to stay at home.
body: Friends Amelia (left) and Beatrice (right) are living at home when they start university this September More new students are choosing to live at home for university this year than in the last nine years, new data shows. Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application that they intended to live at home this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - just over one in three students in that category. In 2017, it was closer to one in five. The figures vary across the UK - with 48% of applicants in Scotland intending to live at home, compared with 20% in Wales - but the trend is rising across the board. Students told the BBC the rising cost of living was a major influence in deciding what to do after school or college. For friends Beatrice and Amelia, who are from St Helens, Merseyside, the cost of accommodation was a big factor in their decision to live at home while studying. Both are heading to university in September, but neither will be moving into student accommodation. Beatrice is going to the University of Manchester to study maths and plans to commute by train, a journey which can take about 50 minutes in total. "My first choice was Manchester and then my second was Liverpool, so I knew I could commute," she says, adding that the price of accommodation would have been "a few grand a year". Amelia, who is going to study at Liverpool John Moores University - approximately 20 minutes away by train - says the accommodation she found was between £300 and £400 a week. Although neither is looking forward to the commute, both are still hoping they can get the full experience of university while living at home. My three-hour university commute is worth the £7,000 saving on halls However, fellow student Jessica, who is also going to study at Liverpool John Moores University, feels she will miss out. She says she would have loved to live on campus and enjoy student life, but the price of renting is "ridiculous" and "insane". "I have a part-time job as everything is so expensive, and then commuting is going to kill a lot of my free time as well," she says. "It is a bit sad really when you think about it." But she is pleased that staying at home means she will still be able to have her mum and dad's cooked dinners. Earlier this year, BBC News followed the daily journey of one first-year student who said she was saving over £7,000 on accommodation by commuting 90 minutes into Manchester each day from home. The figures were recorded on results day and are expected to rise over the coming month as more students accept university places through clearing. A record number of UK 18-year-olds have been accepted into university this year. But student rents have risen sharply in recent years, alongside other living costs. The Higher Education Policy Institute (Hepi) said last year that students needed £61,000 over the course of a three-year degree in order to have a "minimum socially acceptable standard of living" - and that's excluding tuition fees. Its report found that in 2024 the cost of renting in university-owned accommodation ranged from £108 per week, for 40 to 44-week contracts in Northern Ireland, to £338 a week for the shortest contracts in London, where rent makes up nearly half (46%) of students' costs. In most areas it was between £140 and £180 a week, with private halls usually being more expensive. Many students are eligible for a maintenance loan, which can help with the cost of accommodation, but the average annual price of a room on campus is increasing much faster, according to some student unions. Hepi says most young full-time students now work in paid employment during term time to make up the difference between their maintenance loan income and the cost of living. For some students, it means a rethink about what university looks like. The Open University, which offers distance learning and online courses, says more teenagers than ever are starting courses with it. Almost 3,400 18-and 19-year-olds joined the university last year – making up 9.5% of new starters, compared with 5.7% six years ago. Traditionally, it has been popular with mature students wanting to continue working while studying from home. Its vice-chancellor, Prof Dave Phoenix, says it points to a shift in how younger people are thinking about university, adding that studying online "means they can avoid moving costs and high accommodation bills and, for others, it means keeping a job". But a recent report, external by Prof William Whyte, from the University of Oxford, argues that the value of on-campus life extends far beyond the price of accommodation, and plays an important role in personal development and the wider university experience. "The question isn't simply where students live. It's what they gain from living and learning together as part of a university community," he says. "Currently, we have no real policy on accommodation for the overwhelming majority of students who want to leave home for study. It's time for a serious debate about the role accommodation plays in the university – and how we will pay for it." A spokesperson for the Department for Education says the government recognises that too many students are facing financial hardship. They say they are increasing maximum maintenance loans and reintroducing maintenance grants to help with living costs, as well as working with universities and councils to improve access to student housing. title: 'Relentless' GCSE resit cycle 'simply not working', school and college leaders say
description: Pass rates for maths and English resits remain significantly lower than students taking them for the first time.
body: The "relentless" cycle of pupils in England failing and then resitting their GCSEs in maths and English is "simply not working", a leading education union has said. The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) said a "significant proportion" of students fall short of passing those subjects, and that most who retake those exams "face the miserable experience of falling short once again". Thursday's results data showed nearly one in four maths and English GCSEs in England were taken by students aged 17 and older, mostly young people resitting exams they had previously failed. The government said it wanted to stop the "endless treadmill of unnecessary resits". It said it would introduce a new "stepping stone" qualification from 2028 at Level 1 - one level below GCSEs - for students who do not achieve a pass in GCSE maths or English. Currently, many courses and jobs remain dependent on students securing GCSE passes in those subjects. But those that miss the grade can find themselves in a continuing loop of resits as they try and try again to pass. Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of ASCL, said the fail-resit cycle was like "force feeding" students a "relentless diet of GCSE English and maths". "This limits their education and career options and is very likely to be a factor in the large number of young people who end up not in employment, education or training," he said. Pass rates for students aged 17 and older in English and maths are much lower than 16-year-old students taking the exams for the first time, bringing down overall GCSE grades for all ages across England, Wales and Northern Ireland as a result. While resitting is not a requirement, according to the Department for Education (DfE), colleges will generally enter students into exams when they think they are ready. For Marianne, from Cambridgeshire, results day has been a "mixed bag" as both of her sons collected GCSE results. While her younger son achieved a grade 8 in maths, his older brother, Tobias, did not get the pass he wanted after sitting the exam for a fifth time. Despite picking up good A-level results last week, Tobias is stuck in a GCSE resit loop with maths "He was very upset," Marianne said. "He turns up for his lessons, he puts great effort in, there's just something about maths he doesn't get. What do we do now?" Last week Tobias, collected A-level results in which he achieved a B in history and two Cs in politics and criminology - but his ambitions to apply to university to become a history teacher are on ice without that pass in maths. "It's horrendous making him keep doing it. I don't think it's fair, the pressure on them to keep resitting it," mum Marriane said. The new stepping stone qualification would offer an alternative route for students like Tobias to keep moving forward. Although the details are scant, the DfE said a student could be directed to it once they had sat maths and English GCSE but did not achieve a pass. It said it would "give students the essential knowledge and skills" before they resit their GCSEs, and then "only be entered into exams when they are ready". It is hoped it would provide a solution for students like Abdi, 17, from east London, who failed to pass his exams in maths and English for the third time. "I have to get my retakes right next time, or they won't let me complete my course at college," he said. "My school has provided extra classes to help prepare for the exams, but you have to be self-disciplined because juggling resits and college is not easy." Abdi plans to resit his maths and english GCSEs in November after learning he did not pass them for the third time Catherine Sezen, from the Association of Colleges, said the stepping stone qualification sounded positive, but that it should become an option for students long before they fail their GCSEs. "We have to look at what happens probably from reception right the way through, because young people who don't achieve very well in their SATs at 11 are really unlikely to achieve a grade 4 at 16." She said this year's resit figures were "disappointing and slightly demoralising for everybody" but not a "huge surprise". "I think we're still also seeing the legacy of the pandemic," she said. "These young people would have been in Years 6, 7 and 8, and so possibly haven't necessarily got the basic foundations in these subjects which are really fundamental." Unexpected GCSE results? This interactive guide runs through your options Five key takeaways from GCSE results day 2026 But the resit cycle is not always an inevitable one. Amandeep, 17, did not pass her maths or English language GCSEs this time last year. But on results day on Thursday, the student at Sandwell College, in the West Midlands, found out she had passed with a grade 5. "I teared up, I thought my patience had paid off," she said. "It happened for a reason, it was meant for me this year." Amandeep's results mean she is now able to move on to study a T-level in health and social care. Amandeep was one of the resit students who managaged to get the grades she needed for her next step in life While the majority of resit students are aged 17 to 19, some are also mature students. Wynne Hindle, 52, a grandmother from Sudbury, in Suffolk, celebrated having passed her GCSE maths on Thursday after taking it for a fifth time and achieving a grade 4. "I was very happy and shocked to pass," she said. "I just wanted to achieve something and I'm a resilient person." Hindle, who previously worked as a nanny and nursery nurse, now hopes to work in a school and said it was all "part of a journey". She said her message to others who might be stuck in the resit cycle is: "Keep at it". Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? Share your experiences. title: Meet the men applying for the 'hardest job in British politics'
description: Labour MSPs Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are making their pitches as they aim to succeed Anas Sarwar.
body: Michael Marra and Joe Fagan are squaring off in the Scottish Labour leadership contest Wanted: one leader for Scottish Labour. Must enjoy long hours, complex trade-offs and difficult questions. That may not be the official job description for Scottish Labour leader, but it's perhaps not far from the truth. After all, Anas Sarwar described this gig as "the hardest job in British politics". Despite this health warning, two candidates are on the ballot paper vying to take on the challenge - Michael Marra and Joe Fagan. I sat down with both of them for the Scotcast podcast to learn a bit about who they are, where they think Labour has gone wrong, and their prescription for fixing things. Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions Lennon criticises 'nasty' Scottish Labour as leadership bid fails But before we got into the nitty gritty of politics, I wanted to know a bit more about these two candidates. We started with an ice-breaker: If they had to give a Ted Talk (an online lecture about a topic they're passionate about), what would their subject be? For Michael Marra, it was his beloved football team, Dundee United. Given they've just endured back-to-back 4-0 defeats, there's a joke here about the North East Labour MSP backing lost causes. Joe Fagan opted for a lecture on Cold War Berlin. And there was even a comparison about the "eerie resemblance" between Stasi HQ in East Germany and the office he occupied when he was the leader of South Lanarkshire Council. This video can not be played Labour leadership: Marra says party must work for Scotland But we weren't here to talk about DUFC's glory days or the fall of the wall. This was a conversation about everything that's been going on with Scottish Labour. The most newsworthy reflection probably came from Fagan, the South of Scotland MSP, who was critical of Sarwar's decision to leave Holyrood and take a place in the House of Lords. He wished Sarwar well on a personal level, but said it "wasn't a good look" for him to stop being a Glasgow MSP and head to Westminster's upper chamber. Fagan said that he would never personally take a seat in the Lords. And not just because he thinks the robes look "ridiculous". But he did concede that it would be difficult to turn down the offer of a ministerial post from the prime minister. Anas Sarwar accepted a peerage after stepping down as Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra also had some criticisms of Anas Sarwar's approach as leader. He praised his work ethic and communication abilities, but said that the party had been too focused on Sarwar in the last five years. Privately other party figures have said that same – that the party's style was too "presidential" in recent years, rather than showcasing a team of spokespeople. Marra told me the party had "lost definition as to who the Labour Party is" and had become "too narrow in our leadership and the circle of influence around the leader". A big question hanging over these interviews was what will the approach of these candidates be to independence? While Scottish Labour isn't going to support that sort of constitutional change any time soon (or perhaps ever), there are voices inside the party who argue it's time to engage with the debate around the grounds for a second referendum. But both Michael Marra and Joe Fagan don't have much time for this argument. Fagan said it would be "obvious" when the will of the Scottish people had changed, but we weren't at that point. He insisted that debates around the process for independence was a relic of the "Sturgeon era", and that that period was now "history". Marra told me he wasn't clear how a trigger for a second referendum would work, arguing that people are more concerned with issues like the cost of living and the NHS. This video can not be played Labour leadership: Fagan says indyref calls and Sturgeon era 'over' This leadership contest has – somewhat unexpectedly – focussed on the issue of gender in recent days. When Glasgow MSP Monica Lennon failed to make the ballot, she released an explosive statement suggesting the other two had been "punching down on trans people". Both Marra and Fagan have rejected that accusation. But they both have strong views on the issue of gender reform. Remember, MSPs passed a bill in 2022 that would have made it easier for someone to change their legally recognised sex – so-called "self-ID". It was ultimately blocked by the UK government, a decision upheld in the courts. Labour MSPs at the time were whipped to support it. Some gave up their spokesperson positions in order to vote against. Marra came to a deal with Sarwar – he was allowed to abstain. But he told Scotcast he felt so strongly about the issue that he would've been willing to resign over it. Monica Lennon did not secure the nominations required to make the leadership ballot Fagan wasn't in Holyrood at the time, but his view watching from outside was that Labour MSPs shouldn't have backed it. When it came to the economic side of Scottish politics, both candidates expressed the view that some Scots – especially middle earners – are paying too much tax. But that doesn't necessarily mean cuts across the board. Fagan argued that there's a case for "widening" the tax base through some new approaches, such as environmental taxes. And Marra – whose professional background is in economics – said that he was willing to consider looking at a wealth tax. And when it comes to oil and gas both wannabee leaders think the UK government should go ahead with extracting at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields. title: Students get their GCSE and BTec grades as app launches for 750 schools in England
description: Some pupils in England will be able to see their grades on their phones from 11:00 BST on Thursday.
body: Pupils in England, Wales and Northern Ireland have received their GCSE, BTecs and other Level 2 results. Schools and colleges have been distributing grades in person, while pupils at more than 750 schools in England will also be able to see their grades on an app on their phones, which has been rolled out nationally for the first time. Results this year come as the government in England plans to boost technical education and address a growing number of English and maths GCSE resits. The overall GCSE pass rate has remained stable - with 67.3% of all grades across England, Wales and Northern Ireland at 4/C and above, down very slightly from 67.4% last year. Students across England, Wales and Northern Ireland receive their GCSE and BTec results The pass rate for National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher exams in Scotland rose across the board at the start of the month. And top A-level results increased slightly again last week – with 28.5% of all grades across England, Wales and Northern Ireland marked at A* or A. Students have also received results for BTec Tech Awards, BTec Firsts and BTec Level 2 Technical courses on Thursday, as well as for Cambridge Nationals. Last year, more than 360,000 results for vocational and technical qualifications were given out. Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants to make more technical subjects available to teenagers, and has announced plans for schools and colleges in England to offer subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning from Year 10. Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Thursday morning, Education Secretary Lucy Powell said that for too many pupils GCSEs had been "a barrier" rather than a "gateway". She said the government would bring in a new foundation qualification to help bring down the number of pupils resitting GCSE English and maths each year. This year, pupils at more than 750 secondary schools in England are able to see their results on their phones. The Department for Education (DfE) said pupils would still go into school to get their results in envelopes first, but that they would also be able to access their results through the Education Record app from 11:00 BST. A record of their results will stay in the app for colleges and future employers to review, in a move the government hopes will reduce paperwork for students and teachers. In England, pupils who do not get at least a grade 4 in GCSE English and maths must continue studying for it alongside their next course, whether this is A-levels, a T-level, or something else. Resitting is not a requirement, according to the DfE, but colleges will generally enter students into exams when they think they are ready. GCSE English and maths resits take place in November and May or June. This year, nearly a quarter of maths and English GCSEs in England were taken by people aged 17 and older this year, making up 24.3% of grades – up from 23.4% last year. A government-commissioned report in May cited research suggesting that half of 18 to 25-year-olds in England without level 2 qualifications - including GCSEs at grade 4/C and above - have spent time not in employment, education or training. Skills minister Baroness Jacqui Smith said in October that the DfE planned to introduce a new qualification as a "stepping stone" to GCSE resits, helping students who "too often have been on this demoralising roundabout of taking exams and failing them". How do the 9-1 GCSE grade boundaries work in England Schools to offer technical subjects to pupils from age 14 in England, Burnham says Are girls being left behind in school? Experts are sounding the alarm Data shows that girls are more likely than boys to pass GCSEs, but this year the gap between them was the lowest on record - with girls' pass rates dropping and boys' pass rates rising very slightly. The gap between the highest- and lowest-performing regions in England has widened, with London having the highest pass rate and the West Midlands the lowest. Disparities in GCSE results are often framed through the lens of a North-South divide, but there are also challenges facing children in coastal and rural parts of England. For example, in South West England, 40% of children eligible for free school meals obtained a grade 4 in maths and English at GCSE compared with 56% of the same cohort in London. This is the third year that grading has returned to pre-pandemic standards across all three nations. The proportion of GCSE passes rose in 2020 and 2021 when exams were cancelled and results were based on teachers' assessments. That was followed by a phased effort to bring them back down to 2019 levels. Are you happy with your exam results? Have you decided what to do next? Do you have any questions?
